pages.title: Build an App
pages.description: How an agent writes a Page, saves it as an App and gives it named actions on a Connection, a Data Store or a Workflow, and how the App's code calls them.
pages.body:
This page is the technical guide an agent follows. [Apps for people](/automate/apps/) says what a person clicks. An App is a Page that is kept. An agent writes the Page's files in its execution workspace, saves the folder with `page.save` and shows it beside the conversation. When the person asks to keep it, `page.save_as_app` makes it an App with a draft. A person publishes the draft; an agent never publishes. A quick Page may show data the agent wrote into it. Live data comes through named actions: one file per action in the folder `actions/`, which the build compiles into the manifest. The browser calls an action by its name and nothing else: it never calls a Connection, a Data Store or a Workflow directly, and it never holds a key. ## The folder ```text / app.yaml the manifest index.html a plain HTML App: its entry src/routes/__root.tsx a React App: TanStack Router file routes src/routes/index.tsx src/components/*.tsx optional actions/.action.yaml a call of a Connection's operation, or the start of a Workflow actions/.sql a statement on the App's Data Store assets/ images and other static files ``` Write the files with the workspace file tools, then save the folder with `page.save`, giving the Page a name and the folder that holds `app.yaml`. A save builds the Page. It answers the revision, or the build errors with file and line: fix the files and save again. After `page.save_as_app`, each later `page.save` of the same Page name writes the App's next draft, so keep working in the same folder. A React App imports only its own files, `react`, `react-dom`, `@tanstack/react-router` and `@work-shape/catalyst-app-kit`. Nothing is installed. A plain HTML App names `entry: index.html`; inline scripts work, inline event handler attributes such as `onclick` do not. ## The manifest `app.yaml` names everything the App reaches. A Connection or a Data Store that the manifest does not list cannot be called. | Key | What it holds | | --- | --- | | `id` | Lowercase letters, digits and `-`, at most 63 characters. | | `name` | The name people read. | | `description`, `icon` | Optional. | | `kit` | The exact kit version. Use `1.4.0` for a new App; actions on a Connection need `1.1.0` or later and `workflow` actions `1.3.0` or later. | | `entry` | `index.html` for a plain HTML App. A React App leaves it out. | | `connections` | The Connections the App's actions call, by name. | | `dataStores` | The Data Store the App's `sql` actions use: `{ name, minSchema }`. One at most while the App has `sql` actions. | | `actions` | One line per `sql` action: `{ name, file, effect }`. Optional for the other kinds. | | `externalHosts` | Internet hosts the browser code may fetch from, such as `api.example.com`. | Any other key is refused. `pages` is derived from `src/routes/` and is not written by hand. ## Named actions An action's name is the name of its file without the ending: `actions/load-bookings.action.yaml` is the action `load-bookings`. A name has lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `_`. | Kind | File | Reaches | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `connection` | `actions/.action.yaml` with `connection`, `operation`, `effect` | One operation of a Connection the manifest lists | Written in the file | | `sql` | `actions/.sql` plus a line under `actions` in `app.yaml` | The Data Store the manifest lists | Written in the manifest line | | `workflow` | `actions/.action.yaml` with `workflow` | A run of the published Workflow | Always `changing` | Every call runs as the person who looks at the App, through the platform's policy and audit. In the published App the viewer needs the right to use the App; in its draft, the right to write it. Beside that, for a `connection` action the viewer needs the right to use the Connection, for a `workflow` action the right to use the Workflow. An `sql` action of a published App needs no right on the Data Store: the person who published the App answered for it. Server code of an App's own, beyond these three kinds, is planned and not available. ### A `connection` action ```yaml connection: exampledata operation: list_bookings effect: reading description: The bookings of one client in one month. input: schema: type: object properties: client: { type: string, maxLength: 40 } month: { type: string, description: "The month as YYYY-MM" } required: [client] mapping: clientId: "{{client}}" period: "{{month}}" ``` - `connection` is the Connection's name, which `connections` in `app.yaml` lists. - `operation` is the name of one operation of that Connection, exactly as the Connection lists it. For an MCP Connection that is the name of the server's tool. Only an operation an editor accepted on the Connection's page, enabled and offered to Apps (exposure `bridge`), can be called. `platform.assets.operations` with `for: app` lists the operations an App may call, as far as the person may use them, each named `connection..` with its effect: write the two parts as `connection` and `operation`. `platform.assets.get` on the Connection shows all its accepted operations with name, effect and exposure, where the person may read the Connection. Without these tools, ask the person for the operation's name. - `effect` is `reading` or `changing`, as the operation was accepted. A `reading` action that stands for a changing operation is refused. - `input.schema` declares the parameters the browser passes: JSON Schema with `type: object` and `properties` of type `string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean` or `array` of one of them. A parameter not declared is refused at the call. - `input.mapping` is the operation's input. A value `"{{name}}"` stands for the parameter `name`; every other value is passed as written. A mapping computes nothing: a text that holds `{{` other than as the whole value is refused by the build. A parameter the caller leaves out leaves out its key. The answer's `result` is the MCP tool's result: `{ content, structuredContent }`, where `content` is a list of blocks such as `{ type: "text", text }` and `structuredContent` is there when the tool gives one. A tool that answers an error rejects the call. ### An `sql` action The statement is one file. Its first lines declare the parameters, and the statement names each as `$name`: ```sql -- @param client text optional select id, client_id, title, created_at from findings where $client is null or client_id = $client order by created_at desc limit 100 ``` The manifest says what the statement does, with one line for it: ```yaml actions: - { name: list-findings, file: actions/list-findings.sql, effect: reading } ``` - A parameter line is `-- @param `, with `optional` after it where a call may leave it out. A type is `text`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean`, `date` or `timestamp`, or one of them followed by `[]` for a list. - A `reading` statement is one `SELECT` or `WITH`. - A `changing` statement is one `INSERT` of one row whose values are all parameters, with `on conflict do nothing` after it where an existing row is skipped. An `UPDATE` or a `DELETE` is not available yet. - A value is bound to its place in the statement and never written into it. A reading statement answers `{ columns, rows, truncated }`: `rows` is a list of objects by column name, at most 1,000 rows and 2 MiB, and `truncated` says the result was cut; page with `limit` and `offset` parameters. A `numeric` value comes as text. An insert answers `{ table, inserted, skipped }`. ### The Data Store The App lists its Data Store under `dataStores` in `app.yaml`, by name, with `minSchema` where it needs at least that migration of the store. The `dataStores` module has to be on. The agent cannot create a Data Store or its tables: a person creates it with its migrations (`store.yaml` and `migrations/0001_.sql`, written with `catalyst data-store put` and published), and the statements read and write the tables those migrations made. Ask the person which Data Store to use, or to create one. An `sql` action runs only in an App: in a Page a reading `sql` action is refused with `data_store_needs_app`, and a changing one with `draft_safe_mode`. In the App's draft it runs with the viewer's own right on the store: to read it, and for an insert, which the draft simulates, to insert. ### A `workflow` action ```yaml workflow: monthly-check description: Checks the bookings of one client. input: schema: type: object properties: client: { type: string } required: [client] mapping: client: "{{client}}" ``` `workflow` is the Workflow's name. The mapping makes the input the Workflow declares. The call starts a run of the Workflow's published revision as the viewer, who needs the right to use that Workflow. The answer's `result` is the Workflow Run; follow it with `useWorkflowRun(result.id)` from the kit, or `workflowRuns.get(result.id)` in a plain HTML App. A `workflow` action has no `effect` key and no `connection`; it needs kit `1.3.0` or later. ## Effects, drafts and publishing A `reading` action runs live everywhere, with the viewer's rights. A `changing` action is carried out only in the published App; before that it runs in safe mode: - In the draft of an App, a `changing` action of each kind is simulated. It changes nothing and answers `{ status: "dry_run", message, result }`: `message` says what the call would have done, and whether live it would wait for another person's approval; `result` is the input it would have done it with. The call goes through the viewer's rights and the policy as a live call would, so a call that would be refused live is refused here too, and it leaves an Operation Run with the target `dry_run`. Show `message` as it is. - "Run live once" on the App's Actions list, under "Technical details" on the draft page, carries out the next call of one changing action of the draft for real. A person who may write the App switches it on for themselves; it covers only their own next call of that action, and every save or discard of the draft clears a switch nobody used, so a `page.save` clears it too. A call it sends live that the policy holds for another person's approval is refused with `approval_unavailable`, since a draft cannot wait. An agent cannot switch it on: when the person wants to try a change for real, tell them where the switch is. - In a Page that is not yet an App, a changing `connection` or `sql` action is refused with the code `draft_safe_mode`, and nothing is called. A `workflow` action answers `{ status: "dry_run", message, result }` as in a draft, but leaves no run. A changing call passes `{ idempotencyKey }` in the draft as in the published App. The published App carries out every action. An action may ask for a stricter `policy` than the instance sets (`confirm`, `approval` or `deny`), written in the action file or, for an `sql` action, in its manifest line. A call that waits for another person's approval answers `status: "pending_approval"` without a result. An agent never publishes. Tell the person to publish the draft: with the Publish button on the App's page, or with `catalyst app publish --revision --workspace `. Publishing needs the right `app.publish`, which administrators hold. It checks again what a save checked, and that each Data Store is published, at `minSchema` or later, readable (for an insert, `data_store.insert`) by the person who publishes, and of the App's workspace; a retired store, or one of another workspace, is refused. Guardrails may answer the publish too. Saving checks what it can: when a save writes the App's draft, it refuses a Connection that does not exist, a Data Store that does not exist, an operation the Connection does not accept and a `reading` action on a changing operation. `page.save` then answers the Page as saved and, under `app`, `saved: false` with what was found: fix it and save again. Whether the operation is enabled and offered to Apps (exposure `bridge`) is checked only at the call, which is refused as forbidden: check the operation's exposure on the Connection's page first. ## Calling an action from the App Import `actions` from `@work-shape/catalyst-app-kit`. `actions.call(name, params, options)` calls a named action and answers `{ runId, status, result }`. `result` is what the action answered, as described for each kind above: check its shape before using it. A call that is refused or fails rejects with an `AppCallError`. Show its `message` as it is, since it is the platform's sentence in the viewer's language, and offer no button to try again when `retryable` is false. A changing call passes `{ idempotencyKey }`: make the key when the person acts, and send the same key again when the answer was lost. In a draft the answer to a changing call is `{ status: "dry_run", message, result }` unless "Run live once" sent it live: show `message`, which says what the published App would have done. `getContext()` answers the viewer, the locale and, under `can`, what the instance says for each action: `allow`, `confirm`, `approval` or `deny`. The server asks again at every call. ## A complete example A dashboard of one ExampleData client: it reads bookings from the Connection `exampledata`, lists findings kept in the Data Store `findings`, adds a finding and starts the Workflow `monthly-check`. Replace the names of the Connection, its operation, the Data Store and the Workflow with those of the instance, and the mapping with the input the operation declares. ```yaml title="app.yaml" id: exampledata-dashboard name: ExampleData dashboard kit: 1.4.0 connections: - exampledata dataStores: - name: findings actions: - { name: list-findings, file: actions/list-findings.sql, effect: reading } - { name: add-finding, file: actions/add-finding.sql, effect: changing } ``` ```yaml title="actions/load-bookings.action.yaml" connection: exampledata operation: list_bookings effect: reading description: The bookings of one client in one month. input: schema: type: object properties: client: { type: string, maxLength: 40 } month: { type: string, description: "The month as YYYY-MM" } required: [client] mapping: clientId: "{{client}}" period: "{{month}}" ``` ```sql title="actions/list-findings.sql" -- @param client text optional select id, client_id, title, created_at from findings where $client is null or client_id = $client order by created_at desc limit 100 ``` ```sql title="actions/add-finding.sql" -- @param client text -- @param title text insert into findings (client_id, title) values ($client, $title) ``` ```yaml title="actions/run-check.action.yaml" workflow: monthly-check description: Checks the bookings of one client. input: schema: type: object properties: client: { type: string } required: [client] mapping: client: "{{client}}" ``` ```tsx title="src/routes/__root.tsx" import { createRootRoute, Outlet } from "@tanstack/react-router"; export const Route = createRootRoute({ component: () => }); ``` ```tsx title="src/routes/index.tsx" import { createFileRoute } from "@tanstack/react-router"; import { useEffect, useState } from "react"; import { AppCallError, actions, useWorkflowRun } from "@work-shape/catalyst-app-kit"; import { Button } from "@work-shape/catalyst-app-kit/ui"; export const Route = createFileRoute("/")({ component: Dashboard }); const CLIENT = "10023"; /** A message to show for a failed call: the platform's own where it gave one. */ function messageOf(error: unknown): string { return error instanceof AppCallError ? error.message : "The call failed."; } function Dashboard() { const [bookings, setBookings] = useState(); const [findings, setFindings] = useState(); const [error, setError] = useState(); const [note, setNote] = useState(); const [runId, setRunId] = useState(); const { run } = useWorkflowRun(runId); const load = () => { actions .call("load-bookings", { client: CLIENT, month: "2026-09" }) .then((answer) => setBookings("result" in answer ? answer.result : undefined)) .catch((failure: unknown) => setError(messageOf(failure))); actions .call("list-findings", { client: CLIENT }) .then((answer) => setFindings("result" in answer ? answer.result : undefined)) .catch((failure: unknown) => setError(messageOf(failure))); }; useEffect(load, []); const addFinding = () => { actions .call( "add-finding", { client: CLIENT, title: "Booking without receipt" }, { idempotencyKey: `add-finding-${Date.now()}` } ) .then((answer) => { // In the App's draft a change is simulated: say what it would have done. if (answer.status === "dry_run") setNote(answer.message); else load(); }) .catch((failure: unknown) => setError(messageOf(failure))); }; const startCheck = () => { actions .call("run-check", { client: CLIENT }, { idempotencyKey: `run-check-${Date.now()}` }) .then((answer) => { if (answer.status === "dry_run") { setNote(answer.message); return; } const started = answer.result; if (typeof started === "object" && started !== null && "id" in started) { setRunId(String(started.id)); } }) .catch((failure: unknown) => setError(messageOf(failure))); }; return (

Client {CLIENT}

Check: {run.status}

{JSON.stringify({ bookings, findings }, null, 2)}
); } ``` ## A plain HTML App The same call from a plain HTML App, with one action on the Connection. ```yaml title="app.yaml" id: exampledata-bookings name: ExampleData bookings kit: 1.4.0 entry: index.html connections: - exampledata ``` ```yaml title="actions/load-bookings.action.yaml" connection: exampledata operation: list_bookings effect: reading input: schema: type: object properties: client: { type: string } required: [client] mapping: clientId: "{{client}}" ``` ```html title="index.html" ExampleData bookings

```

## When a save fails

The build answers each fault with its file and a sentence that names the fix. The common ones:

- `connection_not_declared`: the action calls a Connection that `connections` in `app.yaml` does not list.
- `data_store_not_declared`: an `sql` action and no `dataStores` in `app.yaml`.
- `key_reserved`: a key a later part of Apps will use, such as `rights`, `requires` or an action of `kind: code`; remove it.
- An `sql` file without its line under `actions`: add `{ name, file, effect }`.
- A YAML file in `actions/` without the ending `.action.yaml`: rename it.
- A missing `connection`, `operation` or `effect` in an action file: add it.
- `sql_statement_not_allowed`: a reading statement that is not one `SELECT` or `WITH`, or a changing one that is not one `INSERT` of parameters.

At a call, `action_unknown` means the manifest of the shown revision has no action of that name: save the Page again after adding the file.

pages.title: Apps for people
pages.description: Ask an agent for an App, keep it as a draft, try its actions safely, run one live once, and publish it for your workspace.
pages.body:
An App is a small tool with its own screens, such as a form for new clients or a list of open offers. You get one by asking an agent in a chat. It can show data and, through its actions, read from or write to a connected system, a Data Store or a Workflow.

The German interface shows the labels in quotes. [Build an App](/apps/build/) is the technical guide the agent follows.

## Ask for it in a chat

Describe what you need: who uses it, what it shows, what it should let people do. For example: "Build a page where I can enter a new client and see the last ten."

The agent builds a **Page** and shows it beside the chat. **Preview** ("Vorschau") shows it working; **Files** ("Dateien") shows what it is made of. Keep asking for changes in the chat; each one the agent saves is the Page's newest revision.

A Page belongs to its conversation. It cannot yet change anything in other systems. To keep it and share it, save it as an App.

When you have no App yet, the **Apps** page offers **Build an app in chat** ("App im Chat bauen"), which starts a chat for this.

## Keep it as an App

1. In the Page's header, click **Save as app** ("Als App speichern").
2. Give it a **Name** and an **ID**. The ID is part of the App's address and cannot change later.
3. Click **Save** ("Speichern").

The Page becomes the **draft** of a new App in your workspace. Nothing is published yet: only administrators see it until you publish.

You can also simply tell the agent "keep this as an app".

After that, changes you ask for in the same chat go into the App's draft by themselves. When that did not happen, for example because someone changed the draft elsewhere, the Page offers **Update app** ("App aktualisieren"): **Replace draft** ("Entwurf ersetzen") puts the Page as it is now into the draft.

## Try it safely

Open **Apps** in the main rail and the App, then **Edit** ("Bearbeiten"). The draft opens on its **Preview**. **Technical details** ("Technische Details") beside it shows two more tabs, **Files** and **Actions** ("Aktionen"); your browser keeps them open until you fold them again.

In a draft, nothing changes for real:

- An action that only reads gets real data.
- An action that would change something is **simulated**. It answers with what it would have done and changes nothing. In the **Test** dialog the result says **Not carried out in the draft** ("Im Entwurf nicht ausgeführt").

On the **Actions** tab, **Test** ("Testen") calls one action with input you give.

## Run one action live once

To check that a changing action really works before you publish:

1. On the **Actions** tab, find the action and click **Run live once** ("Einmal live ausführen"). The button shows on actions that change something and are allowed to run without someone else's approval.
2. It now says **Your next call runs live.** ("Dein nächster Aufruf läuft live.")
3. Use the action once, in the preview or with **Test**. That one call is carried out for real, under the instance's usual rules. The next one is simulated again.

The switch is yours alone: it does not affect anyone else trying the draft. Saving or discarding the draft clears it. A call that would need someone else's approval is refused here, because a draft cannot wait for one.

## Publish it

1. On the draft, click **Publish** ("Veröffentlichen").
2. The dialog names the workspace that gets it, such as "Everyone in Sales gets revision 3 when they open the app.", and lists the Connections it uses and the outside hosts it calls.
3. Click **Publish** ("Veröffentlichen") in the dialog.

Now everyone in the workspace finds it on the **Apps** page, and up to five published Apps appear under **Apps** in the main rail. In a published App, every action runs for real, with the rights of the person using it. An action that starts a Workflow is the exception: the Workflow runs with its own account.

An agent never publishes. A person decides.

Later changes go to the draft again. The App shows **Unpublished changes** ("Unveröffentlichte Änderungen") until you publish them. **Discard** ("Verwerfen") throws the draft away, and **Revisions** ("Revisionen") under **More actions** ("Weitere Aktionen") shows every saved state.

## Who may do what

- Everyone in the workspace can open a published App.
- Saving a Page as an App, editing the draft, **Run live once** and publishing are rights of the administrator role today. They cannot be given to one person yet. If you do not see **Save as app** or **Publish**, ask an administrator.
- An action reaches only what the person using the App may reach. The App's screens never hold a key: they call actions by name, and the instance makes the call.

pages.title: Workflows
pages.description: Let the platform do work by itself, step by step, on a schedule or when you start it; try it with a test run and publish it.
pages.body:
A Workflow is work the platform does by itself, step by step: every morning, or when someone starts it. It runs without a chat. Each step reads or changes something, for example in a connected system or a Data Store.

The German interface shows the labels in quotes.

## Find your Workflows

Click **Workflows** in the main rail. The row shows when the instance has Workflows switched on and you may see at least one, or may write Workflows. The list shows each Workflow with its last run.

Open one to see its page:

- The **Workflow** tab shows the steps as a canvas, from **Starts** ("Startet") at the top down to the last step. A step is marked **Reads data** ("Liest Daten") or **Changes data** ("Ändert Daten").
- The **Runs** tab ("Läufe") lists every run, with what each step did.
- The trigger says when it runs: **Started by hand only** ("Startet nur von Hand") or the schedule, such as "Every day, 07:00 AM" ("Jeden Tag, …").

## Make or change a Workflow

A new Workflow is created with the CLI (`catalyst workflow put <name> --from … --if-revision new`); see [the CLI](/configure/cli/). After that, change it with **Edit with the agent** ("Mit dem Agenten bearbeiten") on its page. A chat opens that is about this Workflow: describe what should change, and every change the agent saves becomes the next draft.

A change is always a **draft** first. The banner says **Draft, not published yet** ("Entwurf, noch nicht veröffentlicht") or **Draft differs from published** ("Entwurf weicht von der veröffentlichten Version ab"). Runs keep using the published version until the draft is published.

## Try it with a test run

1. On the draft banner, click **Test run** ("Testlauf").
2. Read the dialog and click **Start test run** ("Testlauf starten").

A test run reads real data, but only what both you and the Workflow may see. Steps that would change something are only simulated: each says what it would have done, and nothing is changed. Each step shows where its call went: **Live**, **Test** or **Simulated** ("Simuliert"). A test run writes no new draft and changes nothing about the published version.

To try one changing step for real:

1. On the page of the test run, select the step.
2. In its panel, click **Run live once** ("Einmal live ausführen").
3. Click **Test again** ("Erneut testen"). That step runs for real once, under the instance's usual rules. The others stay simulated.

A step marked "A published run asks for approval here" needs someone's approval under the instance's rules. A published run stops at this step, because a run cannot wait for an approval. Change the step before you publish.

## Publish it

Click **Publish** ("Veröffentlichen") on the draft banner. The revision becomes the version that runs, by hand and on its schedule. **Discard** ("Verwerfen") takes the draft back to the published version.

A Workflow runs with its own account, not with yours, so it can read and change what you cannot. That is why publishing is held tight: today it takes a superadmin.

## Start it by hand

Click **Start now** ("Jetzt starten") on a published Workflow, fill in what it asks for, and click **Start** ("Starten"). The run appears under **Runs**. On a run's page, **Run again** ("Erneut starten") starts the published version once more.

## Who may do what

An administrator gives these rights under **Settings > Instance > Access** ("Einstellungen › Instanz › Zugriff"), for one Workflow:

| Right | What the Access page says |
| --- | --- |
| Read workflows | See the Workflow, its steps and its runs. |
| Use workflows | Start the Workflow. It then runs with the Workflow's own rights, not with this person's. |
| Write workflows | Change the draft of the Workflow. A draft does not run until it is published. |
| Publish workflows | Make a draft the version that runs. Today this also needs the superadmin role and the right to manage API access. |

Administrators hold every right; publishing also needs the superadmin role. A test run needs the right to write the Workflow.

pages.title: Agents and skills in Studio
pages.description: Create, edit, restore and delete agents and skills in Studio, connect outside systems, and read the other lists Studio holds.
pages.body:
**Studio** is the area of the interface where agents and skills are made. It stands in the main rail as a row of its own and opens at `/build`. The old address `/admin/config` leads there. Beside **Agents** (German: **Agenten**) and **Skills**, Studio lists **Connections** (**Verbindungen**), **Data stores** (**Datenspeicher**) and **Guardrails** (**Leitplanken**), each for a person who may read one. Apps and Workflows are not in Studio: each has a row of its own in the main rail.

Studio works on the [asset API](/reference/api/assets/): it reads a list page by page, reads one asset when its page opens and writes one asset at a time. It never loads the whole set of agents and skills.

## Who sees Studio

The Studio row shows for a person who holds a right on at least one agent or skill:

- `config_assets.read` or `config_assets.write` on the instance, or
- a grant in a [Namespace](/operate/rights-and-namespaces/).

A person with a grant in a Namespace sees the assets of that Namespace and nothing else. A person with no such right has no Studio row, and the address says that Studio is not available.

A grant on one single asset, or on what one workspace owns, is checked by the instance on every read and write. The interface learns only that the person may read some asset of the kind: a read grant gives the Studio row and the list of the kind, which holds the assets the person may read. Such an asset opens read-only. A grant that allows another action and no reading gives no Studio row.

On an instance with the module [`connections`](/configure/modules/#connections) on, Studio also lists Connections for a person who may read every Connection of the instance, which the administrator role allows, and for a person with a read grant on one Connection, who sees that Connection. A read grant written earlier in a Namespace or on a workspace shows the Connections it covers until it is revoked. A grant to use a Connection gives no entry in Studio. A row shows the connector type, whether the instance or a workspace owns the Connection, and whether it is enabled. A row opens the [page of the Connection](#the-page-of-a-connection). The list is **Studio > Connections**; the German interface names it **Studio › Verbindungen**.

## Connecting an outside system

[Connect a system](/connect/connect-a-system/) walks through these steps for the person who sets it up.

A Connection reaches a remote MCP server (connector type `mcp`) or a REST interface that it reads by GET (connector type `http_api`). An MCP server lists its tools itself. A REST interface lists nothing: each operation is declared in the Connection's definition with its path and parameters, as [release config](/configure/release-config/#a-rest-interface-http_api) shows. An agent may write such declarations from a vendor's public OpenAPI description into the conversation; a person pastes them and saves, because an agent never saves a Connection. A REST interface that must be written to needs a [custom tool](/extend/custom-tools/) in the client assembly for now.

1. **New connection** in Studio > Connections takes a name, the server's https address with the path of its MCP endpoint, and the authentication: none, a bearer token, or a key in a header the server names.
2. The key is entered in that form or later on the Connection's page under **Credential** (German: **Zugangsdaten**), with **Enter the key** or **Enter a new key**. It is stored encrypted and never shown again, to anyone. A key is never typed into a chat: an agent cannot take it, and an agent that asks for one is wrong. Give the key on the Connection's page only.
3. The instance reads the tools the server offers. On the Connection's page, accept the operations agents may call. **Test connection** checks the address and the key.
4. Give an agent the tools, as the next section says.

The rights this needs:

| Step                                                                          | Right                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| See Studio > Connections and a Connection's page                              | `connection.read`                                                                                    |
| Create a Connection, enter or replace its key, test it, accept its operations | `connection.write`, which the administrator role holds; the Access page does not grant it            |
| Delete a Connection                                                           | `connection.delete`, which the administrator role holds                                              |
| Give an agent a tool of the Connection                                        | `agent.write` on the agent, and `connection.read` to see the Connection in the agent's Tools section |
| Have an agent call the tool                                                   | `connection.use` for the person the agent works for: an agent acts with that person's rights         |

The administrator role holds every right on Connections. Beside the rights, the operator must have turned the module [`connections`](/configure/modules/#connections) on, listed the server's host in [`egress.allow`](/configure/release-config/#egress) and set a [Secret Store key](/configure/release-config/#secret-store-keys); without the host on the list the save is refused with `egress_denied`. A Connection that comes from the release config is read-only on the instance, and its credential comes from the instance's environment.

## Giving an agent the tools of a Connection

The **Tools** section of an agent's page lists the instance's own tools under **Instance tools** and then, under **Connections**, one group for each Connection you may read (`connection.read`). A group holds a check box for each operation that agents may call and that is enabled and ready, with its description and whether it reads or changes. Ticking a box gives the agent the tool `connection.<name>.<operation>`. A group with more than 12 operations starts folded and shows how many of its operations the agent holds, and so does every group the agent holds nothing of when there are more than 6 groups.

A tool the agent already holds whose Connection or operation is gone, switched off, not offered to agents or not visible to you stays on the page in a group **No longer available** at the end of the section. Saving keeps it until you remove it. At run time the agent goes on without such a tool.

The instance checks on save that a name starting with `connection.` has the form `connection.<name>.<operation>`. It does not check that the Connection or the operation exists, because Connections change without a release.

The list is read once when the page opens, in one answer without pages. A Connection accepts at most 100 operations (`CONNECTION_MAX_ACCEPTED_OPERATIONS` in `packages/core/src/connections.ts`).

## The page of a Connection

A Connection made in Studio is changed on its page by a person who may change Connections (`connection.write`): its address and authentication under **Settings**, its key under **Credential**, and the operations agents may call. A Connection that comes from the release config opens read-only and says so; it is changed in the release config. The page never shows a credential or a reference to one.

- **Settings**: the connector type, the authentication scheme and the settings of the connector type.
- **Status**: whether the instance reaches the outside system, when it was last tested, and whether the credential is set, not set or unreadable. A Connection has one credential for everyone who may use it, and the page says so. A Connection with the authentication scheme `none` needs no credential, and the page says that instead.
- **Operations**: each accepted operation with its tool name `connection.<name>.<operation>`, whether it reads or changes, who may call it (agents, Apps, Workflows, outside clients or nobody) and its status. On a Connection made on the instance, a person with `connection.write` opens an operation to outside clients with the check box **Outside clients (CLI, MCP)** (German: **Externe Clients (CLI, MCP)**), and closes it again by clearing it. It is off on every operation until somebody ticks it, because what such a call returns is copied to the computer that holds the key. Only an operation with the status **Ready** can be called. **Awaiting discovery** means the instance has not read it from the outside system yet, **Needs review** that the outside system describes it differently than was accepted, **Unknown** that the outside system does not offer it, and **Disabled** that the operator switched it off. On a Connection made in Studio, **Accept new description** clears **Needs review**, and **Remove** takes an operation away.
- **Discovered tools** (German: **Gefundene Tools**), for a person who may change the Connection: the tools the server offers. For each, check **What it does** (**Was es tut**: Reading or Changing), untick **Agents can use it** (**Agenten dürfen es nutzen**) if agents should not call it, then **Accept** (**Akzeptieren**) to add it as an operation. **Read tools again** asks the server once more.
- **Used by**: the agents that carry a tool of the Connection, of those the reader may read.
- **Who may use it**: the people and service principals given this Connection by itself. Rights on a whole Namespace are on the Access page.

**Test connection** asks the connector type to check the Connection and records the answer. It is offered to a person who may change Connections (`connection.write`); a person who may only read sees the recorded state. A test that a policy holds for an approval has not run: it waits in the Inbox.

What to do depends on where the Connection comes from. A Connection made in Studio is repaired on its page; one from the release config needs the operator.

| Status | What it means | Made in Studio | From the release config |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ready | The outside system answered the test. | Nothing. | Nothing. |
| Not tested | Nobody has tested the Connection yet. | Test it. | Test it. |
| Testing | A test runs. | Wait for it. | Wait for it. |
| Unauthorized | The outside system refused the credential. | Enter a new key under **Credential**, then test again. | The operator sets a new credential in the instance's environment and restarts the instance. |
| Network denied | The host is not in [`egress.allow`](/configure/release-config/#egress), or it resolves to an address the instance may not reach. | The operator adds the host to `egress.allow`, or for a public HTTPS host on port 443 sets `egress.allowPublicHttps`, and restarts the instance. | The same. |
| Unavailable | The outside system did not answer. | Check the address under **Settings** and change it if it is wrong. | Check the address under **Settings**. The operator changes it in the release config. |
| Not configured | The credential is missing. | Enter the key under **Credential**, then test again. | The operator supplies it in the instance's environment and restarts the instance. |
| Credential unreadable | A credential is stored and the instance cannot read it. | Enter the key again under **Credential**, then test again. | The operator restores the Secret Store key it was stored with, or supplies the credential again, and restarts the instance. |
| Failed | The test failed for a reason the instance does not name. | Test again, then ask the operator. | Test again, then ask the operator. |

## The list

Each kind has a list. For **Agents** and **Skills** a row shows the name, the Namespace if the asset is in one, the id and when it was last changed. A row is a link, so it opens in a new tab like any other link.

- **Search** asks the instance for names and ids that contain the text.
- **Namespace** narrows the list to one Namespace. It shows when you hold rights in more than one.
- **Show more** reads the next 50 rows.

The names in the list are in the instance's default language.

## Create

**New agent** or **New skill** opens a dialog for the name and the id. The id follows the name until you change it. It cannot be changed after the asset is saved.

If you hold the write right in a Namespace, the dialog offers that Namespace and the id starts with its prefix. Only Namespaces you may write in are offered. The choice **No Namespace** is offered to people who may write every asset of the instance.

**Continue** opens the page of the new asset. Nothing is stored until you press **Create agent** or **Create skill** there.

## Edit

An asset page has sections, and an index of them beside the content or above it on a narrow window. The save bar appears with the first change. It counts the changed fields and offers **Discard**.

Texts that exist in English and German are written in one language at a time. **Texts in** switches the language for the whole page. The switch marks a language in which texts are still empty. A field left empty in one language shows the text of the other one to people, and the field says so.

If you may read an asset but not change it, the page says so and has no save bar.

### When a save is refused

- **A tool, model or skill that is not allowed.** A Namespace can limit the tools and models of its agents. The refusal stands under the field it concerns, and the form keeps what you typed.
- **Somebody else saved first.** The page saves against the revision it loaded. If the asset changed in between, nothing is overwritten. A notice offers **Load the newer version** and asks before it replaces what you typed, so you can copy what you need first. Until then the page saves nothing. If the newer version cannot be loaded, the page says so and keeps your text.
- **Somebody deleted it.** The notice says that the asset was deleted. Your text stays so that you can copy it, and the notice leads back to the list.
- **A skill you may not read.** An agent can only be given skills you may read yourself. A skill it already has stays when you save other changes.
- **Anything else** is shown in the words of the instance, above the save bar.

## History and restore

**History** opens a panel beside the editor with the saved revisions, the newest first, 50 at a time. **Restore** makes the content of an older revision the newest one. The asset gets a new revision, so a restore can itself be restored. After a restore the page says which revision it restored. While somebody else's newer version waits to be loaded, History restores nothing.

## Delete

**Delete** is in the menu beside History, for people who hold the delete right on the asset. An asset that another one still refers to is not deleted, and the page says which reference stands in the way.

## Limits

| What                                                                 | Value     |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- |
| Rows read per list request                                           | 50        |
| Wait after typing before a search                                    | 250 ms    |
| Skills offered per search in an agent's skill picker                 | 50        |
| How long the list of your Namespaces is kept before it is read again | 5 minutes |

The list never holds more than the pages you asked for. The Namespace filter and the create dialog list the Namespaces you hold rights in. History reads 50 revisions of the one asset when it opens, and **Show more** reads the next 50.

pages.title: The Catalyst CLI
pages.description: Install the public catalyst command from one file and use it against an instance.
pages.body:
`catalyst` is the command line tool for an instance. It is the public package `@work-shape/catalyst-cli` under the MIT licence and needs Node 22 or later.

## Install

Install the release tarball you were handed:

```sh
npm install --global ./work-shape-catalyst-cli-<version>.tgz
catalyst --help
```

A team that keeps its tooling with its working copy installs the same file as a development dependency and runs `npx catalyst`.

The package installs from that one file. It depends on two third-party packages, `js-yaml` and `zod`, and on no private package: the asset schemas, the API contract and the API client it uses are built into it. No registry account and no token are needed to install it.

## What it does today

The `config` commands synchronize agents and skills between a folder and an instance. [Config assets](/configure/config-assets/) describes the working copy, the commands and what a push does.

```sh
catalyst config pull
catalyst config diff
catalyst config validate
catalyst config push
```

## Log in

On an instance with the module `personalApiKeys` on, a person logs the tool in with a key of their own:

```sh
catalyst login --instance https://chat.example.com
```

The tool prints an address and a code such as `BCDF-GHJK`. Open the address, signed in as yourself; it leads to **Settings > You > API keys** (German: **Einstellungen › Du › API-Schlüssel**). Check that the code is the one your terminal shows, choose what the key may do and until when, and confirm. The tool then collects the key and saves it. Nothing is pasted anywhere: the code you confirm cannot be used to sign in, and the key travels only from the instance to the tool. A code expires after 15 minutes and is collected once.

A key acts as you, narrowed to its scopes. A scope is a right such as `agent.write`, optionally limited to one Namespace: `agent.write:tax-`. A key never does more than you may at the moment of each call: a right an administrator takes from you is gone from the key on its next call. A key lives at most a year. A new key starts with no scope ticked: tick the ones the key needs. **Settings > You > API keys** lists your keys and revokes them; a revoked key is refused on its next call. Whoever administers API access sees and revokes every person's keys. No key issues another key.

`catalyst logout --instance <address>` removes the saved key from this machine. It stays valid until you revoke it under **Settings > You > API keys**.

`catalyst setup <claude-code|codex|other> --instance <address>` logs in the same way where no working key is saved, then writes the Catalyst skill for an AI tool on your computer. [Connect a local agent](/getting-started/local-agent/) describes it.

A command without `--instance` works on the `defaultInstance` of the working copy's `catalyst.yaml`; one without a default is refused with the instances it names, and a saved key never chooses among them. Outside a working copy it works on the one instance a key is saved for, unless `CATALYST_API_KEY` is set. With none or several saved it names the saved ones and asks for `--instance`. `catalyst --version` prints the version of the tool.

A working copy that belongs to one Namespace names it beside the instance:

```yaml
instances:
  production:
    url: https://chat.example.com
    namespace: tax-
defaultInstance: production
```

Its `push` names the Namespace, as the instance asks of everyone but the holder of the release right, and never changes the instance's default agent. Its `pull`, `diff` and `list` read only the agents and skills the key may read, and neither the instance's version nor its default agent, which only a reader of every agent and skill may read; a key of one Namespace pulls, diffs and lists its Namespace.

A working copy can instead belong to one Shared Workspace: then the agents and skills it pushes are the workspace's own, and a pull reads only what the workspace owns. Bind an empty working copy once with its first pull:

```sh
catalyst config pull --workspace <workspace-id>
```

The pull writes `workspace: <workspace-id>` beside the instance's `url` in `catalyst.yaml`, and every later command of that working copy names the workspace. A working copy is bound once: one bound to another workspace, one of a Namespace and one that already pulled the instance's own assets are refused, so pull another workspace into a directory of its own. Its `push` is never a release and never changes the instance's default agent, which only an agent of the instance can be; an agent it creates starts hidden until an instance admin offers it, and a guardrail it creates belongs to the workspace as well. A workspace's agent may name the workspace's skills and the instance's skills you may read; no agent outside the workspace may name the workspace's skills.

## One command per asset operation

Every operation on assets has a command, for every kind the instance registers: agents, skills, Apps, Workflows, Connections, Data Stores, guardrails. The kind is the first word, by its id, its plural or with dashes (`data-store`). The instance names its kinds; a kind a later release adds works without a new CLI.

```sh
catalyst context                  # the instance, your rights in Namespaces and workspaces, its kinds
catalyst kinds                    # each kind: lifecycle, folder or definition, rights
catalyst references               # models, efforts and tools a definition may name
catalyst agent list --prefix tax-
catalyst agent show tax-vat
catalyst agent history tax-vat
catalyst skill validate --from skills/tax-guide
catalyst skill put tax-guide --from skills/tax-guide --if-revision new
catalyst agent put tax-vat --from agents/tax-vat.agent.yaml --if-revision 3
catalyst app put offers --from offers --if-revision 4 --workspace <workspace-id>
catalyst app publish offers --revision 5 --workspace <workspace-id>
catalyst agent revert tax-vat --to 2 --if-revision 4
catalyst agent delete tax-vat --if-revision 5
```

`--from` takes the forms of the working copy: an `.agent.yaml` or any YAML or JSON definition, a skill's folder with its `SKILL.md`, or the folder of a kind whose revisions hold files, such as an App. A write names the revision it was made against with `--if-revision`, or `new` to create; read it with `show` or `history`. `discard-draft`, `set-availability` and `set-default` complete the list; `catalyst --help` shows each with its options. `--json` prints the instance's answer as it came.

Guardrails have four commands of their own beside `put`:

```sh
catalyst guardrail test no-iban --text "DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00"   # or --from <file>, --asset skill:<name>
catalyst guardrail dry-run no-iban                 # what the draft would have done in the last 14 days
catalyst guardrail publish no-iban --revision 2    # shows the dry run first
catalyst guardrail unpublish no-iban               # stops it; the draft stays
```

`test` checks the draft, or `--revision <n>`, and keeps no hit. A first `publish` of a guardrail that would have blocked or held actions asks for `--confirm <n>` with the number the dry run counted. [Guardrails as assets](/configure/config-assets/#guardrails-as-assets) says who may do what.

The instance decides every right, revision and check. A `revert` needs the read right on the asset beside the write right, as it restores content. A refusal is printed as the instance gave it, with each asset, issue or item it names:

```text
Refused by the instance (HTTP 403 FORBIDDEN): Missing the right 'agent.write'
```

The exit code is 0 when the call was applied, 1 when it was refused or failed, 2 when the command line was wrong and nothing was sent, and 3 when the call waits for another person's approval and has changed nothing yet.

## The key

The tool takes its key from the variable `CATALYST_API_KEY` when it is set, which is how automation runs it, and otherwise from the key `catalyst login` saved for the instance's address. It never takes a key as an argument and never writes one into the working copy.

- A saved key is kept in `~/.config/catalyst/credentials.json` (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/catalyst`, or `$CATALYST_CONFIG_HOME`), readable by you alone. A file others may read is refused until you `chmod 600` it.
- The key is sent only to the instance you name, and only over HTTPS. Plain HTTP is accepted for `localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8` and `::1`.
- The key is exchanged once for a short-lived access token. Every other request carries the token, not the key.
- An error message never repeats the key, and the tool never prints it.

## What is not in it

`catalyst config local-key` is no longer a command of this tool. It created a key on a local development instance by reading the release config and its secrets, which the public tool does not do. A client repository runs its `config:local-key` script instead, which calls `catalyst-local-key` of the private `client-assembly` package.

## For maintainers

`pnpm release:check` packs the tool and reads every file of the tarball. It fails when the tarball depends on a workspace package, holds source of a private package, holds what looks like a credential or a file that stores credentials, or has no licence file. `pnpm release:check:public` runs the same check alone and then installs the tarball with npm in an empty directory.

The workflow `Publish public CLI` publishes the tarball to npm. It is switched off until the repository variable `PUBLISH_PUBLIC_CLI` is `true`. It refuses a commit whose version is on npm already, so each version is published once, from the commit that carries it.

Settings, Connect a local agent installs the CLI version that `PUBLISHED_CLI_VERSION` in `packages/api-contract/src/public-cli.ts` names, and only one that is on npm. While it is unset the page says the command is not available yet. A release that offers the command goes in this order:

1. Bump the version all packages share, in a commit of its own.
2. Run `Publish public CLI` on that commit.
3. Set `PUBLISHED_CLI_VERSION` to that version and commit it.
4. Deploy that commit.
5. Only then switch on the module `personalApiKeys` on the instance.

pages.title: Client assembly
pages.description: Keep customer-specific code thin and source-controlled.
pages.body:
A client assembly app imports platform packages and wires them to one organization's config, tools, and deployment settings.

It should not copy platform internals.

## Recommended Shape

```text
client-instance/
  package.json
  Dockerfile
  docker-compose.yml
  .env.example
  src/
    client.ts
    server.ts
  agents/
    support-agent.yaml
    instructions/
      support-agent.md
  tools/
    lookup-order.ts
    update-ticket.ts
  config/
    app.yaml
    ui.yaml
    model-providers.yaml
  deploy/
    compose.prod.yaml
    Caddyfile
```

## Assembly Code

The client object imports platform packages, points at release config, registers tool factories, validates the assembly, and starts the chat API.

```ts
import { defineClientInstance } from "@vivd-catalyst/client-assembly";
import { createDocumentProcessingCapability } from "@vivd-catalyst/document-processing";
import { lookupOrderToolFactory } from "../tools/lookup-order";
import { updateTicketToolFactory } from "../tools/update-ticket";

export default defineClientInstance({
  rootDir: new URL("..", import.meta.url),
  capabilities: [createDocumentProcessingCapability()],
  tools: [lookupOrderToolFactory, updateTicketToolFactory]
});
```

```ts
import client from "./client";

await client.listen();
```

Every process of the instance starts from the same client object, so each one is assembled
from the same tools, Connector types and capabilities. A worker entry point is one call:

```ts
import client from "./client";

await client.runWorkspaceCommandWorker();
```

`runAgentRunWorker()` and `runArtifactPreviewWorker()` start the other two workers. A process
that is assembled without a capability stops when the release config turns a module of that
capability on.

The frontend entry calls `renderStandaloneChatApp` from `@vivd-catalyst/chat-ui/shell`. Its `toolActivityLabels` option names a tool in the activity line, and its `labelOverrides` option takes `resourcesCustomerData: { en, de }` to word the heading of the structured data in the resources, which reads "Data" without it.

Exact APIs may evolve while the platform is still early. The boundary should remain the same: platform packages provide reusable behavior, and the client assembly app provides source-controlled customer choices.

## Startup Validation

The assembly should fail before listening when:

- an agent references a tool that is not registered
- a configured tool is enabled but has no implementation
- a disabled tool appears in an agent allowlist
- an enabled tool has the permission mode `approval_required`, which this release cannot run, see [Permission Policy](/extend/custom-tools/#permission-policy)
- required auth, model provider, retention, or database settings are missing

Validation is part of the product model. A broken instance should not start and surprise users at runtime.

## What Belongs In The Client Layer

Keep these in the client assembly app:

- customer-specific tools
- agent instructions and suggested prompts
- release config and UI copy
- customer system credentials and scoped secret references
- domain output mappings
- deployment env examples and compose overrides

Keep these in platform packages:

- chat server behavior
- API contracts
- UI primitives and shells
- config schema
- tool SDK and tool execution contracts
- auth adapter contracts
- usage governance
- audit and storage interfaces
- datasource registry, adapters, guardrails, and generic datasource query tools
- capability SDK, managed file, conversation attachment, and managed artifact extension surfaces

Reusable capabilities that are not part of the open platform live in capability packages. Document processing (`@vivd-catalyst/document-processing`, part of the paid capabilities and not in the open repository), for example, owns its preprocessing config under `capabilities.documentProcessing`, its document tools, and its document-specific model-context hints while using platform-managed files and conversation attachments.

pages.title: Config assets
pages.description: Agents, skills, Apps and guardrails live in the database; edit them in Studio, write them through the asset API, or synchronize them with the Catalyst CLI.
pages.body:
Agents, skills, and the default agent are **config assets**: they live in the client instance's database, not in config files. The server never reads agent or skill files — a release config that still contains `agents`, `agentFiles`, `skills`, `skillFiles`, or `defaultAgentName` fails validation with a pointer to this workflow.

This gives config assets a different lifecycle than release config:

- **Release config** (`app.yaml`) ships with a deployment and owns infrastructure: auth, model providers and bindings, usage budgets, tool enablement, workspaces.
- **Config assets** change at runtime — in [Studio](/configure/build/) or with a `catalyst config push` — and apply to new conversations immediately, without a deployment. A running conversation keeps the agent snapshot it started with.

Skill content is read on demand by the `read_skill` tool, so edits are visible to reads after the edit even within an already-running conversation; the agent's system prompt, model selection, and tool list remain on the run's snapshot. A skill is one atomic package: its required `SKILL.md` root may include selectively readable UTF-8 text resources. The root read returns a compact resource manifest, and a second `read_skill` call can load one exact listed path.

Every mutation is validated against the full resulting asset set before it is stored (unknown tool or skill references, missing default agent, duplicate names, and skill use without the `read_skill` tool are all rejected), appended to a per-asset revision history, and audited. A fresh instance boots with zero assets; the chat UI shows a "not configured" notice until the first push.

## The CLI working copy

[The Catalyst CLI](/configure/cli/) says how the `catalyst` command is installed.

The repo's YAML and Markdown files are a **working copy**, not the live configuration. Nothing you edit locally is live until you push it:

```sh
catalyst config pull        # replace the working copy with the live assets
catalyst config diff        # show local changes, remote newer assets, and conflicts
catalyst config validate    # schema + cross-reference check without writing
catalyst config push        # merge changed local assets into the live instance
```

A `catalyst.yaml` manifest in the working-copy root names instances and the asset file globs. The database is the live authoring source; the folder is a pulled working copy. `.catalyst-state.json` (gitignored) records each pulled asset's revision and content hash, plus the default agent. Skill hashes cover the root and all resources. YAML formatting and provenance comments do not count as edits.

`push` sends only assets changed locally since their last pull, in one `assets.sync` call that is applied completely or not at all. Each asset names the revision of its last pull, and an asset the working copy never pulled names none: it is a creation, which the instance refuses when it holds the name. Unchanged files leave instance edits alone. Assets missing locally stay on the instance unless you use `--prune`, which deletes them at the revision of the last pull; an asset that appeared on the instance since is reported as a conflict instead of being deleted. `--prune` cannot be combined with `--only`, and a push whose listing of the instance fails deletes nothing.

A working copy that never pulled from an instance pushes every asset as a creation, so a first release to an empty instance needs no pull. Each pulled asset is recorded with its revision and with the id of the asset on the instance, and a push names both. A working copy that was pulled from another database, or whose asset was deleted for good and made again on the instance, is refused for that asset, on the CLI before anything is sent and on the instance with `409 CONFLICT` and `details.reason` `asset_replaced`: the revision numbers of two assets say nothing about each other. The CLI names the asset and the command that repairs it, `catalyst config pull --only <kind>:<name>`, which reads the asset again whenever its id differs. A `.catalyst-state.json` written by an earlier CLI holds no ids and is refused the same way until the assets are pulled once.

There is no `--force`. A push never overwrites a change it did not read: the flag is refused with the procedure below. A deleted asset keeps its name with its history. `pull` records the revision of a delete it sees, and the next push that creates the asset again names it; without that pull the creation is reported as a conflict with the delete.

The CLI reads with `assets.list` and `assets.get` and writes with `assets.sync`, the operations under [The asset API](#the-asset-api). Each push is one Operation Run in the name of whoever the key belongs to: the person or the service principal. A push whose answer is lost on the way is sent again under the same idempotency key, so it is applied once. One push holds at most 2,000 assets and 20 MiB, and one asset in it at most 2 MiB; a larger release is pushed in parts with `--only`. `validate` asks `assets.sync_check` whether a push of the whole working copy would be accepted and writes nothing. On an instance whose policy holds a release for approval, `push` reports the waiting Operation Run and exits with 1; pull after the approval.

If a touched asset was updated, deleted, or created on the instance since its baseline, the server rejects the **whole push** without applying anything. The CLI lists every conflicting asset with its current revision, whether that revision is its delete, who wrote it and when, then prints a scoped pull command. A key that may not read an asset is told its name only:

```sh
catalyst config pull --only skill:support_review --only agent:assistant
```

Commit or stash local edits in git before running that command: pull overwrites the selected files and removes selected assets deleted on the instance. Re-apply your edits to the pulled content, review with `diff`, and push again. There is no automatic content merge or conflict resolution.

`diff` labels assets **changed locally**, **remote newer**, or **conflict** when both sides changed. Remote-newer assets are not local updates. A full pull refreshes all written asset baselines and the manifest's default agent; `pull --only` refreshes only the selected assets. The default-agent pointer is guarded only when you change it locally. Resolving a default-agent conflict requires a full pull.

State files from an older CLI remain readable, but their global version is not a per-asset baseline. Pull before a guarded push.

CLI and server ship together. The addresses the CLI used before, `/api/v1/instance/config/export`, `/import` and `/validate`, are gone: an older CLI is answered `404` with the sentence to upgrade it. This CLI against an older server reports that the instance does not serve the asset operations it uses. `push` and `validate` need the instance on the release of this CLI or later: they send the batch to `assets.sync_check` first, where the instance checks it and writes nothing, and against an instance that has `assets.sync` without the check they say so and write nothing.

The canonical skill package layout is:

```text
skills/support_review/
├── SKILL.md
└── references/
    ├── escalation.md
    └── response-format.json
```

The CLI recursively includes `.md`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.yaml`, and `.yml` resources below each matched skill directory. It validates them as UTF-8 text, includes them in pull/diff/push, and rejects unsupported files instead of silently dropping them. Resource paths are normalized relative paths; absolute paths, traversal, duplicate paths, and a second `SKILL.md` resource are invalid. The working copy carries a skill's text files only. A skill with other files, such as images or scripts, is written from its folder with `catalyst skill put --from <folder>` or the asset API; see [A skill as a folder of files](#a-skill-as-a-folder-of-files).

A working copy holds the instance's [guardrails](#guardrails-as-assets) where `catalyst.yaml` lists their files under `guardrails`, such as `guardrails/*/guardrail.yaml`; each is a folder with its `guardrail.yaml` and, for a `model_judge` check, its instruction in `check.md`. Without that list, pull, diff and `push --prune` leave the instance's guardrails alone. `pull` brings the draft and `--only guardrail:<name>` selects one. Guardrails are no part of a release: after the `assets.sync` batch of agents and skills, `push` writes each changed guardrail as its next draft with `assets.put` against the revision of its last pull, and `push --prune` deletes one with `assets.delete`, so the key needs `config_assets:write` and the instance the module `assetManagement`. `validate` leaves guardrails to the instance's check at that write. Publishing stays a step of its own, and the guardrails of release config are never part of a working copy.

The front matter of `SKILL.md` holds `title`, `description` and, optionally, `name`, `summary` and `starters`. The two texts have different readers:

- `description` is for the agent. It says when to use the skill.
- `summary` is for people. It is one sentence on one line, at most 120 characters, that says what an agent with the skill knows how to do, such as "Knows how to write short, easy sentences in German and English." The agent editor and the Skills list show it under the title. A skill without a summary shows its title alone.

A skill is instructions the agent follows. It adds no tools, so a summary never names something only a tool can do.

`starters` are first requests the empty chat offers under the composer for an agent that has the skill. A skill carries at most two:

```yaml
starters:
  - title:
      en: Check an invoice
      de: Rechnung prüfen
    hint:
      en: Required details and tax rate
      de: Pflichtangaben und Steuersatz
    prompt:
      en: "Check this invoice for the required details and the right tax rate:"
      de: "Prüfe diese Rechnung auf Pflichtangaben und den richtigen Steuersatz:"
    tools:
      - workspace.read_file
```

- `title` and the optional `hint` are one line of at most 60 characters each. `prompt` is the text that fills the composer when the starter is chosen. Nothing is sent until the person sends it. Each of the three is one text or one text per language (`en`, `de`).
- `tools` is optional. A starter shows only for an agent that holds every tool it names, so it never offers what the agent cannot do.
- The chat shows at most four starters for an agent, the skills in the order the agent lists them. An agent whose skills carry none shows the empty chat as before.

The server URL can come from a named `catalyst.yaml` instance or directly from `--instance https://catalyst.example.com`. The CLI signs in one of two ways:

- **A person** runs `catalyst login --instance <url>` once and confirms the code in the browser, under **Settings > You > API keys** (German: **Einstellungen › Du › API-Schlüssel**). The CLI saves a personal key that acts as that person. This needs the module `personalApiKeys`. See [Log in](/configure/cli/#log-in).
- **Automation**, such as a CI job, sets `CATALYST_API_KEY`. The variable wins over a saved key.

```sh
export CATALYST_API_KEY='the-one-time-value-from-api-access'
catalyst config diff --instance production
```

Create the key for automation once, as a superadmin, under **Settings > Instance > API access**:

1. Create a service principal such as `Catalyst CLI` with `config_assets.read` and `config_assets.release`.
2. Create a key restricted to `config_assets:read` and `config_assets:release`. A push is a release only with both: the right on the principal and the release scope on the key. Under a key with `config_assets:write` instead, the same principal syncs as any writer does, inside one Namespace and within the editing limits.
3. Copy the secret when it is shown once and expose it as `CATALYST_API_KEY` in the operator environment or CI secret store.

For a local development instance, one script of the client repository does these steps:

```sh
pnpm config:local-key
```

The script calls `catalyst-local-key --instance <url>`, a command of the private `client-assembly` package. It is not part of the public `catalyst` tool, because it reads the release config and its secrets. It signs in as the seeded superadmin of the development config (`config/app.yaml`, or `--config <file>`), creates the service principal `Local config CLI` and a key with the two config scopes, and writes the key as `CATALYST_API_KEY` into `.env` (`--write-env <file>`, `--env-name <variable>`). The key is not printed. A later call reuses the principal and replaces the key in the file, so run it again after a database reset. The command takes the address of the instance as a URL and refuses any host other than `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `::1`, and any config whose environment is not `development`.

The CLI sends the API key only to `POST /api/v1/auth/access-token`, then uses the returned short-lived access token for config operations. It refuses to send an API key over plain HTTP except to `localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, or `::1`; remote instances must use HTTPS. A key belongs to a service principal but is independently named, audited, expirable, and revocable. Create separate keys for developer machines and CI jobs so they can be rotated without disrupting one another.

Do not pass the key on the command line or put it in `catalyst.yaml` or `.catalyst-state.json`. A key that `catalyst login` saved is kept in `~/.config/catalyst/credentials.json`, readable by you alone; [The key](/configure/cli/#the-key) says more.

The exchange needs `SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET` set on the server; without it the instance has no API access and the exchange answers 404. A personal key is exchanged at the same address. A CLI with neither `CATALYST_API_KEY` nor a saved key stops before it sends a request and says to run `catalyst login` or set the variable; `CATALYST_SERVER_CREDENTIAL` and `CHAT_SERVER_CREDENTIAL` are not read.

## Skills that ship with the release

Some skills come with the release rather than with a working copy: the platform's documentation (`platform-docs`), `workflow-authoring` where Workflows are on, and the skills a capability of the deployment ships, such as `spreadsheets`, `documents`, `presentations` and `pdf` with the artifact helpers. The API process stores each at start as a read-only skill marked as the platform's, with its own icon, and only where the instance has the tools the skill names. No pull brings one, no diff shows one and no push writes or deletes one; an agent lists one in `skillNames` like any other skill.

The name of a shipped skill is taken. A write of a skill of the instance's own under that name is refused, and a start that finds one, because the release ships a skill the instance already holds as its own, stops with the name of the skill. Remove the instance copy with `catalyst config push` while the previous release still runs: pull, delete the skill's folder, take its name out of the agents' `skillNames`, `push --prune`. Then start the release, and add the name to the agents again with a pull and a push. The start never deletes a skill of the instance's own.

## A skill as a folder of files

A skill follows the public Agent Skills convention, so a folder taken unchanged from a public skill library saves, reads and round-trips byte for byte: `SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter and Markdown, and whatever lies beside it, commonly below `scripts/`, `references/` and `assets/`, and also files at the root such as `LICENSE.txt` or `reference.md`. The asset API writes and reads the whole folder: `assets.put` with `files` (each `{ path, text }` or `{ path, base64 }`, `SKILL.md` among them) and `assets.get` with `files=true`, which answers every file with its hash and its content as it was written.

**Frontmatter.** `name` and `description` are required; a file without a `name` takes the name of the asset. `title` is optional: where it is absent the skill is shown under the first Markdown heading of its content, or else under its name with spaces for hyphens and a capital first letter. `summary` and `starters` are read as fields of the skill, as before. Every other key (`license`, `metadata`, `allowed-tools`, `compatibility`, anything else) is kept as it is, returned as `frontmatter` of the config, and read by nothing; a `frontmatter` of a config that holds one of the skill's own fields is refused. The file is stored as its bytes, so nothing reorders or reformats it.

**Names.** Every name of the convention is accepted (lowercase letters, digits and hyphens), and so is what a skill here could always be named: letters, digits, dots, underscores and hyphens, starting with a letter or a digit. A write of a skill whose name is outside the convention or longer than 64 characters, or whose description is longer than 1,024, is answered with a warning (`skill_name_not_portable`, `skill_description_not_portable`) and is not refused.

**Files.** Any normalized relative path is a file of the skill. A file whose extension says script or text (`.py`, `.js`, `.mjs`, `.ts`, `.sh`, `.rb`, `.md`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml`, `.xml`, `.html`, `.css`, `.csv`) is UTF-8; every other file is bytes.

The config of a skill stays where its text is read from: `content` from `SKILL.md`, and `resources` for every text file with a resource extension (`.md`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml`) outside `scripts/`, at whatever path it lies. Every other file is kept in the file set of the revision, and the config names it in `files`, an index of `path`, `sha256`, `bytes` and `mediaType` without content. So a skill that is text alone has the config it always had, `read_skill` and a proposal of an agent work on it unchanged, and a write of the config alone (a release sync, the interface, an approved proposal) changes the text and leaves the other files and the further frontmatter of the skill where they are. Reverting to a revision brings its files back with it. What a caller sends as `files` in a config is not read; `frontmatter` is, and an empty one clears it.

A folder is refused with the path and a reason of its own:

| Reason | What is refused |
| --- | --- |
| `skill_manifest_missing`, `skill_manifest_invalid` | no `SKILL.md`, or one whose frontmatter does not read or lacks a description |
| `skill_frontmatter_alias`, `skill_frontmatter_too_deep`, `skill_frontmatter_too_large` | a frontmatter that uses a YAML anchor with an alias or a merge key, nests deeper than 8 levels, or holds more than 8,192 characters beside the fields of the skill |
| `skill_path_invalid`, `skill_path_duplicate` | a path that escapes the folder or is not normalized, is longer than 240 characters or has a segment longer than 100, a `SKILL.md` below the root; two paths that differ in case alone, a path that is the folder of another one |
| `skill_file_not_text` | a file whose extension says script or text and whose bytes are no UTF-8 |
| `skill_file_executable` | a compiled program by its first bytes (ELF, Mach-O, and PE by both of its headers), whatever its name |
| `skill_file_lfs_pointer` | a Git LFS pointer in place of the file |
| `skill_file_too_large` | a file over 2 MiB |
| `files_too_large`, a schema issue on `files` | more than 8 MiB in all, more than 500 files: the limits of every write of files of the API, which are the skill's too |
| `files_unavailable` | a file the config cannot hold, on an instance without a `files` object store |

The two limits of a whole folder are answered by the API's general limits of a write of files, before any file is decoded and for every kind alike, so a call over one costs nothing; the skill's own `skill_too_large` and `skill_too_many_files` name the same numbers and answer a caller that reaches the rule another way. A YAML anchor with an alias is refused outright in a frontmatter, as in `store.yaml`, `workflow.yaml`, `app.yaml` and an App's action files: a reader answers an alias as the object its anchor made, so a few lines of nested aliases are a value of any size, and no file the platform reads needs one.

An instance without a `files` object store holds skills as their text, as before. An agent's proposal stays with instruction text: it creates and changes no file below `scripts/` and no file that is not a text resource. The audit event of a write of a folder names each file by path, hash and size and holds no content. `read_skill` does not list the other files yet, and an agent's workspace does not hold them yet.

## Interactive editing and field ownership

Agent `name` is the stable technical identifier used by config references and
agent selection. Use `displayName` for the user-facing name and an optional
localized `description` for the short explanation beneath it in the agent
selector. `displayName` and `description` accept a plain string or an `en`/`de`
map. Keep `welcomeMessage` and `welcomeSubtitle` for the conversation's empty
state.

Two boolean release-config settings decide what the chat shows of its agents.
`ui.showAgentName` is `true` by default and puts the selected agent's name
beside its icon on the start page; with `false` the start page shows the icon
alone. In a conversation the chat always shows the icon alone, which opens the
selector when the pointer is on it. `ui.showAgentDescriptions` is `true` by
default and lists each description in the selector; with `false`, or for an
agent without a description, the selector shows only the display name.

The **Agents** page, the row under New chat in the main rail, shows every agent
a person may use in the open workspace as a card: the agent mark, the display
