name, the description in two lines at most, and **Start chat**. Start chat
opens a new conversation with that agent selected, where its starter prompts
wait. The card always shows the description, whatever
`ui.showAgentDescriptions` says, and it marks the workspace's default agent. A
person who may read agents in Studio also finds **Edit in Studio** on each card.
A person who may create one finds **New agent** in the page head, when
`allowAgentCreation` is on and the person holds the right to write one: it opens
the dialog that names the agent on the page itself, and **Continue** leads to the
new agent's page in Studio, where it is written. Cancel stays on the page.

People with the `config_assets.write` permission, or with a grant in a Namespace, edit assets in [Studio](/configure/build/). The module `assetManagement` turns that on, and release config decides how much of an agent is interactively editable:

```yaml
modules:
  assetManagement:
    enabled: true

administration:
  agentConfiguration:
    editableAgentFields:
      - displayName
      - description
      - welcomeMessage
      - welcomeSubtitle
      - instructions
```

Fields outside `editableAgentFields` are owned by the CLI workflow: the UI shows them read-only and the server rejects interactive writes that change them. `catalyst config push` requires the separate `config_assets.release` permission and may change everything.

Five agent fields are not governed by `editableAgentFields`: `modelBindingId`, `reasoningEffort`, `fastMode`, `userSelectableModelBindingIds`, and `modelReasoningEfforts`. They are editable exactly when the caller holds `agent_models.manage`, and read-only otherwise. Listing `modelBindingId` or `reasoningEffort` in `editableAgentFields` is still accepted but has no effect.

One exception: a Namespace can carry a list of allowed model bindings. A user who may write agents in such a Namespace sets `modelBindingId` to a binding on that list without holding `agent_models.manage`. A binding that is not on the list is refused for every writer. An agent there that names a provider or no model is refused unless the writer holds `agent_models.manage`. The other four fields keep the rule above.

`fastMode` (boolean, default `false`) runs the agent on the provider's priority tier, billed at the rate card's fast rates. It is valid only when the agent's model binding declares `supportsFastMode` in release config. The CLI writes `fastMode: true` to the agent YAML and omits the key when it is off.

### Models users may choose

`userSelectableModelBindingIds` (list of binding ids, default empty) names the models chat users may pick for this agent instead of its own:

```yaml
modelBindingId: primary
reasoningEffort: high
userSelectableModelBindingIds:
  - fast
modelReasoningEfforts:
  fast: low
```

- Every id must be a binding agents may use (`agentSelectable` not `false` in release config); anything else is a validation error when the list is saved or pushed. The binding-level `userSelectable` key has no effect. The agent's own `modelBindingId` is always available and need not be listed.
- Studio shows the models in the agent's **Model** section: **Default model** picks `modelBindingId`, and a tick per model under **Models people can choose in chat** fills this list. The default is always offered and has no tick of its own. Changing the default leaves the other ticks as they are, so tick the previous default to keep offering it.
- The composer shows a model picker with the agent's own model first, followed by the list. With an empty list there is no model to choose; the picker then appears only if the agent's own model offers a choice of reasoning effort, see [what the model picker shows](/configure/release-config/#what-the-model-picker-shows). Switching the agent updates the options and falls back to the new agent's own model when it does not offer the current pick.
- The server rejects a run that requests a model the resolved agent does not offer.
- An id whose binding is later removed or set to `agentSelectable: false` is ignored instead of failing the agent. It stays in the stored config until the list is next changed.
- Reasoning effort is set per model. `reasoningEffort` is the effort of the agent's own model. `modelReasoningEfforts` maps a listed binding id to the effort for runs where a user picked that model; without an entry the binding's own default applies. The agent's `reasoningEffort` is never applied to a model the user picked instead. Every key must be in `userSelectableModelBindingIds`; anything else is a validation error.
- In Studio each model in use (the default and the ticked ones) has its own reasoning-effort select. When the default changes, each effort stays with its model.
- The CLI omits both keys from the agent YAML when they are empty.

Set `enabled: true`, leave `editableAgentFields` empty, and set all interactive mutation flags (including `allowSkillEditing`) to `false` for a readable, release-controlled Config tab. Agents, complete skill packages, and revision history remain inspectable while create, save, delete, default-change, and restore controls are hidden. Enabling skill editing later exposes the same atomic package through a root/reference editor; no storage migration is required.

Optimistic concurrency protects both surfaces, per asset: a save in Studio carries the revision the page loaded, and a save after somebody else's write of the same asset shows a notice that names who saved first and when, with "Load the newer version" and "Open history", instead of overwriting. A save of another asset never blocks it.

## Agent skill changes

Agents can propose small changes to their assigned skills through
`propose_skill_change`. Enable the policy in release config, enable the tool
in `tools`, and add it to the agent's `toolNames` alongside `read_skill`:

```yaml
administration:
  agentConfiguration:
    agentSkillChanges:
      enabled: true
      allowSkillCreation: true
```

Both switches default to `false`. Remove `propose_skill_change` from every agent's `toolNames` before setting `enabled` back to `false`. This policy is independent of interactive
skill editing and editable agent fields. Any user of an agent with the tool
can propose a change. Skills are shared by all users; proposals must never
include personal or customer-specific data.

A proposal stays pending until someone with `agent_skills.approve` approves it.
Admins and superadmins hold this permission by default; individual grants and
revocations also apply. Reviewers see whole paragraphs for replacements and
the added text for additions, as source text exactly as the agent will read it. Approval applies the operations to the current skill. A request becomes
superseded only when its operations no longer apply cleanly, or a proposed new
skill already exists. Independent changes to the same skill can both be approved. The original preview remains available in history.

Approval writes a skill revision with the approving user as actor and the
request ID and summary as provenance. Creating a skill adds it to the proposing
agent in the same atomic write. A proposal for a new skill may also carry its
supporting files, such as `references/checklist.md`, as `create_resource`
operations after `create_skill`. Proposals are limited to 20,000 characters per
operation text, 60,000 per root or resource, and 30 resources per skill.

The same permission allows reverting an approved request. Revert writes a new
revision restoring the previous content and records the reverting user. It is
blocked if the skill has newer revisions, and where a guardrail on
`asset.before_write` blocks the restored content; the request then stays
approved. Reverting a newly created skill
removes it and its agent reference together; other agents' references must be
removed first. Reverting retains the original approval and proposal history.

## The asset API

Every asset is read and written at one address, `/api/v1/assets/{kind}/{name}`, where `kind` is a registered kind such as `agent` or `skill`. Studio uses these operations, and so can a script or an outside editor. Each changing call is one Operation Run with its actor and outcome. A read is checked the same way and leaves a run only when it is refused or fails. The [API reference](/reference/api/) lists the fields.

| Operation                 | Address                                      | Right                |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| `assets.list`             | `GET /api/v1/assets/{kind}`                  | `<kind>.read`        |
| `assets.get`              | `GET /api/v1/assets/{kind}/{name}`           | `<kind>.read`        |
| `assets.put`              | `PUT /api/v1/assets/{kind}/{name}`           | `<kind>.write`       |
| `assets.delete`           | `POST /api/v1/assets/{kind}/{name}/delete`   | `<kind>.delete`      |
| `assets.revisions.list`   | `GET /api/v1/assets/{kind}/{name}/revisions` | `<kind>.read`        |
| `assets.revert`           | `POST /api/v1/assets/{kind}/{name}/revert`   | `<kind>.write`       |
| `assets.validate`         | `POST /api/v1/assets/{kind}/validate`        | `<kind>.read`        |
| `assets.publish` | `POST /api/v1/assets/{kind}/{name}/publish` | `<kind>.publish` |
| `assets.discard_draft` | `POST /api/v1/assets/{kind}/{name}/discard-draft` | `<kind>.write` |
| `assets.sync`             | `POST /api/v1/assets/sync`                   | per item             |
| `assets.sync_check`       | `POST /api/v1/assets/sync/check`             | per item             |
| `platform.context.get`    | `GET /api/v1/context`                        | any signed-in caller |
| `platform.references.get` | `GET /api/v1/context/references`             | a right on any kind  |

The right is decided for the one asset: an instance right, a grant in the Namespace of its name, or a grant on the asset. `assets.list` answers only the assets the caller may read, as summaries without content, in the order of their names. It filters by `prefix` (a name prefix such as a Namespace) and by `text` (a part of the name, in any case), and pages with `limit` and `cursor`. It is built for up to 10,000 assets of a kind.

A write names the revision it was made against, for every asset it writes. `assets.put` with a number in `expectedRevision` replaces the asset at that revision; with `null` it creates the asset and is refused when the name is taken. `assets.delete` and `assets.revert` take a number. A write that leaves `expectedRevision` out is answered `428 PRECONDITION_REQUIRED` with `details.assets`, the assets it named no revision for, and changes nothing: no call overwrites what it did not read.

When the asset stands at another revision the call answers `412 REVISION_CONFLICT` and changes nothing; read the asset again and repeat the call. `details.conflicts` holds one entry per stale asset with its `kind` and `name`. A caller who may read the asset's history, the right `assets.revisions.list` asks, is also told `currentRevision` (`null` where the name was never stored), `deleted: true` where that revision is the delete of the asset, and `changedBy` and `changedAt` of that revision. Everyone else is told the name they sent and nothing more.

A write is refused for the first of these that applies, in this order: a right the caller lacks, on the asset and beside it (the right to manage model settings, the right on the instance for a change of its default agent); then the missing `expectedRevision` with `428`; then the stale revision with `412`. A caller without a right is told that and nothing of the revision.

A caller who may write or delete an asset and may not read it is told nothing the instance holds of it. A delete of an asset that is not there, of one that is deleted and of one at another revision are answered the same `412` with the name alone, where a reader is answered `404` for the first two. A name that another owner holds, such as a workspace, is answered that `412` too, where a reader of that asset is answered `422` with `details.reason` `invalid_scope`. That a stored asset takes no write at all (`read_only_origin`) is told only against the revision the asset is at. One thing cannot be kept back, since a name is unique on the instance: a create with `expectedRevision: null` of a name that is taken is refused with the name alone, so its caller learns that the name is used, and not by whom, at which revision, or whether it is active or deleted. An App's id is answered `409` `app_id_taken` in the same case.

The revision a write answers is the one that write was given, not what the asset is at when the answer is built. A write that was committed is answered as made even when its audit row could not be written: the failure is logged with the correlation id.

A deleted asset keeps its name, its history and the revision of its delete. `null` creates only a name that was never stored: creating a deleted asset again names the revision of its delete, which the conflict tells to who may read it. An App is the exception: deleting it removes it with its files, and its name is free again. The four writing operations answer the new `revision`, the configuration `version` and a list `warnings`, which is empty today.

`assets.sync` applies up to 200 puts and deletes for one registered Namespace, named by its prefix in `namespace`. Each item is checked like the single call: the right on that asset, its revision, its content. An item may also carry `expectedAssetId`, the id of the asset its revision was read from; where the instance holds another asset under the name the batch is refused with `409 CONFLICT` and `details.reason` `asset_replaced`. Each applied item answers the `id` and the `revision` it wrote. One put item holds at most 2 MiB as JSON (`ASSET_SYNC_ITEM_MAX_BYTES`). Every item carries `expectedRevision` as the single call does, and the answers are the same two: `428` with `details.assets` when an item names none, `412` with `details.conflicts` when an item is stale. The rights are decided first, those beside the right on the item included, so a caller without a right learns nothing of a revision. The whole set is validated against what the transaction's lock protects: a write that another write made invalid between its check and its commit is refused. An asset the batch does not name is not read for its revision and never refuses the batch. The batch is applied completely or not at all, in one transaction: an agent may name a skill the same batch creates. A kind with a draft and a published revision has its draft moved by a put; the published revision and the version of the asset set stay. An App is refused as an item, since its files are built per write. When any item is refused the answer carries `details.items` with one entry per item, `refused` with its error or `not_applied`, and nothing is written. An item whose name does not start with the prefix is refused for every caller, an administrator included. The right on every item is decided before the instance's policy is asked, and a policy setting narrowed to a kind or to a Namespace applies to a batch that names an asset of that kind or in that Namespace.

A holder of `config_assets.release` whose key carries the scope `config_assets:release` may leave `namespace` out. That batch is a release, which is what `catalyst config push` sends: it may name any agent or skill of the instance, holds up to 2,000 items, may carry `defaultAgentName` and `expectedDefaultAgentName`, is not bound by `editableAgentFields` or the right for model settings, and is checked against the whole stored set instead of what its key may read. A delete of an asset that is not there is answered `absent` and refuses nothing, unless the asset was created meanwhile. Every batch answers `hiddenAgentNames` for agents it wrote that no workspace offers.

`assets.sync_check` takes the body of a sync, runs every check of it and writes nothing. It answers `{ "valid": true }` or the refusal the sync would answer.

A request body over one megabyte is answered `400` with `details.reason` `body_too_large`. `assets.sync` and `assets.sync_check` take up to 20 MiB (`ASSET_SYNC_BODY_MAX_BYTES`).

A definition is checked against what its caller may read. A reference to an asset the caller may not read, such as a skill of another Namespace, is answered like a reference to an asset that does not exist, by `assets.validate` and by a write. An asset may always refer to the assets beside it in its own Namespace, and a reference an asset already carries is kept when somebody edits it who may not read its target. A name with a NUL byte is refused with `422`.

The writing operations and `assets.sync` belong to the module `assetManagement` and follow the same rules as edits in Studio: `editableAgentFields`, the lists of a Namespace, and the rights for the default agent and for model settings. Only a release, as described above, is exempt, so `catalyst config push` also works where interactive editing is narrowed or off.

`platform.context.get` tells a caller where it is: the instance, its release, the asset kinds with their rights, and the Namespaces in which the caller may do something. It answers a person and a service principal. An action is named only when the credential's scopes allow it: `config_assets:read` for reading, `config_assets:write` for writing and deleting.

A new agent starts in the workspace it is made in. `assets.put` takes `availableIn`: `{ "workspaceId": "…" }`, a Shared Workspace the caller is a member of, or `"all"`, which needs the right to write agents on the whole instance. A call of an agent in a conversation is made in that conversation's workspace without naming it. A new agent made in no Shared Workspace is hidden everywhere, and the answer carries the warning `agent_hidden`. `assets.sync` without the release right is made in no workspace, so the agents it creates start hidden and its answer names them in `hiddenAgentNames`. A write of an agent that exists refuses `availableIn`: its availability is set with `assets.set_availability`.

`assets.list` and `assets.get` mark the instance's default agent with `isDefault: true` and leave the field out on every other asset. `assets.get` of an agent also carries its `availability`, the workspaces it is offered in, when one is stored.

`assets.set_default` (`POST /api/v1/assets/{kind}/default` with `{ "name": "…" }`) makes one asset the instance's default of its kind, and `assets.set_availability` (`PUT /api/v1/assets/{kind}/{name}/availability`) sets the workspaces one asset is offered in. Only the agent kind takes either today. Both are Operation Runs of the module `assetManagement`, and both need the right to write the kind on the whole instance: a grant in a Namespace or on one asset does not answer it, and a deny on the named asset refuses. The default also needs `allowDefaultAgentChange`. A changed availability moves the version of the asset set, and the next run that starts reads it. Either call may name what it was decided against: `expectedAssetId`, the id of the asset as it was read, and for the availability `expectedAvailability`, the availability as it was read or `null` for none. Where the instance holds something else by then, the call answers `409` and writes nothing, which matters for a call that waited for an approval. Without the fields the call replaces what is stored.

`platform.references.get` answers what a definition may refer to on this instance: the model providers and bindings, the reasoning efforts, the enabled tools, and the tools whose module is off. It answers a caller who holds at least one right on an asset kind, on the instance or in one Namespace, with a credential that carries `config_assets:read` and the scope of that right. It writes no Operation Run, so an editor may read it each time it opens a definition.

### Apps: a draft and a published revision

An App is the asset kind `app`, on an instance with the module `apps` on. Two things set it apart from an agent or a skill, and the kind list of `platform.context.get` reports both: its `lifecycle` is `draft_published`, and its `representation` is `files`.

A write moves the draft and nothing else. The revision the members of the App's workspace are served is the published one, and only `assets.publish` moves it. `assets.list` and `assets.get` answer `draftRevision` and `publishedRevision`; the second is absent before the first publish. `assets.publish` names the revision number to publish. Publishing an earlier number is the way back, so `assets.revert` answers `use_publish` for such a kind. `assets.discard_draft` moves the draft back to the published revision. The discarded revision keeps its number and can still be published, and the next write takes the highest number plus one. A draft write leaves the configuration `version` as it is.

`assets.put` for an App carries `files`, the whole source set of the App with its `app.yaml`, and no `config`: `[{ "path": "index.html", "text": "..." }, { "path": "logo.png", "base64": "..." }]`. One call carries at most 8 MiB of decoded files (`ASSET_PUT_FILES_MAX_BYTES`). The instance builds the files as it builds a Page and waits up to 60 seconds. A set that does not build answers `422` with `details.issues`, each with its file and line. A build that did not end in time answers `504 TIMEOUT` with `build_timeout`; nothing was written, and the `Idempotency-Key` of that call is used up, so send the write again under a new key. In both cases the draft is the revision it was. The answer of a write names `fileSetId` and, for every source file, `path`, `sha256` and `bytes`. The Operation Run keeps those and never the contents. Without `expectedRevision` the call creates the App in the workspace named by `workspaceId`; an App belongs to one workspace, and a write without one answers `scope_unavailable`. `assets.sync` takes no App. Where a policy holds `assets.put` for an approval, a write whose input is above 256 KiB (`HELD_OPERATION_INPUT_MAX_BYTES`) cannot be held: it answers `422` with the reason `input_too_large_to_hold` before a file is stored or built. `assets.publish` answers `422` with `revision_files_removed` for a revision whose built files are not stored, and the published revision stays the one it was.

`assets.get` reads one revision of an App: `revision` is `draft` (the default), `published` or a revision number, and `contentRevision` in the answer names the revision that is shown, while `revision` stays the number of the draft that a write names. With `files=true` the answer carries the source files of that revision in the order of their paths, each with `path`, `contentType`, `sha256`, `bytes` and its content as `text` where the bytes are UTF-8 text and as `base64` otherwise, so the files of an answer can be put again as they are. One answer carries at most 8 MiB of files (`ASSET_GET_FILES_MAX_BYTES`); for a larger set it carries the index without contents and `filesOmitted: true`. The published revision needs `app.read`; the draft and a numbered revision need `app.write` or `app.publish`. A read that names no revision answers the draft to whoever may read it. Everybody else who holds `app.read` or `app.use` is answered the published view: the published revision's config, `revision`, `contentRevision` and `publishedRevision` all naming that revision, and no `draftRevision`. `assets.list` shows a holder of `app.use` alone the same view of every published App, with the title it was published under, and no App that has only a draft. Through `app.use` no files are read. `assets.revisions.list` holds every draft and needs `app.write` or `app.publish`. `published` before the first publish answers `404` with `not_published`, an unknown number `revision_unknown`, and a revision whose files are not stored `revision_files_removed`. For a kind without files `files=true` answers `422` with `no_files`, and any `revision` but `draft` answers `no_draft`.

`apps.create_from_page` (`POST /api/v1/apps`) saves the newest revision of a Page as an App with a draft. It copies the files, so the App stays when the conversation of the Page is deleted. The source files become the first commit of the App's git repository, and the audit event `app.created` names the asset, the revision and the commit. The commit is made by the workspace command worker with the git of the runner image: on a runner image older than the release the call is refused with `409` and `details.reason` `runner_image_outdated`, and without a worker with `commit_unavailable`. The revision records the Page as its `origin`: `{ "kind": "page", "conversationId", "pageId", "fileSetNumber" }`. The Page an App is updated from is the one its newest revision with such an origin names.

`apps.update_from_page` (`POST /api/v1/apps/{app}/update-from-page`) writes the newest revision of that Page as the next draft revision of the App. It needs `app.write` on the App and read access to the Page, and it names `expectedRevision`, the draft revision the caller last read. Nothing is published, and the App keeps its title. The update is the next commit of the App's repository, made as the commit of a save is and refused as one is. An App that is updated from another Page or from none answers `409` with `details.reason: "app_not_from_page"`; that includes every App saved before a release with this operation. With `"link": true` such an App is written too and is this Page's from then on; the audit event `config_asset.updated` of that write carries `pageLinked: true`. A draft that moved since answers `412 REVISION_CONFLICT`, and a call with the new number replaces it.

`apps.get_from_page` (`GET /api/v1/conversations/{conversationId}/pages/{pageId}/app`) answers the App of a Page, or `null`: among the Apps updated from the Page that the caller may write, the one the caller wrote from it last, and otherwise the one created first. `draftFromPage` is `false` where the draft was last written another way than from this Page. With `?app=<id>` the answer also carries `candidate`: that App where the caller may write it, with `page` saying whether it is updated from `none`, `this` Page, an `other_page` of the conversation or one of an `other_conversation`; `null` otherwise. In the interface the header of a Page with an App offers Update app in place of Save as app, and Save as app under the id of an App the reader may write offers to update that App from the Page.

With the module `apps` on, every conversation offers its agent `page.save`, `page.save_as_app` and the file tools a Page's folder is written with (`workspace.write_file`, and `workspace.edit_file` and `workspace.read_file` where the release enables them), whatever the agent's `toolNames` list; without `workspace.write_file` in the release none of them is offered. The surface beside the chat opens when the first save starts, as the Page building. `page.save_as_app` is the agent's Save as app: it saves the newest revision of a Page of the conversation as an App of the conversation's workspace, with `app.created` as above, and makes the App what the conversation is about. It is refused in a conversation shared with its workspace, as an open is. From then on each built `page.save` of that Page in the conversation also writes the next draft revision of the App, as `apps.update_from_page` does; its answer carries `app` with `saved: true`, the revision and the `warnings` of guardrails that warn about the draft, or `saved: false` with the reason where the draft was written another way since, another Page was put into the App, the person may not write it, a guardrail blocked it or asked for an approval, which this save cannot wait for (the person's Update app on the Page can), or the write failed. The Page is saved either way. What an administrator sets on `assets.put` for an App holds for both tools, as it does for `platform.assets.put`; a setting on `apps.create_from_page` holds for `page.save_as_app`, and one on `apps.update_from_page` for `page.save` in a conversation about an App.

`apps.preview` (`POST /api/v1/apps/{app}/preview`) answers the address a frame loads, for the mode `published` or `draft`, and `interfacePath`, the path of the App in the interface. `assets.delete` removes an App with its revisions and its files; its Operation Runs and audit events stay.

The address `apps.preview` answers is the credential of the frame it is loaded in: the sandboxed frame has no origin and cannot send the session, so whoever holds the address is served its files. The address names the person it was made for and one file set, is valid for one hour, and that person's right is asked again at most every 30 seconds. A browser keeps a file no longer than the address is valid. Treat the address as a secret of that person and do not pass it on; share the App by its path in the interface (`interfacePath`).

| Right | Who holds it | What it allows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app.read`, `app.write`, `app.delete` | admin, superadmin | Read, write and delete Apps. A writer is shown the draft. |
| `app.publish` | admin, superadmin | Move the published revision. A credential needs the scope `config_assets:publish`, which `config_assets:write` does not include. |
| `app.use` | every member of the App's workspace | Open the published revision, and see it in `assets.list` and `assets.get`. A member is never shown a draft. |

## Guardrails as assets

A guardrail is a check bound to a before-event, with the outcome of a hit, as in [release config](/configure/release-config/#guardrails). Beside the floor of release config, guardrails are written as assets of the kind `guardrail`. A working copy keeps one as `guardrails/<name>/guardrail.yaml`, with the instruction of a `model_judge` check in `check.md` beside it:

```yaml
# guardrails/no-iban/guardrail.yaml
name: no-iban
displayName: No IBAN in skills
on: asset.before_write
filter:
  kind: skill
check:
  kind: pattern
  pattern: "(?i)\\bDE\\d{2}(?:\\s?\\d{4}){4}\\s?\\d{2}\\b"
  reason: Skills hold no bank account.
outcome: block
```

A guardrail belongs to the instance or to one Collaboration Workspace (`--workspace <id>` on `catalyst guardrail put`). A write makes a draft, which checks nothing. `catalyst guardrail test <name> --text <content>` (or `--from <file>`, `--asset skill:<name>`) answers what the draft would say, and `catalyst guardrail dry-run <name>` counts what it would have blocked, asked an approval for or warned on in the last 14 days, by actions and by people, never naming anyone. A dry run checks again the writes and publishes of assets of that period, a `model_judge` at most the newest 200; calls of operations and requests for an approval are counted and not checked, since their content is not kept. Neither keeps a hit. Testing needs `guardrail.write`, and a judge's model usage counts for the guardrail's scope: a workspace guardrail's for its workspace.

`catalyst guardrail publish <name> --revision <n>` shows the dry run first. A first publish that would have blocked anything goes ahead only with `--confirm <n>` naming that number; publish a draft with the outcome `warn` first to watch it. Publishing takes `guardrail.publish` at the guardrail's scope. Administrators hold it at instance scope; an administrator grants it for one Shared Workspace (`permissions.grant`, scope `workspace`) to let someone set that workspace's rules. No workspace right carries it. `catalyst guardrail unpublish <name>` stops a guardrail; its draft stays. Publish and unpublish are audited as `guardrail.published` and `guardrail.unpublished` with the guardrail, the revision, its scope and who.

A workspace guardrail answers the events of its workspace only. Its filter may narrow them, by `kind`, `operation`, `origin`, `agent` and `workspace`, and a filter that names another workspace, an agent the workspace does not offer or an operation of an asset another workspace owns is refused at save. Every guardrail that applies runs, from the floor, the instance and the event's workspace, and the strictest answer wins. Guardrail assets never run on writes, publishes or deletes of guardrails, nor on their tests; only the floor does, so no published guardrail can stop the change of guardrails.

## Permissions

| Permission              | Grants                                                                       | Default roles              |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `config_assets.read`    | View assets and revisions                                                    | admin, superadmin          |
| `config_assets.write`   | Interactive edits within `editableAgentFields`, skill editing, default agent | admin, superadmin          |
| `config_assets.release` | Release synchronization via `catalyst config push`                           | none (service tokens only) |
| `agent_models.manage`   | Interactive changes to an agent's model settings and user-selectable models  | superadmin                 |

Effective permissions resolve from role defaults plus the rights given to one person or service principal on the Users and API access pages, such as `config_assets.write`, or taken away, such as `!config_assets.write`. They are stored as instance-wide grant rows, one per action the key stands for: `config_assets.write` is `agent.write`, `agent.delete`, `skill.write` and `skill.delete`.

Beside these, an administrator can allow or deny one user read, write or delete on agents or skills in a Namespace (a registered name prefix) or on one asset, through the operations under `/api/v1/instance/access`. A deny on an asset belongs to its name: it stays until it is revoked, also when the asset is deleted and created again, and the grant list keeps showing it. Allow rows on an asset are removed when the asset is deleted.

pages.title: Modules
pages.description: Turn an optional feature on or off for a whole instance with one switch.
pages.body:
A module is one optional feature of the product together with everything it contributes: its operations, agent tools, job kinds and screens. Each module has one switch in release config, `modules.<name>.enabled`. The switch applies to the whole instance. It grants no rights: who may use an enabled feature is still decided by roles, permissions and workspace availability.

```yaml
modules:
  documents:
    enabled: true
  resources:
    enabled: true
  assetManagement:
    enabled: true
  userInvitations:
    enabled: false
```

## The Modules

| Module            | What it turns on                                                                                        | Needs                                                                             |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `documents`       | Attached documents: preprocessing, the tools that read them and their page previews.                    | The document processing capability in the client assembly.                        |
| `resources`       | The Resources panel of a conversation.                                                                  | Nothing.                                                                          |
| `assetManagement` | Changing agents and skills in the interface. Running agents and `catalyst config push` work without it. | Nothing. `administration.agentConfiguration` still says what a person may change. |
| `userInvitations` | Inviting a user by an emailed link to set a password.                                                   | A mail sender under `infrastructure.mail` and standalone password sign-in.        |
| `apps`            | Pages an agent builds in a conversation, and Apps: the asset kind `app`, Save as app, the Apps row in the main rail. See [Build an App](/apps/build/). | `executionWorkspaces.enabled`, a running workspace command worker and a runner image of the same release. See [Page builds](/operate/deployment/#page-builds). |
| `connections`     | Connections to outside systems: the asset kind `connection`, its rights and its list in Studio.         | `secretStore.keys` and `egress.allow` once `connections` names a Connection.      |
| `workflows`       | Workflows: the asset kind `workflow`, its runs, schedules and code steps, and the Workflows row in the main rail. | Nothing for steps that call operations. Code steps run in the sandbox of the workspace command worker. |
| `dataStores`      | Data Stores: the asset kind `data_store`, one Postgres database per store, and the operations on its rows. | A key under `secretStore.keys` and a platform database role with `CREATEDB` and `CREATEROLE`. See [Data Stores](/configure/release-config/#data-stores). |
| `knowledge`       | Reserved for Knowledge Bases. It is registered and adds nothing yet.                                     | Nothing.                                                                          |
| `personalApiKeys` | Keys a person issues that act as them, and `catalyst login`. See [the CLI](/configure/cli/).            | Nothing. Off, no personal key signs in; stored keys stay.                         |

The document processing capability is part of the paid capabilities and not in the open repository. The other modules ship with the open platform.

### Connections

A Connection is one configured access to an outside system, stored as an asset of kind `connection`. With the module on, **Studio > Connections** lists the Connections of the instance, and **Settings > Instance > Access** grants `connection.read` and `connection.use`. With the module off, the kind does not exist for any caller: `GET /api/v1/assets/connection` answers `404` with `details.reason: "module_off"`, and stored Connections stay as they are.

A Connection comes from release config: [`connections`](/configure/release-config/#connections) names each one, and the API process writes them into the store when it starts. Such a Connection is read-only on the instance. A put, a revert or a delete of it through the interface, the API or the CLI is refused with `403` and `details.reason: "read_only_origin"`; change it in release config and restart. A Connection of a remote MCP server can also be created on the instance, in **Studio > Connections** (German: **Studio › Verbindungen**) or with `assets.put`; [Studio](/configure/build/#connecting-an-outside-system) walks through it and names the rights. MCP is the only connector type: there is no HTTP connector. Its address must be on [`egress.allow`](/configure/release-config/#egress), or the save is refused with `egress_denied`. Its key is entered once, on the Connection's page or with `connections.set_secret`, never in a chat, and is never shown again; a new key replaces it. Such a Connection is changed and deleted there too, and a delete is refused while an agent carries one of its tools.

A Connection never holds a credential. Its definition holds `secretHandle`, an opaque reference into the Secret Store, and the handle opens nothing by itself. A secret reaches a Connection in exactly one place, the field `secret` of its release config entry, and only as the name of a secret, never as a value. The settings are typed by the connector type: a key the type does not declare is refused, and the type never declares one for a credential. A header or query value that authenticates is produced from the stored secret when a call is made and is no setting.

As a second net, a definition that carries a credential anywhere else is refused: an address with a user name or a password, a header named like a credential, a setting named like a credential whatever stands under it (a text, a number, a list or an object; only a switch such as `requiresToken: true` is kept), an `Authorization` value. That check reads names and shapes and is not the boundary. `displayName` and `description` are free text and are stored and shown as written, so write no credential into them.

A module that a later release adds is off until its entry says otherwise.

## What Off Means

A module that is off is off for every caller and on every surface:

- Each of its operations answers `404 NOT_FOUND` with `details.reason: "module_off"` and the module's name in `details.module`. The caller is authenticated first: a call without a valid credential gets `401` as on any route and learns nothing about modules. The module is checked before any right.
- Its agent tools are not offered to the model and cannot be called, also for an agent that still lists one. A write that adds or changes an agent that names such a tool is refused with a message that names the module. An agent stored before the module was turned off keeps its entry and runs without the tool: the instance starts, and a write to another agent or to a skill is not held up by it. The agent editor shows such an entry as not available, with the module, and lets it be removed.
- Its job kinds are not claimed. Jobs of such a kind that are already queued stay queued. **Settings > Instance > Jobs** shows each with the module it waits for, and `GET /api/v1/instance/jobs` names it in `waitingForModule`. They run when the module is on again.
- Its screens, panels and buttons are absent from the interface.

Turning a module off deletes nothing. Its stored data is there when the module is turned on again.

## Reading The Modules Of An Instance

**Settings > Instance > Modules** (German: **Einstellungen › Instanz › Module**) lists every module the product knows with its state, what it adds and its config key. The page is shown to holders of `audit.view` and changes nothing: the switch is release config. `GET /api/v1/instance/modules` returns the same list. A module whose code is not part of the build is listed as off with `shipped: false`.

## What Is Checked At Startup

The API and every worker resolve the same switches before they open the database or start a service. Startup stops with a message that names the module when:

- `modules` names a module the product does not know,
- a module is enabled but the build ships no code for it, for example `documents` without the document processing capability,
- a module is enabled and a module it requires is off. Nothing is turned on implicitly.

`GET /api/v1/instance/config` lists every module with its state under `modules`.

## Moving From The Old Switches

Before the `modules` section, the four modules were switched by other keys. For one release those keys keep working, and an instance whose config is not changed runs exactly what it ran before:

| Old key                                     | Without the old key the module was             | New key                           |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| `capabilities.documentProcessing.enabled`   | off                                            | `modules.documents.enabled`       |
| `ui.resources.enabled`                      | on                                             | `modules.resources.enabled`       |
| `administration.agentConfiguration.enabled` | off                                            | `modules.assetManagement.enabled` |
| none                                        | on wherever mail and password sign-in were set | `modules.userInvitations.enabled` |

When only the new key is set, it applies. When both are set to the same value, the config loads. When they are set to different values, the config is refused with a message that names both keys; remove the old one.

The release after this one removes the old keys. From then on a module without an entry under `modules` is off. Before that upgrade, write the four switches into `modules` with the state the instance runs today and delete the old keys. The `features` object of `GET /api/v1/instance/config` is derived from `modules` during the same release and leaves with the old keys.

pages.title: Release configuration
pages.description: Use source-controlled config as the source of truth for instance behavior.
pages.body:
Static release config defines the code-deployed ceiling of a client instance. It is version-controlled, validated at startup, and deployed with the client assembly app.

Agents and client skills are separate versioned configuration assets. The Catalyst CLI synchronizes their complete YAML and Markdown working copies with the active instance. Static release config decides which of their fields and operations are additionally editable through interactive administration.

## What Release Config Owns

Release config should cover:

- tool enablement and tool parameters
- model providers and approved model bindings
- which optional features run, as [modules](/configure/modules/)
- capability settings
- interactive agent-configuration policy
- supported locales and default locale
- client branding and theme
- welcome copy, placeholders, and suggested prompts
- retention and deletion policy
- audit retention
- usage budgets and safeguards
- built-in tool enablement

## Example

```yaml
version: 1
clientInstance:
  id: example-support
  displayName: Example Support Chat

modules:
  assetManagement:
    enabled: true

administration:
  agentConfiguration:
    editableAgentFields:
      - displayName
      - welcomeMessage
      - modelBindingId
      - reasoningEffort
      - initialPrompts
    allowAgentCreation: false
    allowAgentDeletion: false
    allowDefaultAgentChange: false
    allowSkillEditing: false

ui:
  clientName: Example Company
  faviconUrl: /favicon.svg
  defaultLocale: en
  supportedLocales: [en, de]
  welcomeMessage:
    en: How can I help with your support case?
    de: Wie kann ich bei deinem Supportfall helfen?
  theme:
    accentColor: "#0f766e"
    backgroundColor: "#f7f7f4"
    surfaceColor: "#ffffff"

retention:
  conversationDays: 90
  expireConversations: true
  extendOnActivity: true
  auditDays: 730
  allowUserDelete: true

usage:
  budget:
    dailySpendLimit: 50
    monthlySpendLimit: 400
    costSafetyMultiplier: 1.3
  safeguards:
    modelCallsPerDay: 1000
    tokensPerDay: 2500000
  costs:
    customer:
      id: example-customer
      version: "2026-07"
      currency: EUR
      models:
        - providerId: openai
          model: gpt-5.5
          uncachedInputPricePerMillionTokens: 5
          cachedInputPricePerMillionTokens: 0.5
          outputPricePerMillionTokens: 30
```

### Retention

| Key                             | Default | Meaning                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `retention.conversationDays`    | `30`    | How long a Conversation is kept, in days.                                                                                                      |
| `retention.expireConversations` | `true`  | `false` keeps every Conversation a user started, whatever its date. Abandoned drafts are still removed.                                        |
| `retention.extendOnActivity`    | `true`  | `true` counts `conversationDays` from the last message a user sent. `false` counts from the creation of the Conversation: a fixed maximum age. |
| `retention.auditDays`           | `365`   | How long audit events are kept.                                                                                                                |
| `retention.allowUserDelete`     | `true`  | Lets users delete their own Conversations.                                                                                                     |

With `extendOnActivity: true`, every message a user sends moves the deletion date to `conversationDays` after that message, and never to an earlier date. Opening, reading, renaming or moving a Conversation, the generated title and background jobs do not move it. A Conversation someone keeps writing in is therefore never deleted for age. Set `extendOnActivity: false` when the instance has promised a maximum age: the date set at creation then stands, whatever is written later.

Changing `conversationDays` or `extendOnActivity` does not rewrite the dates of existing Conversations. A Conversation takes the new period with its next message, when `extendOnActivity` is on.

In its last seven days, or the last half of a period shorter than fourteen days, a Conversation carries a clock in the list, and the open Conversation shows one line above the message field with the deletion date. With `extendOnActivity: true` the line adds that a new message keeps the Conversation.

The conversation Resources panel appears only after a user enters a persisted Conversation. It is the module `resources`; turn it off with `modules.resources.enabled: false` when a deployment must opt out of that surface. [Modules](/configure/modules/) lists every optional feature and its switch.

Daily and monthly spend limits use `usage.costs.customer.currency`. Set it to the invoice currency and express every configured model and web-search price in that same currency.

`costSafetyMultiplier` is a private enforcement buffer. Budget checks multiply the persisted customer billable total by this value, while stored usage records and customer-facing billable costs remain unchanged. It defaults to `1`.

The customer rate card uses exact `providerId` and `model` rows and prices uncached and cached input separately. Its `version` must change when any rate changes. Usage Governance persists the applied rates and billable amount with every new usage event, so changing the active card affects only future usage.

A model row may carry a `fast` block with the same three prices for fast-mode calls:

```yaml
usage:
  costs:
    customer:
      models:
        - providerId: openai
          model: gpt-5.5
          uncachedInputPricePerMillionTokens: 5
          cachedInputPricePerMillionTokens: 0.5
          outputPricePerMillionTokens: 30
          fast:
            uncachedInputPricePerMillionTokens: 10
            cachedInputPricePerMillionTokens: 1
            outputPricePerMillionTokens: 60
```

Every model binding with `supportsFastMode: true` needs these rates; startup validation fails without them. The usage event records both that the call was requested in fast mode and the service tier the provider reported. A fast request is settled with the `fast` rates unless the provider explicitly reported another tier, for example `default` after a downgrade to standard processing; then it is settled with the normal rates. When the provider reports no tier, the `fast` rates apply. The usage view marks a call as fast only when it was billed that way. Adding or changing fast rates is a rate change and needs a new card `version`; earlier usage is not re-rated.

## Guardrails

`guardrails` defines the checks the instance runs before an action happens. It defaults to none. Each entry is keyed by its name: lowercase words of letters and digits joined by hyphens or underscores, at most 64 characters. The name stays the guardrail's id in Studio, in its hits and on an approval request it checked.

```yaml
guardrails:
  no_personal_data:
    displayName: No personal data in skills
    description: Keeps customer details out of shared skills.
    on: approval_request.before_create
    filter:
      kind: skill_change
    check:
      kind: model_judge
      modelBindingId: guardrailCheck
      instruction: Check whether the proposed content contains personal data.
    outcome: warn
  no_iban_in_assets:
    displayName: No IBAN in assets
    on: asset.before_write
    check:
      kind: pattern
      pattern: '(?i)\bDE\d{2}(?:\s?\d{4}){4}\s?\d{2}\b'
      reason: Assets hold no bank account numbers. Remove the IBAN and save again.
    outcome: block
  no_iban_in_apps:
    displayName: No IBAN in published Apps
    on: app.before_publish
    check:
      kind: pattern
      pattern: '(?i)\bDE\d{2}(?:\s?\d{4}){4}\s?\d{2}\b'
      reason: Apps hold no bank account numbers. Remove the IBAN and publish again.
    outcome: block
```

A guardrail answers one event. A rule that should hold wherever content can go live needs one entry per event: the IBAN rule above stops an asset write and, with its second entry, the publish of an App, so an App whose revision was written before the rule existed cannot go live with an IBAN either.

| Field                        | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `displayName`, `description` | What Build shows. Without `displayName` the name is shown.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `on`                         | The event the guardrail answers: `asset.before_write` (a save, a push, a revert, an App written from a Page, an agent's save and the skill change it proposes, again when that change is approved), `operation.before_call` (every call of an operation), `app.before_publish`, `workflow.before_publish`, `data_store.before_publish` (the revision a publish makes live, with its files) or `approval_request.before_create`. |
| `filter`                     | Narrows the event: `kind` (the asset's kind, or the request's kind such as `skill_change`), `operation` (a name or a prefix ending in `.*`), `origin` (`agent`, `user`, `cli`, `mcp`, `app`, `workflow`, `schedule`) and `agent`, as far as the event knows them. Without it, everything at the event.                                                                                                                          |
| `check`                      | `pattern`: an RE2 expression (no backreferences, no lookaround), with the `reason` a person is shown. `model_judge`: a model of `modelBindingId` reads the content against `instruction` (at most 8,000 characters, any language) and answers with no tools. Either may name the event's `fields`: `name` and `content` of an asset, `input` of a call, `summary` and `newContent` of a request.                                |
| `outcome`                    | What a hit does: `allow`, `warn`, `require_approval` (a changing call waits for an approval in the Inbox; the App draft an agent's `page.save` writes cannot wait, so there it is a `block`) or `block`. Every guardrail that applies runs, and the strictest answer wins.                                                                                                                                                      |

Content longer than 2 Mi characters is not read in part: a guardrail that blocks or asks for an approval answers it as a match; one that warns warns. A text file in UTF-8, or in UTF-16 with its byte order mark or without one where at least 90% of the bytes at one parity of its first KiB are NUL and at most 10% at the other, is read as text. Any other file is read by a `pattern` as its printable runs (printable ASCII, tab and line ends) of at least 4 characters, as `strings` finds them, so text beside a NUL byte is still found and a photo adds next to nothing. A `model_judge` reads the text files and, of an image or a font (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, ICO, WOFF, WOFF2, TrueType, OpenType), the printable runs of at least 16 characters, which a photo has next to none of and text put into the file has throughout; any other file that is no text leaves it nothing it can judge, which a judge that blocks or asks for an approval answers as a match. Such a refusal does not say to try again, as nothing about it is temporary; a judge that failed or timed out does.

All guardrails bound to an event run concurrently. For skill changes, the summary and proposed new text are sent to the configured model provider; existing skill text and replaced text are excluded. Select a provider and binding approved for that content. Each check is a model call of the instance: it counts toward the usage budgets and safeguards and leaves one usage record with the purpose `guardrail_judge`, also when it fails or times out. The record names the originating conversation when there is one and never an agent run.

`warn` stores a visible warning and leaves the decision with the approver. `block` refuses a violating proposal and returns the reason to the agent without storing a request. If a check cannot be evaluated, including provider failures or the 60-second timeout, `warn` stores a neutral warning and `block` refuses the proposal, so a blocking guardrail never lets unchecked content through. When a usage limit of the instance refuses the check, the reason given to the agent says that the limit is reached. When a skill change is approved, the skill as the approval would write it is checked again at `asset.before_write`: a block then leaves the skill unchanged, and the request ends as not applied with the guardrail's reason. Undoing an approved change writes the earlier revision back, which is checked the same way: a block refuses the undo and the request stays approved. A call that waited for an approval is checked again before it runs. Request kinds without a proposed-content extractor are not checked.

Every warning and block is kept as a hit: the guardrail, the outcome, its one-sentence reason and the kind of request, never the checked content and never the person. A block that answered a `require_approval` where the action could not wait for an approval, such as the App draft an agent's `page.save` writes, says so (`convertedFrom: require_approval` of `guardrails.list_hits`; "Blocked: approval could not wait" on the guardrail's page). The judge is told to word its reason without quoting the content. Studio > Guardrails lists the guardrails read-only, and a guardrail's page counts its hits for the last 7 and 30 days and lists the newest 50, for holders of `guardrail.read` (administrators). Hits are counted by rule and period and never listed by person, because a list of who tripped which rule would let the instance monitor employees, which in Germany needs the works council's co-determination (§87(1) no. 6 BetrVG). Who made a request is in the audit log: `approval_request.created` for a request a guardrail warned on, and `operation.failed` of the agent's `propose_skill_change` call for one it blocked. Hits are deleted with the audit events, after `retention.auditDays`. Creation audit metadata contains only guardrail names and statuses, never proposed content or reasons. Stored check messages remain part of the approval request.

The API seeds the guardrails into the asset store when it starts, published, so a change of `guardrails` shows in Studio after a restart. They are the operator's floor: they cannot be changed, unpublished or deleted through the asset operations or the CLI, and they run from release config itself. Further guardrails are written as assets and published by a holder of `guardrail.publish` (see [config assets](/configure/config-assets/#guardrails-as-assets)); they add checks to the floor and never remove one. A name of release config that a guardrail asset holds already is left to the asset in Studio and logged at start; the floor's rule of that name runs all the same.

### From `approvalChecks`

`guardrails` replaces `approvalChecks`. For this release a config that still has `approvalChecks` loads each check as the guardrail it became: `id` becomes the name, `appliesTo` the `filter.kind`, `modelBindingId` and `instruction` the `model_judge` check, and `onFail` the `outcome`, with `on: approval_request.before_create`. A config with both keys is refused at start. The next release refuses `approvalChecks`.

## Sharing Config Across Environments With `extends`

A config file can start from another config file and override only what differs:

```yaml
# app.staging.yaml
extends: ./app.base.yaml
clientInstance:
  id: example-staging
  environment: staging
auth:
  standalone:
    baseUrl: https://staging.example.test/api/auth
```

Merge rules:

- Objects merge recursively; the extending file wins on conflicts.
- Arrays and scalars replace the base value wholesale — overriding one list entry means restating the whole list.
- `extends` chains are allowed; cycles fail validation with a clear error.
- Relative paths in the merged result (such as `uiFile`) resolve against the entry file's directory, not the extended file's.
- When a merged config has both `uiFile` and inline `ui`, the file supplies the base UI config and inline `ui` overlays it with the same object and array merge rules.

Keep everything shared in one base file and put only genuine per-environment differences in the environment files. Reading an environment file should answer "what makes this environment different?" at a glance.

## Tool Configuration

Each tool entry controls whether a stable tool name is available in the client instance. The optional `config` object is passed to the matching configured tool factory and validated by that factory's schema during startup.

```yaml
tools:
  - name: support.lookup_ticket
    enabled: true
    config:
      permissionRef: support-ticket-reader
      endpointEnvName: SUPPORT_API_URL
  - name: support.create_escalation
    enabled: false
```

Use `config` for customer-specific values such as permission references, default currencies, endpoint names, model-facing labels, allowlists, and secret environment variable names.

Do not put secret values in `config`. Put secret values in environment files or a secret manager, and reference them by name.

Startup validation fails when:

- an enabled tool has no registered implementation
- a configured tool's `config` does not match its schema
- an agent references a disabled or missing tool
- an enabled tool has the permission mode `approval_required`, which this release cannot run

## Web Access

`webAccess` holds the instance switches for reaching the web. Everything is off by default.

```yaml
webAccess:
  enabled: true
  search:
    enabled: true
  fetch:
    enabled: true
```

- `webAccess.enabled` is the gate for both search and fetch.
- `webAccess.search.enabled` lets agents that list the tool `web_search` search the web. The
  search is the model provider's own: whether a model can search is declared by its provider,
  not set in config. An `openai-compatible` entry with `api: responses` can; an entry on
  `chat_completions` and the `deterministic` provider cannot. An agent whose model cannot
  search runs without the tool, and saving that agent is refused with "the model of this agent
  cannot search the web". There is no search provider run by the platform.
- `webAccess.fetch` enables the `web_fetch` tool and bounds what one fetch may read.

`webAccess.search.mode` and `webAccess.search.managedProvider` were removed. A config that
still sets either is refused at startup with one message naming every such key; delete them.

An agent with `web_search` also needs a customer price for web search calls of its provider
under `usage.costs.customer.webSearch`.

## Links And Images In Replies

A reply in the chat and a Markdown file in the preview load nothing from another address. An image, whether written in Markdown or as HTML, remote, relative or a `data:` address, is never loaded; its description is shown in its place. A link stays a link when it points to the instance itself, is a `#fragment` or a `mailto:` address. `replies.allowedLinkHosts` names the other hosts links may point to:

```yaml
replies:
  allowedLinkHosts:
    - example.com
    - "*.example.com"
```

An entry is a host name, or `*.` and a domain for every subdomain of it but not the domain itself. A link to any other host is shown as text followed by its address, so a person can still read and copy it. The default is an empty list. The setting applies when a reply is shown, so it also governs replies written before a change.

The renderer is not the only line. A Mermaid diagram draws into the page outside it, and a node label, an image shape or the diagram's theme CSS can name an image. The interface's page therefore carries a content policy in a meta tag that the chat UI's Vite plugin writes into `index.html` at build: images, media, fonts and connections come only from the interface itself, `data:` and `blob:` addresses, the API when the build names another origin (`VITE_CHAT_API_URL`, or `VITE_CHAT_API_PORT` on the page's host), and the hosts of `ui.logoUrl`, `ui.logoUrlDark` and `ui.faviconUrl`. A logo on another host therefore needs a new build of the interface image after a change. Scripts, styles and frames are not limited by it: generated views and Apps run in documents with policies of their own.

## Generated Views

A view an agent shows with `show_view` loads Tailwind CSS and Lucide from the instance and no script from any other host. `views.allowedScriptSrc` names the hosts views may load scripts from besides the instance, as HTTPS origins or paths:

```yaml
views:
  allowedScriptSrc:
    - https://cdn.jsdelivr.net
```

The default is an empty list, and `"*"` allows every HTTPS host. The setting applies when a view is shown, so it also governs views saved before a change. Earlier releases read script settings from the `show_view` tool's own `config`. That tool takes no config now, and any key left there fails validation with a message that names `views.allowedScriptSrc`.

### What A View Can Reach

A view cannot by itself load from, move its frame to or send HTTP or WebSocket requests to a host the instance has not allowed. A view that holds private rows also carries no address a person could open from it.

Three things hold this.

- **The view's content policy.** The interface composes it each time it shows the view. It refuses every load and every connection except scripts from the instance's view runtime and from the hosts in `views.allowedScriptSrc`.
- **The shell.** Every view is framed in a small document the instance serves under `/app-runtime/view-shell/<version>/`, whose `Content-Security-Policy` header carries `frame-src 'none'`. A view that sets `location`, carries a refresh tag or has a script follow a link would move its own frame to another address, and no policy of the view itself can forbid that. The browser checks the move against the policy of the framing document and refuses it before it sends a request, to addresses of the instance as well. Because the policy is a header of the instance, it also holds when another site embeds the chat widget.
- **The allowlist for views with private rows.** A view of kind `private_hydrated_view` runs no script, and its rows are written into its HTML on the server. Such a view needs no script to send rows away: a link carries them in its address, and a click with a modifier key or the middle button opens it in a new tab, outside the frame. So the interface does not show the stored HTML of such a view. It reads it with the browser's parser and writes the body anew from a list of allowed elements and attributes, each time the view is shown. Row text is already part of the stored HTML at that point, so whatever it became is held to the same list.

What a view with private rows keeps:

| Kept                                                                 | With                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Text, headings, paragraphs, sections, `pre`, `blockquote`, `details` | `class`, `id`, `style`, `title`, `lang`, `dir`, `role`, `hidden`, `aria-*`, `data-*`                                                 |
| Lists and tables                                                     | also `colspan`, `rowspan`, `headers`, `scope`, `span`, `start`, `value`                                                              |
| Inline formatting, `time`, `meter`, `progress`                       | their value attributes                                                                                                               |
| `a`                                                                  | its text, never an address                                                                                                           |
| `img`                                                                | `alt`, `width`, `height`, and `src` only when it is a `data:` address of type `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/gif` or `image/webp` |
| `style` blocks and `style` attributes                                | only without `url(` other than `url(#id)`, `@import`, `image-set(`, `image(`, `src(` or a backslash                                  |
| Inline `svg` with shapes, `text`, gradients and clip paths           | geometry and paint attributes, no `href`                                                                                             |

Everything else is left out with what is inside it: `script`, `link`, `meta`, `base`, `area`, `form` and its controls, `iframe`, `object`, `embed`, `canvas`, `video`, `audio`, SVG `a`, `image`, `use` and `foreignObject`, every event handler attribute, `href`, `ping`, `target`, `srcset` and `srcdoc`.

The limits:

- **WebRTC.** A view that runs scripts can send UDP packets to a host its script names. No content policy and no sandbox flag of current browsers forbids WebRTC. The view's bootstrap removes `RTCPeerConnection` and its prefixed variants from the view's window. That is hardening and not a boundary: a script gets the constructor back in a frame it writes itself.
- **Links in a view that runs scripts.** The view's bootstrap takes the address from every link, image map area and SVG link, and cancels a click on one that still has an address. That is hardening and not a boundary: a script can put a link back where the bootstrap does not run, in a frame it writes itself, and a click on it with a modifier key or the middle button then opens the address in a new tab. A link inside a closed shadow root keeps its address, because the bootstrap does not look into shadow roots. Opening a link from the context menu and dragging a link out of a view have not been tested.
- **A static view is static.** A view with private rows shows HTML and CSS. A chart drawn by a script on a canvas does not appear, and the frame keeps a fixed height and scrolls inside, since nothing in it can report its height.
- **DNS.** Whether a view can cause a DNS lookup for a host of its choosing has not been observed. A view with private rows keeps no `link` or `meta` element, so it carries no resource hint. For a view that runs scripts this is open.
- **Allowed script hosts are data destinations.** A host named in `views.allowedScriptSrc` receives the requests a view makes for its scripts, and a view chooses the address, so data can leave in it. Name only hosts you would send the data to.
- **A view navigates nowhere.** A link in a view has no address, `#fragment` included, and a view that moves its frame anyway shows the browser's own notice for a refused address.
- **Sites that embed the widget.** The shell is a frame from the instance. A site that embeds the chat widget under a content policy of its own must allow the instance's origin in `frame-src`, or no view is shown there.
- **Browsers.** All of this is tested in Chromium only. Firefox and Safari are untested. The shell relies on the browser applying `frame-src` of the framing document to a navigation of the frame, and on a `srcdoc` frame taking over the policies of the document that holds it.

The shell answers only requests a browser makes for a frame: a request whose `Sec-Fetch-Dest` header names anything else gets `403`. The shell runs under `sandbox`, so it and the view have an opaque origin and neither can read anything of the instance. The requests for the shell and for script files are still requests to the instance, and a browser may attach eligible cookies to them. The routes read none. A reverse proxy in front of the instance must route `/app-runtime/*` to the API. When it does not, views stay on "Loading view…".

## Agent And Skill Configuration Assets

Agents and client skills remain source-controlled YAML and Markdown, but runtime reads them from the versioned configuration-asset store. A `catalyst.yaml` manifest selects the working-copy files and target instances:

```yaml
instances:
  staging:
    url: https://catalyst.example.test
defaultInstance: staging
defaultAgentName: support_agent
agents:
  - agents/*.agent.yaml
skills:
  - skills/*/SKILL.md
```

Use `catalyst config pull`, `diff`, `validate`, and `push` to synchronize the complete entities. Push uses the last pulled version and conflicts when the active instance changed in the meantime. The CLI release path has full entity access; ordinary administration writes are limited by `administration.agentConfiguration` and enforced by the server.

An agent YAML file contains its behavior and grants:

```yaml
name: support_agent
displayName: Support Agent
instructions: Help users with support cases.
modelBindingId: primary
reasoningEffort: medium
toolNames:
  - read_skill
  - support.lookup_ticket
skillNames:
  - support_review
initialPrompts: []
```

Each skill file starts with YAML frontmatter:

```md
---
title: Support Review
description: Use when the user asks to review support case details and plan next checks.
---

# Support Review

...
```

The model sees only the allowed skill name, title, and description. It calls `read_skill` to load the full Markdown body when a skill matches the task.

A skill directory may also contain UTF-8 text resources such as `references/policy.md`. The root `read_skill({ name })` response lists these paths without loading their content; the agent can then call `read_skill({ name, resourcePath })` for one relevant resource. The CLI synchronizes the entire directory as one revisioned skill package. Supported resource file extensions are `.md`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.yaml`, and `.yml`; binary files are intentionally excluded.

## UI Branding

Clients own their favicon and should serve it from `public/`, reference it from `index.html`, and set `ui.faviconUrl` so runtime branding stays explicit. The platform includes `packages/chat-ui/assets/favicon.svg` as an optional fallback asset; pass it as `faviconPath` to `vivdCatalystChatUiPlugin()` when a client intentionally wants that default copied into its build. `ui.faviconUrl` may be an absolute URL or a root-relative path served by the client.

### Documentation address

`ui.docsUrl` is the address the interface's links to the documentation start from: the Documentation item of the account menu, and the "Learn more" links on pages such as Access.

```yaml
ui:
  docsUrl: https://docs.workshape.ai/catalyst
```

- It has no default. An instance that leaves it out shows no Documentation item and no "Learn more" link, and no empty row in their place.
- Set your own address to send people to your own handbook. The account menu opens the address as it is. A "Learn more" link adds the path of a page of this documentation to it, such as `/operate/how-rights-work/`, so an address of your own needs the pages at those paths.
- `docsUrl: null` clears an address that a base file set, for one environment that [extends](#sharing-config-across-environments-with-extends) it.
- Only an `http` or `https` address is taken. Anything else, such as a path, a bare host or a `javascript:` address, stops the start with a validation error.

The address is part of the public branding the interface reads, so it is not a place for a link that carries a token.

## Model Provider Configuration

OpenAI-compatible providers keep API-specific request shapes behind the model-provider boundary. Agents and tools still see Workshape Catalyst's provider-neutral messages, tools, tool calls, tool results, and usage.

Tools reach an OpenAI-compatible provider under a readable name derived from the tool name (dots become underscores), shortened with a short suffix when the name is too long or would clash.

Use `api: responses` for OpenAI reasoning models that combine reasoning, tool calling, or multi-turn workflows. Leave the field unset, or set `api: chat_completions`, for legacy OpenAI-compatible endpoints that still expect `/chat/completions`.

```yaml
infrastructure:
  models:
    openai:
      provider: openai-compatible
      region: global
      api: responses
      model: gpt-5.5
      reasoningEffort: high
      baseUrl: https://api.openai.com/v1
      credentialSecret: OPENAI_API_KEY
      contextManagement:
        compaction:
          compactThresholdTokens: 270000
modelBindings:
  - id: primary
    providerId: openai
    model: gpt-5.5
    agentSelectable: true
    supportsFastMode: false
```

`contextManagement.compaction` enables provider-native server-side compaction
for `api: responses` providers. Catalyst sends the configured threshold as
`context_management[].compact_threshold`, retains the encrypted checkpoint for
later model requests, and keeps the durable conversation transcript unchanged.
Do not configure this block for `api: chat_completions`; startup validation
rejects that unsupported combination.

Agent configuration may override a binding's default with one of Catalyst's product-owned reasoning efforts: `none`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`. Only bindings with `agentSelectable: true` are valid agent choices; set it to `false` for internal bindings such as conversation-title generation. The server validates model-binding references and reasoning values; the UI does not accept arbitrary model identifiers.

An agent's `modelBindingId`, `reasoningEffort`, `fastMode`, `userSelectableModelBindingIds`, and `modelReasoningEfforts` are editable in Studio exactly when the caller holds the `agent_models.manage` permission, and the server rejects an interactive change to any of them without it. Superadmins hold the permission by default; a superadmin can grant it to individual users. `modelBindingId` and `reasoningEffort` remain valid `editableAgentFields` values for compatibility but no longer have an effect. `catalyst config push` is unchanged and may set all five.

Set `supportsFastMode: true` on a binding whose provider deployment offers a priority processing tier. It defaults to `false`.
