Instance > Infrastructure shows the sandbox as failed with the time of the last report once the workers were silent for 30 seconds, and `codeExecution` of `GET /instance/infrastructure` says whether code runs and since when. Both recover when a worker is back.

The same rule holds for a save. When a build has been due for 30 seconds and the workers reported nothing for 30 seconds, the save fails and says that no workspace command worker takes Page builds. A worker that reports is waited for; a save whose wait runs out behind it says that the workers are busy.

A build that is published is published once. The revision and the result of the build are written in one transaction while the worker holds the job; a job that is delivered again after a worker stopped finds the result and stores nothing, and a save that gave up gets no revision.

A worker that is killed can leave a build's directory under `WORKSPACE_COMMAND_TEMP_ROOT` and, with the Docker sandbox, its container. Every worker removes directories named `catalyst-page-build-*` and containers named `catalyst-workspace-command-page-build-*` that are older than 15 minutes when it starts and every 10 minutes while it builds.

| Setting                  | Default | Meaning                                                                         |
| ------------------------ | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PAGE_BUILD_CONCURRENCY` | 2       | Builds one worker process runs at once. One conversation never has two at once. |
| `PAGE_BUILD_TIMEOUT_MS`  | 60000   | A build that runs longer is stopped, its container removed, and the save fails. |

A build takes at most 500 files, 2 MiB per file and 25 MiB in all, and may leave 500 files of 50 MiB in all, in at most 2,000 files and folders nested 32 deep. Memory, CPU and process count are those of the sandbox (4 GiB, 1 CPU and 128 processes by default); there is no disk quota on the build's directory beyond the timeout. A save waits five minutes for its build; when no worker takes it in that time the save fails and a worker that comes later stores nothing.

## Deployment Flow

Separate publishing from deployment:

```text
run checks
  -> build Docker images
  -> tag release
  -> push images
  -> explicitly deploy target client instance
  -> run migrations
  -> restart services
  -> health check
```

Production deploys should be explicit. A GitHub Actions workflow can call the same deploy script that an operator can run manually with the right credentials.

## Environment Contract

Do not commit production env files.

Document these values per instance:

- database URL
- model provider credentials
- auth token signing or exchange secrets
- object storage endpoint and credentials
- backup bucket
- public origin
- CORS or embed allowlist
- retention and audit env overrides, if any

For machine API access, configure a `SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET` of at least 32 characters before starting the API. Treat it as a server signing secret: keep it stable across restarts and identical across replicas. API keys are separate database-backed credentials created in the API Access control plane and supplied only to callers as `CATALYST_API_KEY`; they do not belong in the server deployment environment.

## Database

Postgres is the baseline application store.

Managed Postgres is preferred for production when available. Running Postgres on the same VPS is acceptable for early instances only when backup and restore are treated as product features.

Minimum requirements:

- persistent volume outside the app container lifecycle
- automated external backups
- documented restore procedure
- migration procedure
- monitoring for failed backups
- least-privilege backup credentials

Database schema changes must be shipped as committed Drizzle migration files. Do not use `drizzle-kit push` or any direct schema-push workflow.

Migrations run as an explicit step before the API and the workers start. Each client builds `dist/migrate.js`, and the Compose `migrate` service runs `node <client folder>/dist/migrate.js`. In the operated production Compose files the deploy script runs that service after the pre-deploy backup and before `up`; the services themselves only wait for a healthy Postgres there. In local Compose the API waits for the `migrate` service to complete, and the workers wait for the API. The step holds a Postgres advisory lock on one session, applies each committed migration once, prints the names it applied and names the migration that failed, also when the server ended its connection. While another step holds the lock it waits, and says so on standard error when it starts to wait and every 30 seconds after; it has no deadline.

The API and the workers never migrate. When one starts, it reads the migration state: a database that lacks committed migrations stops it with their names, so a production stack started without the migrate step fails instead of serving an old schema. A database ahead of the release starts, so the previous release keeps serving while a newer one is rolled out. There is no `RUN_MIGRATIONS` switch.

Schema changes expand before they contract. A new migration may hold the additive forms: a new table, type, schema or sequence; a nullable or defaulted column; a column default; a relaxed `NOT NULL`; a constraint added `NOT VALID` and its later validation; inserts and updates; and, in a migration of its own, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS`. Every other statement is a contract step, among them a drop, a rename, a new `NOT NULL`, a column type change, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE` and a `DO` block: it ships in a later migration under `-- contract-after: <tag>`, once the oldest supported release in `packages/postgres-store/migration-policy.json` has reached that tag. A required column without a default and a blocking index build never pass. `pnpm check:migrations` enforces this for every migration the base branch lacks and rejects any change to a committed migration; `pnpm test:compatibility` runs the database tests of the previous and the oldest supported release against the new schema, and `pnpm test:upgrade` migrates a database of the oldest supported release.

A concurrent index build runs outside a transaction. When it fails, the migration is not recorded and the index stays behind as invalid; repair what stopped it and run the step again, which drops the invalid index and builds it anew.

### Data Stores on the database server

With the module `dataStores` on, each Data Store has a database of its own on this server and two roles, named `catalyst_ds_...`. The platform takes from those roles every way to the platform database and to each other's databases. Three things it leaves to you. Every job of a store looks for them and names them on the store's record, and a name goes once its cause is closed. `GET /api/v1/data-stores/<store>` answers them for one store, each with these steps in a sentence, beside the store's migration level, its size against its limit and how its last migration ended:

- `server_databases_open`: a store role can connect to another database of the server, such as `postgres` or `template1`, where it reads the catalog and nothing else. The platform changes no grant of a database it does not own, because the server may hold more than this instance. On a server that is this instance's alone, run `REVOKE CONNECT ON DATABASE <name> FROM PUBLIC` for each such database as its owner. On a shared server add the line below to `pg_hba.conf`, above the lines that admit the platform, and reload Postgres. Postgres shows that file to no ordinary role, so the condition stays.
- `sessions_open`: the platform's database role is no superuser, so it cannot take the functions that list and end sessions from the roles of a store. A query of a store can then see the sessions of the server and end another query of that store.
- `temp_files_unbounded`: the platform's database role is no superuser, so it cannot set `temp_file_limit` on the roles of a store. A statement of a store that sorts or joins without end fills the disk with temporary files until its timeout.

```text
host postgres,template1 /^catalyst_ds_ all reject
```

A role of a store may change its own password. The platform sets it again before it connects as that role, so keep the Postgres port closed to everyone but the platform: whoever reaches it in between logs in with what the role last set.

A store at its size limit takes no further rows. What a refused insert wrote is given back by a `VACUUM` the platform runs as the owner of the store's database; the autovacuum of the server does the rest.

## Health And Readiness

Two unversioned addresses answer without a credential.

- `GET /health` says the process is up. It reads nothing.
- `GET /ready` says whether this process can serve, and is the check for rotation: use it for the proxy's upstream check and for the deploy script's wait after `up`. The container healthcheck stays on `/health`: other services wait for a healthy API container, and a healthcheck on `/ready` would keep the proxy from starting during a database outage. `/ready` answers `200 { "status": "ready", "migration": "<newest migration of the release>" }` when the database answers within two seconds and holds every migration the release was built with. Otherwise it answers `503 { "status": "not_ready", "reason": "database_unreachable" }` or `503 { "status": "not_ready", "reason": "database_behind", "missing": ["<migration>", ...] }`. A database ahead of the release is ready, so the previous release stays in rotation while a newer one is rolled out.

`/ready` checks the database and nothing else. A model or mail provider outage does not take the API out of rotation. The answer names migrations only: no host, no account, no connection string and no driver error. The document worker answers `/ready` on its own port with the same body and status.

The proxy has to forward `/ready` to the API like `/health`; it is outside `/api/*`.

## What The Proxy Routes To The API

Everything else goes to the interface. A deployment with its own proxy routes these to the API:

| Address             | What it is                                         |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `/api/*`            | The product API.                                   |
| `/auth/*`           | Sign-in of an instance with standalone auth.       |
| `/health`, `/ready` | The two checks above.                              |
| `/app-runtime/*`    | The runtime and the shell of a generated view.     |
| `/app-content/*`    | The files of a Page, when the module `apps` is on. |

`docker/Caddyfile` routes all of them.

An address below `/app-content/` holds a token in its path: `/app-content/<file set>/<token>/<file>`. The token is a bearer capability. The API mints it after it has checked that the person may read the Page, and for one hour (`APP_CONTENT_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS`) it serves the built files of that one revision to whoever holds the address, as long as that person may still read the Page. The API asks again every 30 seconds per address (`APP_CONTENT_VIEWER_CHECK_SECONDS`): once the account is deactivated or the person no longer reads the conversation, the address answers `404` at most 30 seconds later. It is not bound to the person's session: signing out does not end it before the hour is over.

So no layer may write these addresses down:

- The API writes no request line for them, whichever way the address is spelled.
- `docker/Caddyfile` writes no access log. If you add a `log` directive, leave these addresses out with `log_skip /app-content/*`.
- `docker/nginx-spa.conf` answers `/app-content` with `404` and `access_log off`, for the case that such an address reaches the interface's server.
- Any other proxy, load balancer or CDN in front must be set the same way, and must not cache these answers: they carry `Cache-Control: private` or `no-store`.

A proxy's error log is not its access log: when the API does not answer, Caddy writes the address of the failed request to its error log, so proxy error logs can hold the address of a Page that stays valid for up to the lifetime of its token.

A Page's own script can read the address it was loaded from. The token is therefore a secret from other people and not from the Page.

## Production Readiness Checklist

Before a real deployment:

- release config validates
- migrations run cleanly
- `/health` answers and `/ready` answers `200` on the API and the document worker
- TLS is configured
- production secrets are not in Git or images
- backups run and restore has been tested
- model provider billing alerts or budgets exist
- retention and deletion behavior is documented
- audit views are permissioned
- user access path is tested
- customer-hosted integrations have timeout and failure behavior

## Release Gate For The `/api/v1` Cutover

The release that moves the product API under `/api/v1` answers 404 at every old path, with no alias. Interface, CLI and server ship together, so the only callers it can break are outside ones: a backend that issues chat session tokens for an embedded chat.

Before deploying that release to an operated instance:

1. Search the instance's access log for `POST /auth/session-token` and `POST /api/superadmin/session-tokens` over the log's whole retention.
2. Record the result with the release: the two paths, the period searched, and per path the request count and the calling hosts. Record metadata only, never request bodies, tokens or the server credential.
3. Move every caller found to `POST /api/v1/instance/session-tokens` in the same release. The `x-server-credential` header and the payload are unchanged.
4. Give every CLI runner a `CATALYST_API_KEY`; the CLI no longer signs in with the server credential. The server needs `SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET` for the key exchange.
5. Tell users to reload open tabs after the upgrade. A tab loaded before it calls the old paths and shows "Operation is not available"; later releases show a notice with a reload action instead.

A reverse proxy that forwards `/api/*` and `/health` needs no change.

pages.title: Operate code execution
pages.description: Operate workspace command workers, runner images, cleanup, and artifact promotion.
pages.body:
Execution workspaces give agents a persistent conversation-scoped file area and a bounded command primitive. Operators should treat the feature as a worker-backed artifact pipeline, not as shell access inside the chat API.

## Runtime Roles

The production-shaped deployment has these roles:

- chat API: validates tool calls, enqueues workspace commands, exposes promoted artifacts, and never runs shell commands
- workspace command worker: runs the job of each command on the job executor, hydrates workspace files, starts a short-lived runner, syncs changed files, and records terminal status
- runner container: executes the agent-authored command with no platform secrets and no network by default
- object storage: stores workspace file bytes and promoted artifact bytes
- Postgres: stores workspace, file manifest, command queue, leases, audit events, and managed artifact records

Commands wait in the durable Postgres queue until worker capacity is available. Each command is a job of the kind `workspace.command`; one workspace runs one command at a time, in the order they were queued. A command runs once: when its worker dies, the command fails with the category `worker_lost` after its lease of two minutes and is not started again; until then the later commands of that workspace wait. `executionWorkspaces.worker.concurrency` is the deployment control for simultaneous runner containers; queued commands are not rejected through separate per-user or global admission caps. Size worker concurrency for the host, and use queue wait time as the signal to add execution capacity.

## Runner Image

The platform Dockerfile exposes a `workspace-command-runner` target for the `infrastructure.sandbox.image` container. It includes `/bin/bash`, Node, Python artifact libraries, LibreOffice, Poppler, fonts, ImageMagick, and common shell utilities so `workspace.exec` can run ordinary script-first DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, and image workflows without package installs at command time.

The image target intentionally does not copy the chat API build or deployment secrets. The `workspace-command-worker` target remains the trusted control process image with Docker CLI access; it starts short-lived runner containers from the configured runner image.

Capability-owned Catalyst helper CLIs such as `docx_render`, `xlsx_scan_errors`, `pptx_render`, `pdf_inspect`, and `promote_artifact` are part of the paid capabilities and not in the open repository. Deployments that license those helpers layer the capabilities helper package onto the platform runner image and publish that layered image tag through `EXECUTION_WORKSPACE_RUNNER_IMAGE`.

## Operational Signals

Workspace command lifecycle audit events use these event types:

- `workspace_command.queued`
- `workspace_command.running`
- `workspace_command.completed`
- `workspace_command.failed`
- `workspace_command.timed_out`
- `workspace_command.cancelled`
- `workspace_command.recovered_stale`

Audit metadata includes command id, workspace id, conversation id, timeout, attempts, counts, error code/category, and duration where available. It must not include command text, stdout, stderr, file contents, or object-store credentials.

The worker also emits operator telemetry logs with `workspace_command.*` event types. These logs include active queued/running/cancelling counts, terminal status, timeout categories, and temp cleanup counts. Use these logs for queue pressure and failure-rate alerting.

## Cleanup

Conversation deletion and retention expiration call execution workspace cleanup before the conversation is marked unavailable. Cleanup deletes internal workspace object bytes, removes workspace file manifests, removes workspace command rows, and marks the workspace deleted.

A periodic cleanup job also scans for active workspace metadata attached to already deleted or retention-expired conversations. This catches interrupted delete/retention paths.

The worker keeps a hydrated local workspace directory after each command and reuses it until `executionWorkspaces.cleanup.hydratedWorkspaceIdleTtlMs` expires. Set the value to `0` to disable reuse. Before every command, the worker reconciles the directory with the durable workspace manifest, and after every command it syncs changed files back to durable storage. Runner containers remain short-lived.

Empty directories remain available while that warm local copy is reused. The durable manifest stores files, so empty directories do not survive cache eviction, worker restart, or execution on a different worker.

The same periodic cleanup removes expired or orphaned directories with the `catalyst-workspace-` prefix. The durable source of truth is object storage plus the workspace manifest, not hydrated directories or runner containers.

## Promoted Artifacts

Users should only receive promoted artifacts. Internal workspace files and logs are visible to agent tools for debugging and follow-up commands, but they are not projected as user-downloadable artifacts until `workspace.promote_artifact` or an expected promoted output creates a managed artifact.

## Incident Checks

For command failures:

- check `workspace_command.failed` and `workspace_command.timed_out` audit events
- check worker logs for queue counts and for commands that failed as `worker_lost`
- verify the workspace command worker is running
- verify the runner image tag matches the release
- verify object storage root or credentials are writable by the worker
- verify Docker can start a no-network runner container

Do not inspect or paste raw workspace files, command strings, stdout, or stderr into support tickets unless the customer has approved that specific data access path.

pages.title: Retention, audit and deletion
pages.description: Run sensitive chat workflows with retention, audit, usage, and deletion controls.
pages.body:
Governance is the minimum set of controls needed to run a sensitive client instance responsibly.

It is not a broad compliance suite. It is explicit behavior for access, audit, retention, deletion, and usage visibility.

## Retention

Define retention for:

- conversations
- messages
- tool call records
- document outputs
- managed file references
- model usage events
- audit events
- backups

A Conversation is deleted `retention.conversationDays` after the last message a user sent in it. Set `retention.extendOnActivity: false` to count from its creation instead, as a fixed maximum age. In its last seven days, or the last half of a shorter period, the conversation list marks it with a clock, and the open Conversation says when it will be deleted. See [release config](/configure/release-config/#retention).

Conversation retention and audit retention may be different. Audit events should avoid raw sensitive payloads so they can safely outlive conversation content where policy requires it.

Audit retention is enforced. Once a day the API process deletes the audit events of its instance that are older than `retention.auditDays` (default 365) and records one `audit.pruned` event with the number of rows it removed. There is no switch: an instance that has to keep audit events longer sets a higher `auditDays`, up to 3650, before it upgrades.

## Audit

Audit events should record governance metadata:

- actor id
- event type
- conversation id
- message id
- tool call id
- file id
- status
- reason code where required
- correlation id
- timestamps

Audit events should not store:

- full prompts or completions
- full document text
- raw file bytes
- secrets or tokens
- unnecessary personal data

## Usage Governance

Model usage is governance metadata, not provider billing truth.

Admin-facing usage views expose consumption volume and customer billable totals: model calls, total and cached input tokens, configured non-financial safeguards, recent model usage metadata, and the persisted rate-card amount the customer should expect to be invoiced. Per-day and per-calendar-month summaries use “Billable” until an invoice is issued. They do not expose applied rates or internal pricing provenance. Web-search costs are displayed only when web search is enabled for the instance.

Record:

- provider id, and the region of the provider entry: `eu`, `global`, or none for a provider that runs inside the instance
- model id, and the model binding the call named
- token counts when reported by the provider
- conversation id, where a conversation caused the call
- agent run id and agent name, or for a call the product made for itself what it was for: `conversation_title`, `guardrail_judge`, `document_extraction`, `knowledge_embedding` (the chunks of a Knowledge Base at ingestion and re-index) or `knowledge_query` (the query of a Knowledge Base search)
- the user who caused the call and the workspace it happened in, where there is one
- correlation id
- persisted customer billable cost and completeness state

Every model call leaves one record, including conversation titles and guardrail checks, and including a call that failed, timed out or was stopped. Titles and guardrail checks count toward the limits of the instance like every other call.

A record has a status:

- `pending`: the call was admitted and has not ended. The Usage page shows it as "Running".
- `settled`: the call ended with usage. The Usage page says where the amounts come from: "Reported by provider", "No usage reported" when the provider answered and reported none, or "Estimated".
- `failed`: the call failed, was stopped or timed out before any of its answer arrived. It counts as one call toward the daily call limit and uses no tokens. The Usage page shows it as "Failed".
- `abandoned`: the process that made the call went away before the call ended. The job `usage.recover_abandoned_calls` runs every 10 minutes and takes a call that is still `pending` six hours after its admission as abandoned. The Usage page shows it as "Abandoned".

A streamed call that is stopped or breaks off after its answer began has cost something, and its provider reports no usage for it. Where the provider had reported the usage before the stream broke off, the call is settled with it. Otherwise it is settled with an estimate: every three characters that were sent and every three that arrived count as one token, a character outside the Latin alphabet counts as a token of its own, the input of a tool call counts as output, the input counts as not cached, and a web search that had started counts as one search. An estimate is at most 10,000,000 tokens of input and as many of output. Its record is marked `estimated`.

### How a call is admitted

A call is admitted against the limits in the database, in one statement on two counter rows: the day's and the month's. Several API and worker processes together admit no more than the limits allow, for calls, tokens and spend. Admission reads no usage record and no process waits for a lock per instance.

At admission a call reserves the most it can use: its input by the size of the request, 16,000 output tokens, and both at the highest price the rate card has for the model. When the call ends, the reservation is replaced by what the call used. A failed or abandoned call releases its reservation.

This has three consequences for how you set limits:

- A call is refused when its reservation no longer fits, so a token or spend limit is reached slightly before it is used up.
- A token limit at or below the 16,000 reserved output tokens would admit no call. The config is refused with a message that names the limit and the reservation.
- With a spend budget, a model without a price on the customer rate card is refused. A `deterministic` provider needs no price: it bills nothing, and its calls reserve no cost. A run that is refused this way fails with the code `MODEL_NOT_PRICED`. The chat tells someone with `usage.view` that the price is missing and to choose another model until the operator has added it under `usage.costs` in release config, and anyone else to choose another model or ask an administrator. Startup validation asks a price of the models agents start on, of conversation titles and of guardrails; it does not ask one of a model an agent only offers for selection, so give every binding of a billed provider a price.

The limits are protective safeguards, not exact caps. A call reserves a fixed amount at admission and settles its real usage when it ends, and the request sets no maximum for the answer, so a call can use more than it reserved. The most a limit can be passed by is the sum, over the calls in flight when it is reached, of what each used minus what it reserved. The reserved output is the constant `MODEL_CALL_RESERVED_OUTPUT_TOKENS` (16,000) in `@vivd-catalyst/core`. Set a limit with that margin in mind, and keep a provider-side budget as the hard stop.

A cost that cannot be settled, such as one whose provider reported no cached tokens, counts toward a spend budget at the highest price of the model. It does not stop later calls.

The Usage page lists the caller and the provider with its region for the recent calls. Its sums are read from daily sums that are kept as each call ends. The summary of the API also answers `attributedUsage`: the last 30 days by day, model, provider, region and purpose or agent.

### What stays after a deletion

Usage records are the accounting of the instance and are kept. When an account is deleted, the user is removed from its usage records together with the conversation id, the agent run id, the operation id and the correlation id. A call that ends or is recorded after the account is gone is written without them. The amounts, the model, the provider and the agent or purpose stay. When a workspace is deleted, the workspace is removed from its usage records and the amounts stay.

### After an upgrade

Records written before provider region, purpose, user and workspace were recorded are filled by a background job, `usage.backfill_attribution`. It needs no action. Until it ends, older records show no region. A record whose provider and model are no longer in `infrastructure.models` keeps no region, because nothing says where it was processed.

Use provider-side billing alerts or budgets as an external backstop.

## Background Jobs

Settings > Instance > Jobs shows what the instance works on in the background: per job kind the
queued, running, failed and dead jobs, and below that the jobs themselves under Failed and dead,
Running and Queued. Everyone with `audit.view` can read it. A job is shown with its kind,
status, attempts, the class of its last error and the id of the record it works on. The page
and its API never show a job's payload or an error message, because either can quote a
provider or a record.

A job is `dead` when its attempts are used up, and `failed` when another attempt could not
help or when a schedule tick failed. A superadmin can retry a failed or dead job. The retry
queues the job again and puts the record it works on back into the state the job starts from,
so a preview that failed is rendered again and a draft attachment that failed is preprocessed
again. There is no retry for a schedule tick, since the next tick does its work, none for a
workspace command, since a command is never run a second time, and none for a kind whose
capability names no way to retry it. Every retry is written to the audit log as
`job.retried`.

## Admin Access

Admin and superadmin access should be explicit, permissioned, and audited.

Default views should show metadata, retention status, usage summaries, audit events, and deletion workflows.

Full message access should require:

- explicit release-config enablement
- stronger permission
- reason capture
- audit event

## Inbox

The Inbox is where a person finds what waits for a decision. It is a section of the sidebar, below Chat, at `/inbox`. The older address `/approvals` leads there. Issuing an API key never waits there, because the key is shown once to the person who asks: under an instance default of `approval` for changing operations the call runs on its caller's own word, and a policy setting for the operation or a guardrail that asks for an approval refuses it.

The sidebar shows the Inbox to a person who may decide a kind of Approval Request, and to a person who has made a request. The number beside it counts the pending requests that person can decide. It does not count unread items.

The Inbox has three lists:

- **To decide**: the pending requests the person can decide, oldest first.
- **My requests**: the requests the person made, in every state, with who decided and the comment.
- **Decided**: the requests of the kinds the person may decide that were decided in the last 30 days. An accepted change is undone from here.

To decide and Decided need a right to decide, such as `agent_skills.approve` for skill changes. A person without one sees their own requests as a single list. Every signed-in person can read their own requests through `approval_requests.list_mine`; `approval_requests.list` stays with the people who may decide.

Opening a row shows the request beside the list at `/inbox/<id>`. A decision is made there or on the card in the conversation; both read and change the same Approval Request. Who may decide is answered by the server for each request.

The lists and the open request ask for their state every 60 seconds. When two people decide the same request, the first decision stands. The second person is told who decided, and a comment they had written stays on the page.

## Deletion

Support deletion as a product workflow, not a manual database habit.

Deletion should cover:

- one conversation
- all conversations for a user where policy allows
- related messages and tool outputs
- related document outputs and file references
- minimal retained audit records where legally or contractually required

The customer or legal owner decides the lawful basis and exact retention durations. Workshape Catalyst provides the mechanisms and evidence path.

The job `usage.reconcile` builds the daily sums of the days before the upgrade from the usage records. Until it ends, the Usage page shows no sums for those days. It takes about 3 seconds per million records and needs no action. Afterwards it runs once a day and at every start, compares the counters and the sums with the usage records from the month of its previous run on, and corrects what differs. After a rollback it therefore reads the months in which the previous release wrote. One comparison of an instance runs at a time; admission and settlement do not wait for it.

During a rolling upgrade a process of the previous release writes usage records that are in no counter and no sum. A limit can be passed by what those processes admit until the next run of `usage.reconcile`. To avoid that, stop the previous release before the new one takes calls.

pages.title: How rights work
pages.description: Who may do what in Workshape Catalyst, explained from the start. Roles, single rights, grants, Namespaces, the checks an action passes, and which screen sets which of them.
pages.body: ## The short version [Rights at a glance](/how-it-works/rights/) explains the same in three pictures. 1. An action is checked before it runs, in a fixed order, whether you click a button, a script calls the API or an agent uses a tool for you. 2. The instance first finds out who is calling, and for an API key what that key may be used for. 3. Then it asks whether the caller holds the right for this action in this place. A right comes from your role, from a single right on the Users page, or from a grant on the Access page. 4. For most changes, a policy decides whether the action runs at once, waits for a person's approval, or is refused. [Which actions take the whole path](#which-actions-take-the-whole-path) lists them. 5. For those actions the instance records each change, each refusal by a right or by the policy, and who decided. This page explains the rights system to a reader who has never seen it. It says what exists today. The last section lists what does not exist yet. For the exact rules of the Access page, see [Rights for one person or asset](/operate/rights-and-namespaces/). Three words come up on every screen, so here they are once. - A **right** is the permission to do one kind of thing, such as "write agents". In the API a right has a short name like `agent.write`. - A **grant** is one row that gives or refuses one person one right in one place. A Service Principal can hold a grant too, see [API keys and Service Principals](#api-keys-and-service-principals). You write grants on the Access page. - A **Namespace** is a registered beginning of a name, such as `tax-`. Every agent and skill whose name starts with it belongs to it, and so does every Connection where that module is on. See [Namespaces](#namespaces). It is not a workspace, as the next section shows. Namespaces are being retired: a new right is no longer given in one, and those already registered keep working until a later release removes them. ## Namespace or workspace? They are two different things. A **workspace** is where people work and what they see: its conversations, their files and the agents they can choose there. A **Namespace** is a name prefix, such as `tax-`, that says which agents and skills a right covers. Since an agent or skill made in a Shared Workspace belongs to that workspace, a right can also be given on what a workspace owns, and the workspace takes over the Namespace's job. In practice they often come together, because a team tends to have a workspace and a prefix, and that is why they get mixed up. ### When they go hand in hand Take the tax team of a company. It has both. - The Shared Workspace **Tax team** is where its twelve people chat. Its owner added them as members, and members reach the shared conversations in it. A private conversation stays with the person who created it. A Superadmin can enter every Shared Workspace without being a member. - The Namespace `tax-` holds the agents the team uses, such as `tax-vat-helper`. Mara and one colleague hold grants in it. They are the two people of the team who build those agents. An Admin or a Superadmin of the instance can change them too. So ten people of the team use the agents and two build them. Membership in the workspace makes nobody a builder, and a grant in the Namespace gives no access to the team's conversations. ### How an agent of the Namespace reaches the workspace Each agent has a setting named **Available in**. It lists the workspaces whose members can choose the agent in the chat. - **All workspaces**: every workspace of the instance, personal ones and future ones included. - **Selected workspaces**: the Personal Workspaces, chosen Shared Workspaces, or both. With nothing ticked the agent is hidden everywhere. A new agent starts in the workspace it was made in. Mara opens Studio while she works in Tax team, or asks the Build Agent in a conversation there, and her new `tax-travel-costs` can be chosen in Tax team and nowhere else. An agent made in a personal workspace, pushed with the CLI, or written through the API without a workspace starts hidden everywhere, and the answer says so. A person with the instance-wide right may choose **All workspaces** in the dialog that starts the agent. To offer an agent in more workspaces, or to show a hidden one, somebody opens it in Studio, goes to **Available in** and chooses **All workspaces**, or **Selected workspaces** with the workspaces ticked. That somebody needs "Edit agent configuration" for the whole instance. Mara's grant in `tax-` does not show her this section, so she cannot do it herself. Two exceptions. The default agent of the instance is always available everywhere, so the first agent of an instance starts there. And an agent that arrives through a release push starts in all workspaces, and hidden when the same push deletes an agent that was limited to selected workspaces, because that is a rename and the new name must not reach more people than the old one did. Nothing links a Namespace to a workspace. You cannot say "the agents of `tax-` belong to the workspace Tax team". What does link an agent to a workspace is where it was made: an agent or skill made in Tax team belongs to Tax team. To offer an agent in further workspaces, the **Available in** setting is the bridge, agent by agent, and only a person with the instance-wide right sets it. A new grant on agents or skills can name a Shared Workspace. It covers everything of that kind the workspace owns, also what is made later, and gives no access to its conversations. A grant to read or use Connections is written on one Connection: the instance owns every Connection, so a grant on a workspace would cover nothing, and the instance refuses one. A Connection grant written on a workspace before keeps applying until it is revoked. It says nothing about agents, skills or conversations. ## The four questions The instance asks four questions about an action. A "no" to any of them stops the action, and the answer says which question stopped it. ### Who are you A caller is one of two things. - A **User** is a person. You sign in to the interface, or the application of your company signs you in to the embedded chat. - A **Service Principal** is an identity for a script or the Catalyst CLI. It has no password. It has an API key, which the script or the CLI exchanges for a short-lived access token before it calls. A call without a valid sign-in or key gets `401 UNAUTHENTICATED` and nothing else happens. An account that is not active has no rights, whatever its role and its grants say. Example: Mara signs in with her email and password. The nightly release job uses the API key of the Service Principal `release-ci`. Both are known callers now. Neither may do anything yet. ### What may your key do This question matters for keys. A key carries **scopes**. A scope is a limit on the key itself, such as `config_assets:read`. The key can never do more than its scopes, even when the Service Principal behind it holds more rights. That lets you hand out a weak key for a task that only reads. A person who signs in to the interface has no such limit. A session of the embedded chat is limited to the chat. A call outside the scopes of its key gets `403 FORBIDDEN` with the text `Missing auth scope` and the name of the scope. Example: `release-ci` holds the right to release agents and skills. Its key for the comparison job has the scope "Read configuration assets" only. That key can pull and compare. It cannot push. ### Do you hold the right here This is the main question. It has two parts: which right, and where. The instance collects everything that speaks about you: 1. Your **role** gives you a fixed set of rights on the whole instance. 2. A **single right** on the Users page adds one right to that set or takes one away, also for the whole instance. 3. A **grant** on the Access page allows or denies one action in one place. A new grant is written on one asset. Grants written before in a Namespace, and Connection grants written before on a Shared Workspace, keep applying until they are revoked. Then it decides: - If any entry that covers this action in this place says **deny**, the answer is no. - Otherwise, if any entry that covers it says **allow**, the answer is yes. - Otherwise the answer is no. Nothing is allowed by default. A "no" gets `403 FORBIDDEN`. The message names the missing right, for example `Missing the right 'agent.write'`. Example: Mara has the role User, which carries no administrative right. A grant allows her to write agents in the Namespace `tax-`. She can save `tax-vat-helper`. She cannot save `hr-onboarding`, because nothing she holds covers that name. ### Does it need a second pair of eyes A caller who holds the right can still be held back. This question is asked for the actions on the [full path](#which-actions-take-the-whole-path). Each of them is either **reading** or **changing**, and a **policy** gives it one of four values: | Value | What happens | | --- | --- | | `allow` | The action runs. | | `confirm` | The caller has to confirm. When you click a button or call the API or the CLI yourself, that call is the confirmation, and the action runs. | | `approval` | The action waits. A person with the right to approve decides it in the [Inbox](/operate/governance/#inbox). | | `deny` | The action is refused with `403 POLICY_DENIED`. | A reading action only knows `allow` and `deny`. Nobody approves a read. The instance ships with `allow` for reading and `confirm` for changing. The operator of the instance changes that in [release config](/configure/release-config/#operation-policy). Example: an instance sets changing actions to `approval`. Mara saves `tax-vat-helper`. Studio says "This change waits for an approval. Nothing was changed yet and your text is still here." An administrator approves it in the Inbox. The instance then checks the call once more and saves the agent as Mara. ## Roles and single rights Catalyst has three roles. The interface calls the role of a person their **Access level**, and you set it on **Settings > Instance > Users**. | Role | What it carries | | --- | --- | | User | Chat, and nothing administrative. | | Admin | Read and change agents and skills, approve changes, manage users, see usage and the audit log. Every right on Connections, where the module is on. | | Superadmin | Everything an Admin has, plus managing API access and the model settings of agents. | The three roles are fixed. You cannot change what a role carries, and you cannot create a role of your own. Below the Access level, the same page has a card named **Rights** with one switch per right. A switch adds a right the role does not carry, or takes away one it does. The card shows where each right comes from: "by role", "granted individually" or "revoked individually". A revoked right stays revoked even though the role carries it. A switch is stored as grants for the whole instance, one per action the right stands for, and each records who set it and when. These grants are changed on the Users page and on the API access page for a Service Principal, not in the Grants list of the Access page, which leaves them out. | Switch on the Users page | Name in the API | Carried by | | --- | --- | --- | | View agent configuration | `config_assets.read` | Admin, Superadmin | | Edit agent configuration | `config_assets.write` | Admin, Superadmin | | Approve skill changes | `agent_skills.approve` | Admin, Superadmin | | Manage users | `users.manage` | Admin, Superadmin | | View usage | `usage.view` | Admin, Superadmin | | View audit log | `audit.view` | Admin, Superadmin | | Manage API access | `api_access.manage` | Superadmin | | Manage agent model settings | `agent_models.manage` | Superadmin | Some things are reserved for a Superadmin. Only a Superadmin gives somebody the Superadmin level, changes another Superadmin, deletes a user, or switches "Manage API access" and "Manage agent model settings" on or off. "Approve skill changes" also lets a person decide an action that waits for an approval. One right is on no switch. Pushing a release with `catalyst config push` needs `config_assets.release`, and only a Service Principal can hold it. See [API keys and Service Principals](#api-keys-and-service-principals). Managing Service Principals, `service_principals.manage`, is on no switch either. Admins and Superadmins carry it with their level. It creates a Service Principal, gives and takes its rights, and switches it on and off. Its keys stay with "Manage API access". Chatting is not on this list. Which conversations you see depends on the Collaboration Workspaces you are a member of and on whether a conversation is private, and not on one of these rights. The one exception is a Superadmin, who can enter every Shared Workspace. The Users page has one more field, **Permission refs**. A tool written for one customer can ask for a reference such as `support-ticket-reader`. An agent can use that tool only for a person who has the same reference in this field. ## Grants A role and a single right always apply to the whole instance. A grant is for everything narrower. It says five things: | Part | Choices today | | --- | --- | | Who | One person. A Service Principal gets its grants on the API access page. | | Kind | Agents, or skills. Connections and Workflows too, where their modules are on. | | Action | Read, write, delete for agents and skills. Read and use for Connections. Read, use, write and publish for Workflows. | | Where | For agents and skills: what one Shared Workspace owns, or one existing asset. For Connections and Workflows: one existing item. Rows written before in a Namespace stay until they are revoked. | | Effect | Allow, or deny. | So the answer to "can rights only be given to single people" is yes, today. A grant names one person or one Service Principal. There are no groups, and a role cannot hold a grant. **Deny wins.** A deny on an asset beats every allow, including the one from the Admin role. Use it for the one agent that even administrators should not change by accident. A deny has limits of its own, which [Rights for one person or asset](/operate/rights-and-namespaces/#grants) lists. **Read and write are separate.** A person who should edit agents needs both. With write alone they cannot open the agent they are meant to change. **Check before you guess.** The tab **Check** on the Access page takes a person and a name and says for each action whether it is allowed and what decided. The name does not have to exist yet. The tab covers agents and skills. To get a result you need "View agent configuration" beside "Manage users", because the tab looks up the assets. ## Namespaces Namespaces are being retired. The **New right** dialog no longer offers one, and a later release removes them. Until then the Namespaces already registered, their lists and the grants that name them keep working, and this section explains them. A Namespace answers the question "which agents belong to this team". It does that through names. You register a prefix, for example `tax-`. From then on every agent and skill of the instance whose name starts with `tax-` belongs to the Namespace. That includes agents somebody creates next month. A grant "write agents in `tax-`" therefore covers the whole family, and you never have to list the members. ### An example A company has a tax team. Its agents are named `tax-vat-helper` and `tax-year-end`, and it has a skill named `tax-audit-notes`. 1. The instance has the Namespace `tax-` with the display name "Tax team", registered before Namespaces were retired. 2. Mara holds read and write on agents in `tax-`, granted at that time. 3. Mara opens **Studio**. She sees the two tax agents and can change them. She does not see `hr-onboarding` or `helpdesk`. 4. Mara creates `tax-travel-costs`. The name starts with the prefix, so her grant covers it at once. 5. Jonas from the same team gets a grant on one asset instead, read on `tax-year-end`. He sees **Studio** with a list of agents that holds this one agent and nothing else. It opens read-only. ### Rules for a prefix - A prefix is made of lowercase letters and digits, in parts joined by single hyphens. It starts with a letter and ends in a hyphen: `tax-`, `tax-team-`. It has 2 to 32 characters. `tax/` is not a valid prefix. - Two Namespaces never overlap. While `tax-` exists, `tax-team-` is refused, so a name belongs to at most one Namespace. - A prefix cannot be changed later. The id of an agent cannot be changed either. Decide the names first. - Deleting a Namespace needs its grants revoked first. The agents and skills stay. ### A Namespace can also limit tools and models A Namespace can carry a list of allowed tools and a list of allowed models. An agent in the Namespace is saved only with tools from the tool list and with model bindings from the model list. One way around the model list is left: a person with "Manage agent model settings" can save an agent that names no model binding, and it then runs on the model the instance uses by default. The lists are checked when an agent is saved. They bind every writer, an administrator and the release push included. They are not rights. They are limits on what an agent in this family may be given. The details are in [Rights for one person or asset](/operate/rights-and-namespaces/#namespaces). ### A Namespace is not a workspace A grant in a Namespace covers what the instance itself owns under that prefix: its agents, its skills or its Connections, depending on the kind of the grant. It gives no access to any conversation. [Namespace or workspace?](#namespace-or-workspace) puts the two side by side. ## The path of one action Here is the whole way, in order. The table below the chart says who sets each step and where. | Step | Set by | Where | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 Sign-in or key | Administrator, Superadmin | Users for people, API access for keys | | 2 Module | Operator | `modules` in [release config](/configure/modules/) | | 3 Rate limit | Operator | `rateLimits` in release config | | 4 Key scope | Superadmin | API access, when the key is created | | 5 Tool list of the agent | Whoever may write the agent | The list of tools in the agent's definition | | 6 Input | Nobody. The action defines its input. | | | 7 Right | Administrator | Users for role and single rights, Access for grants | | 8 and 10 Policy | Operator, and the author of a tool | `policy.defaults` in release config, `permission.mode` on a tool | | 9 Guardrails | Operator (the floor), and whoever may publish a guardrail | `guardrails` in release config; Studio > Guardrails. See [Guardrails](#guardrails) | | 11 and 12 Run and record | Nobody. It is part of every action on the full path. | Read it on Operations and Audit | The chart shows the common exits. A few rarer ones exist. - At step 1, a Service Principal that calls a route meant for people gets `403 FORBIDDEN`, and so does a browser request from an address the instance does not trust. - At step 10, a call that needs an approval and cannot be held gets `403 POLICY_DENIED`. That is every call of a Service Principal and every call that carries a secret. A call whose input is too large to be held gets `422 VALIDATION_FAILED`. - A call that repeats an `Idempotency-Key` gets the answer of the first call again, without new checks. The same key with different input is refused with `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`. Three things about the order are worth knowing. - **The module comes before the right.** A feature that is switched off does not exist for anybody, an administrator included. One switch is narrower. With `assetManagement` off, nobody changes agents and skills in the interface, but they can still be read and a release push still writes them. - **The right comes before the policy.** A caller without the right never learns what the policy says, and never puts anything into somebody's Inbox. - **An approved action is checked again.** An approval queues the call. Just before the call runs, the instance asks for the module, the right, the policy and the guardrails once more for the person who made the call, as that person is at that moment. If they lost the right while the call waited, the call does not run. ### Which actions take the whole path Not every part of the product is on the full path yet. - **All 12 steps:** every tool call of an agent. Reading, saving, deleting and reverting agents and skills in Studio and through the asset API, and the release push. Writing or revoking a grant, and creating, changing or deleting a Namespace. Creating, changing and deleting a user, and changing a user's sign-in identities, password or invitation. Creating and changing a Service Principal, and creating and revoking an API key. The retry of a background job. - **Steps 1 to 4, a simpler input check and step 7:** everything else, for example conversations, workspaces, the lists of grants and Namespaces, the default agent, the **Available in** setting, usage and the audit log. These calls are refused the same way for a missing sign-in, module, scope or right. They have no policy step, cannot wait for an approval and leave no Operation Run. ### Approvals When the policy says `approval`, the action stops before it changes anything. - The caller receives `202` and a reference to the waiting call. In Studio the page says that the change waits and keeps your text. - The call appears in the **Inbox** of everybody who may decide it, as an "Operation call". That is every person with "Approve skill changes". - **Approve** queues the call. The instance checks it again and then runs it once, as the person who made it. If that check fails, the call is refused although it was approved. The record names the approver. - **Decline** ends it. The caller's record shows `DECLINED` and the approver's comment. The caller can also withdraw a waiting call. - A call that nobody decides expires after 7 days. A person who holds the approval right can approve their own call. The instance does not force a second person. Only a person's call can wait. A call made with an API key is refused with `POLICY_DENIED` where the policy asks for an approval, and that includes a release push. A call that carries a secret never waits. These are creating an API key, resetting a user's password, and creating a user with a first password. A held call would keep the secret and show it to whoever decides, and a key shown later reaches nobody. Under an instance default of `approval` such a call runs on the caller's own word. See [operation policy](/configure/release-config/#operation-policy). There is an older, separate approval that works without the policy. An agent can propose a change to one of its skills. That proposal is an Approval Request of the kind "Skill change", and the same people decide it. [Guardrails](#guardrails) can check it before it is filed and warn the approver or block the proposal. See [config assets](/configure/config-assets/#agent-skill-changes). A [guardrail](#guardrails) can also send a call to the Inbox: a call it answers with "needs approval" waits there like a call the policy holds. Agents and approvals do not go together yet. A run cannot pause for a person and continue later. So the instance refuses to start with a tool of the release whose calls would need an approval or a confirmation. Such a tool states `allow` or `deny`, unless the instance default for its kind of action already is one of the two. ### Guardrails A guardrail is a rule that looks at an action just before it happens and answers: let it through, warn, ask for an approval, or block. It sits at step 9, after the right and the first look at the policy, and it can only make the answer stricter. Guardrails run at six points: - before an asset is saved: a save in Studio, a push, a revert, an App written from a Page, an agent's save and the skill change it proposes; - before any operation is called, at step 9 of every action on the full path; - before an App, a Workflow or a Data Store is published; - before a request for approval is filed. Every guardrail that applies runs, and the strictest answer wins. - **Block**: the action does not happen. The caller gets `403 GUARDRAIL_BLOCKED` with the guardrail's reason. - **Ask for an approval** (`require_approval`): a changing call waits in the Inbox, as when the policy holds it. A reading call cannot wait and is refused. Where a changing action cannot wait either, such as the App draft an agent's save writes, it is blocked, and the hit says so. - **Warn**: the action goes on, and the reason is kept beside it. There are two sources of guardrails. The operator's floor is set in [release config](/configure/release-config/#guardrails), always runs and cannot be changed in the product. Further guardrails are written as assets, for the whole instance or for one Shared Workspace, tried on sample content and in a dry run, and made live by a person who may publish guardrails (`guardrail.publish`). Administrators hold that right for the instance, and an administrator can grant it for one Shared Workspace. A workspace's guardrail checks only what happens in that workspace. No published guardrail runs when guardrails themselves are changed; only the floor does. See [Guardrails](/manage/guardrails/) for the steps, and [Guardrails as assets](/configure/config-assets/#guardrails-as-assets) for the format. **Studio > Guardrails** (German: **Studio › Leitplanken**) lists every guardrail with one sentence saying when it runs, such as "Runs before an agent saves a skill, in workspace Finance. Checks the content for a text pattern. Blocks if the check fails." A guardrail's page counts its hits for the last 7 and 30 days. Hits are counted by rule and never listed by person. Beside guardrails, fixed limits protect an instance: | Limit | What it stops | Set in | | --- | --- | --- | | Module switches | A whole feature, for everybody | [release config](/configure/modules/) | | Tool and model lists of a Namespace | An agent with a tool or model off the list | Access, tab Namespaces | | Editable fields of an agent | A change in the interface to a field the release owns | [release config](/configure/config-assets/#interactive-editing-and-field-ownership) | | Usage limits and budgets | Model calls beyond a daily or monthly amount | [Capacity and limits](/operate/capacity-and-limits/) | | Rate limits | Too many requests in a short time | release config | ### What the record shows Every changing action on the full path leaves an **Operation Run**. That is one record of one call: which action, who called, from where, and how it ended. A reading action leaves one only when it was refused or failed. Every tool call of an agent leaves one, a reading one too. A call that is stopped at steps 1 to 4, or for invalid input, leaves none, and neither does an action off the full path. **Settings > Instance > Operations** lists them. The origin says where a call came from: User, CLI or Agent. A call that was refused has the status "Denied" and names what refused it. You need "View audit log" to open the page. Beside the run, the instance writes Audit Events, for example `permission.granted` when somebody writes a grant. The events the product writes hold names, ids and codes, and no content of an agent or a conversation. A tool written for one customer adds its own details to its events and has to keep to the same rule. See [Retention, audit and deletion](/operate/governance/#audit). ## A worked example Mara has the role User and two grants: read and write on agents in `tax-`. The instance runs with the default policy. Now she tries the same on `hr-onboarding`, which a colleague sent her as a link. 1. Sign-in: yes. Module: on. 2. Right `agent.read` on `hr-onboarding`: her grant covers names that start with `tax-`. This one does not. Nothing else covers it. 3. The instance answers `403 FORBIDDEN`. Studio says "You may not read this asset." 4. The refused call is on the Operations page with the status "Denied". ## Give a colleague the right to edit an agent You need "Manage users" yourself. Open **Settings > Instance > Access**, the tab **Rights**, and choose **New right**. In the German interface the button is "Neues Recht". The dialog has five fields. | Field | What you choose | What it means | | --- | --- | --- | | Person | One person from the list | The right is for this person alone. To give it to three colleagues, send the dialog three times. | | Kind | Agents or Skills | One kind per dialog. A colleague who edits both needs the dialog twice. With the modules `connections` and `workflows` on, the dialog offers Connections and Workflows too. | | Actions | Read, Write, Delete | Tick Read and Write for somebody who should edit. Tick Delete only if they should remove the agent too. The dialog writes one row per tick. | | Where and asset | **On one asset** ("An einem Asset"), then the one agent | The right covers this agent, which exists now. **In a shared workspace** ("In einem geteilten Arbeitsbereich") would cover every agent the workspace owns instead, also later ones. | | Effect | Allow or Deny | Allow gives the ticked actions there. Deny refuses them there and beats every allow and every role. For this task choose Allow. | Press **Create right**. Under the default policy the right works at once. On an instance that sends changes to an approval, it works once the approval is given. Your colleague sees **Studio** in the main rail the next time the interface loads, with the agent. If these rights are all they hold, they see nothing else. For a team with several agents, send the dialog once per agent. Three things to know afterwards. - You can send the same dialog again. Rows the person already has are left alone, and the dialog says how many it added. - **Check** on the same page confirms the result. Choose the person, enter the agent's name and read the answer for each action. You need "View agent configuration" for that. - A save can still be refused for a reason that is not a right. Examples are a tool that is off the list of a Namespace the agent's name lies in, or a model setting that needs "Manage agent model settings". The Check tab lists these under its result. To take the right away, open the menu of the line in the list and choose **Revoke** for the action. Once the revocation has run, the next call of your colleague is refused. ## API keys and Service Principals The Catalyst CLI does not sign in as a person. It works as a Service Principal, and so should a script. Whoever manages Service Principals, an Admin for example, creates a **Service Principal** on **Settings > Instance > API access** and gives it one or both of two rights: - "Read configuration assets", to pull and compare agents and skills. - "Release configuration assets", to push them with `catalyst config push`. Only a Superadmin gives this one. Then a person with "Manage API access" creates an **API key** for it and picks the key's scopes from the rights the Service Principal holds. The key is shown once. Nobody gives a Service Principal more than they hold themselves. Giving it a right, switching it back on and issuing it a key each ask whether the person holds every right the Service Principal would act with. Where a personal API key makes the call, its scopes count too. A refusal names the first right that is missing, and the asset only where the person may read it. Taking a right away and switching a Service Principal off ask nothing of it. A Service Principal has no role. Whoever manages Service Principals can allow one to use a single named resource they may use themselves, such as one Connection: a grant with the holder kind `service_principal`, a use right, and that one asset as scope. The use rights are `connection.use`, `workflow.use`, and `data_store.read`, `data_store.insert` and `data_store.execute` for the rows of a Data Store, each where its module is on. No other grant can be written for one: no right that writes, publishes, deletes or manages, no workspace, Namespace or instance scope, and no deny. A Service Principal never writes a grant, also not for itself. Disabling a Service Principal leaves its grants recorded and without effect. The interface does not offer these grants yet; they are written through `POST /api/v1/instance/access/grants`. A release push reaches every agent and skill of the instance and is not held back by the editing limits of the interface. It is still bound by the tool and model lists of a Namespace and by a deny on an asset. See [config assets](/configure/config-assets/#permissions). ## Which screen for what | You want to | Screen | You need | | --- | --- | --- | | Make somebody an Admin or a Superadmin | Settings > Instance > Users, Access level | Manage users. Superadmin for the Superadmin level. | | Give or take one right for the whole instance | Settings > Instance > Users, Rights | Manage users | | Let somebody edit an agent | Settings > Instance > Access, Rights | Manage users | | Change the lists of a Namespace registered before | Settings > Instance > Access, Namespaces | Manage users | | Find out why somebody can or cannot do something | Settings > Instance > Access, Check | Manage users and View agent configuration | | Create a key of your own for the CLI | Settings > You > API keys, or `catalyst login` | The module `personalApiKeys` on | | Create a Service Principal or give it a right | Settings > Instance > API access | Manage Service Principals, and the right you give | | Create a key for a script or CI | Settings > Instance > API access | Manage API access, and every right of the Service Principal | | Decide a call or a skill change that waits | Inbox | Approve skill changes | | See what was called, by whom, and what was refused | Settings > Instance > Operations | View audit log | | See who changed which right | Settings > Instance > Audit | View audit log | | Switch a feature on or off, set the policy | Release config, then a deploy | The operator | ## What the system does not have yet - **Groups and teams.** A grant names one person or one Service Principal. Nothing gives a right to a group. - **Custom roles.** The three roles are fixed. The Rights card on the Users page shows which rights a person has by role, and nothing edits what a role carries. - **Company sign-in with group mapping.** People are not signed in through a company identity provider with its groups. - **Grants on the whole instance, and grants for other kinds.** The **New right** dialog writes a grant on one agent, skill, Connection or Workflow, on the agents or skills a Shared Workspace owns, or the right to publish a Shared Workspace's guardrails. A right on the whole instance comes only from a role or from the Users page. Grants written before in a Namespace, or on a Shared Workspace for Connections, keep applying until they are revoked. Writing, deleting and approving a Connection stay with the Admin role. Data Stores and Apps have no grant for a person. - **Policy settings for administrators.** The instance can already resolve a policy value per action, per Namespace, per workspace and per kind of asset. Nothing stores such settings and no screen edits them. Today the policy is two instance-wide defaults and the mode a tool states. An administrator cannot set "saving in `tax-` needs an approval" in the interface. - **An agent that waits for a person.** A run cannot pause for a confirmation or an approval and continue. - **One path for everything.** Conversations, workspaces and the other areas named [above](#which-actions-take-the-whole-path) are checked for sign-in, module, scope and right, without policy and without an Operation Run.

pages.title: Instance brief
pages.description: The thin documentation every client instance should have before implementation.
pages.body:
Write a short instance brief before configuring a client instance.

This is not a long specification. It is the minimum shared context that keeps tools, prompts, auth, retention, and deployment choices aligned.

## Template

```md
# Instance Brief

## Purpose

What should this chat help users accomplish?

## Users

Who can use it? Which roles or permission refs matter?

## Operating Model

Who operates the dedicated instance?

- operated dedicated instance
- self-operated instance
- mixed, with customer-hosted integrations

## Data

Which sensitive data can enter the chat?

Which data must never enter the chat?

## Agent

What should the agent do?

What should it refuse or escalate?

Which language or tone constraints matter?

## Tools

List each proposed tool:

- stable tool name
- purpose
- source system
- read or write action
- required permission
- expected audit summary
- output shown to the model
- output shown to the user

## Chat Experience

Branding, welcome text, suggested prompts, locales, and domain UI outputs.

## Auth And Access

How does an authenticated user reach the chat?

How are roles or permission refs mapped?

## Retention And Deletion

Conversation retention, audit retention, backup retention, and deletion expectations.

## Model Provider

Provider, model, region, budget, and external billing controls.

## Deployment

Runtime owner, target environment, database, object storage, proxy/TLS, monitoring, and backup owner.

## Open Questions

Anything that must be answered before production use.
```

## Keep It Current

Update the brief when the workflow scope changes, not for every code detail.

Implementation choices belong in release config, tool code, planning docs, or ADRs. The brief exists so everyone can understand the instance boundary quickly.

pages.title: Rights for one person or asset
pages.description: Give one person rights on one asset, and check what a person may do.
pages.body:
Instance roles and the rights set on the Users page apply to the whole instance. The page **Instance > Access** is for everything narrower: one person, one kind of asset, one place. It is shown to users who hold `users.manage` and has three tabs.

## Namespaces

Namespaces are being retired, and a new right is no longer given in one. The Namespaces already registered keep their lists, and the rights that name them keep applying, until a later release removes them. This section describes them for that time.

A Namespace is a registered name prefix such as `sales-`. Every agent and skill whose name starts with the prefix belongs to it. Two Namespaces never overlap: while `sales-` is registered, `sales-x-` is refused, and so is `sa-` for a registered `sa-team-`. The form checks this as you type. A prefix cannot be changed later.

A Namespace can carry two lists. Each is switched on with **Limit tools** or **Limit models**.

| Switch | Off | On with entries | On and empty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Limit tools | Agents may use every tool of the instance. | An agent is saved only with listed tools. | An agent that names a tool cannot be created or changed. |
| Limit models | Only a person with `agent_models.manage` sets the model of an agent. | A person who may write agents here picks a listed model without `agent_models.manage`. A model off the list is refused for everyone. An agent without a model is saved only by a person with `agent_models.manage`. | An agent that names a model cannot be created or changed by anyone. A person with `agent_models.manage` can still save an agent without a model. |

The lists bind every writer: a person who writes through a grant, an instance administrator and the release sync. The one exemption is the last cell of each model column, which belongs to `agent_models.manage`. A list is checked when an agent is created or changed; an agent that is saved unchanged is not checked.

Saving an empty list over agents that already have the prefix stops those saves, so the form names how many agents are affected and asks for a confirmation that names the Namespace before it saves. When the agents of the instance cannot be read, for example without `config_assets.read`, the form counts from the Namespace's own number of agents and skills instead.

A Namespace is deleted only when no grant names it. Until then its row says how many grants do. Deleting it frees the prefix and leaves the agents and skills as they are.

## Grants

A grant gives one person one action in one place. A Service Principal's grants are written on **Settings > Instance > API access**, not here. The **New right** form takes a person, a kind, the actions, the place and the effect, and writes one row per action. For agents and skills the actions are read, write and delete. The places are a shared workspace, one existing asset and the whole instance, in this order, and the form offers only the places where every action of the kind can be written. Today, for agents and skills, that is **In a shared workspace** ("In einem geteilten Arbeitsbereich"), which covers everything of the kind the workspace owns, also what is made later, and gives no access to its conversations; and **On one asset** ("An einem Asset"). For Connections and Workflows it is one existing item, so the form asks for no place and goes straight to the item. No action is offered for the whole instance.

The form offers no Namespace. Rows written in a Namespace before stay in the list, keep applying and are revoked like any other row until the Namespace is retired.

On an instance with the module `connections` on, the form also offers the kind Connections, with the actions read and use. Using a Connection is a right of its own: a person who may read a Connection may not use it, and a person who may use it is shown nothing of it. The place is one existing Connection. The instance owns every Connection, so a right on a workspace would cover nothing: a grant of `connection.read` or `connection.use` on a workspace is refused with `422` and the reason `invalid_scope`. Rows written on a workspace before keep applying until they are revoked. Writing, deleting and approving a Connection belong to the administrator role and are not granted. A Connection that release config no longer names, or names differently, is removed at the next start together with the allow rows written on it; grants on a renamed Connection have to be written again.

On an instance with the module `workflows` on, a grant can also name a Workflow, with the actions read, use, write and publish. Reading shows the Workflow in the list and its runs, using starts it, writing edits its draft, and publishing makes a revision live. The place is one existing Workflow; the instance owns every Workflow, so no grant on a workspace covers one. Publishing a Workflow that runs as a service principal also needs every right that service principal holds: nobody makes a Workflow lend more than they hold themselves. A Workflow that runs as a service principal holding `config_assets.release` is published by nobody. Deleting a Workflow and reading the rows of a run's datasets belong to the administrator role and are not granted.

A row the person already has is left as it is, so the same form can be sent again after it stopped half way: it adds what is missing and says how many rows it added and how many were there already.

The list shows one line per person and scope, with the actions as chips. A deny chip carries its own mark and the word "Denied". Each chip is revoked from the menu of its line.

The effect is **Allow** or **Deny**:

- A deny wins over every grant and role that would allow the same action there.
- A deny is not a wall. A person with instance-wide rights can still export a denied agent or set it as the default, because those are decided for the instance.
- Whoever is denied reading or writing an asset cannot delete it.
- A deny on one asset belongs to its name. Deleting the asset removes the allow rows on it and keeps the deny rows. The list then shows the row as "Asset no longer exists". It applies again when an asset with that name is created, and stays until you revoke it.

**Revoke** removes one allow row at once, **Remove deny** one deny row. Rows held by a superadmin are shown to superadmins only. When the person who wrote a row is hidden from you, "Granted by" reads "Not available". A grant for a person whose account is being deleted is refused with "User account is being deleted".

A row on one asset names the asset only for a reader who may read that kind of asset (`config_assets.read`, or `agent.read` or `skill.read` for the instance). Any other reader sees the asset's id and whether the asset still exists. In the API, `scopeAsset.name` is absent for such a reader.

## Check

Choose a person and enter the name of an agent or a skill. The name does not have to exist yet, which answers "could this person create `sales-helper`?". For each action the tab says whether it is allowed and what decided:

| Reason | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Role | The person's instance role allows it everywhere. |
| Individual right | A right set or revoked on the Users page decides. |
| Given right | A row in a Namespace or on the asset allows it. |
| Deny | A deny row refuses it. |
| No right | Nothing covers it. |

An account that is not active has no rights, whatever its rows say.

The result is the right alone. A save the tab calls allowed can still be refused for a reason outside rights:

- a tool or model list of the Namespace the name lies in. The tab names these lists under the result.
- a changed model setting without `agent_models.manage`
- the first agent of an instance and the last one change the default agent, which needs the instance-wide right to write agents
- agent configuration in the interface is switched off for the instance

A read that is allowed through a grant opens that asset. The overview of all agents and skills and the export need the instance-wide right to read.

The tab gives a result only when it has everything it decides from: the person's rights, the grant rows and the agents and skills of the instance. While one of them loads, or when it could not be loaded, the tab says so and shows no result, because a result without them could miss a deny on one asset. It also gives no result for a name no asset can have.

## API

The page uses the eight operations under `/api/v1/instance/access`. See the [API reference](/reference/api/).

pages.title: Runner security
pages.description: Security boundary and assumptions for execution workspace runners.
pages.body:
