`workspace.exec` is a high-risk capability. The product boundary is that agent-authored commands run outside the chat API, inside a short-lived runner with no broad secrets and no network by default.

## Required Boundaries

Runner containers must not receive:

- platform database credentials
- model provider keys
- customer API tokens
- object-store credentials
- the Docker socket
- internal network access
- outbound internet access

The workspace command worker is the trusted control process. It can read and write the exact workspace objects required for a command, then starts the sandboxed runner with only the mounted workspace and bounded environment variables.

## Docker Policy

Every command in a runner container, an agent's command and a Page build alike, is started by one `docker run` call with:

- `--user 10001:10001`: the command is not root
- `--cap-drop ALL` and `no-new-privileges`: no capabilities, and none to gain
- `--network none`
- a read-only root filesystem
- writable `/workspace`, which is the home directory, and tmpfs for `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` owned by the same user
- CPU, memory, and pid limits
- Docker's default seccomp profile
- bounded wall-clock and idle timeouts
- bounded stdout and stderr previews

None of these is a setting. The runner image should contain approved runtimes and artifact helpers at build time. Agents should not install packages dynamically in production.

## The Runner's User

The user id and the group id are both `10001`, the constants `RUNNER_USER_ID` and `RUNNER_GROUP_ID` in `packages/tool-execution/src/docker-workspace-command-runner.ts`. Both runner images create this user as `catalyst-runner` with the home directory `/workspace` and start as it, so a container started by hand is not root either. The ids on `docker run` are numbers, so a runner image of an older release, which has no such user, still runs commands as `10001`.

The worker is root in its own container. Before each command it gives the directory it filled to `10001:10001`, and afterwards reads and removes the files as before. A link in the directory is given away itself and is not followed. If the directory cannot be given away, the command does not start and fails with `WORKSPACE_COMMAND_SPAWN_FAILED`, or the Page build with "could not be started". It never starts as root instead.

What an operator must know:

- **Ownership on the host.** Files under `WORKSPACE_COMMAND_TEMP_ROOT` belong to user `10001` on the host while a command or build runs. Nobody has to create that user or prepare the directory. Do not give the id `10001` to a person or a service on the host.
- **The filesystem must keep ownership.** The directory has to lie on a filesystem where root may change the owner of a file: a local disk or a Docker volume. A network share that maps root to another user (NFS with `root_squash`) refuses it, and every command then fails as described above.
- **No user namespace.** The product does not turn on rootless Docker or user-namespace remapping. Without them, `10001` in the container is `10001` on the host, and root in the worker's container is root on the host. With either turned on, the worker and the runner must run under the same engine so both see the same mapping; this combination is not tested by a release.
- **The worker holds the Docker socket.** Whoever takes over the worker process can start any container and is as powerful as root on the host. The non-root user protects against a command in the runner, not against the worker.
- **A worker that is not root**, as on a developer's machine, cannot give files away. It runs commands as its own user and group instead, and no ownership changes. This case is not root either.

## Page Builds

With the module `apps` on, the same sandbox builds saved Pages. The build is the fixed command `catalyst-page-build` of the runner image, with a temporary directory of its own instead of a workspace. The files of a Page are written by an agent or a person and are not trusted, and the build tools that read them are third-party code. The sandbox is therefore the boundary: nothing of a Page is parsed or run outside it, and what the command writes is read back as untrusted data. See [Page Builds](/operate/deployment/#page-builds).

## Data Handling

Workspace file contents live in managed object storage and are referenced by manifest rows. Command audit events and operator telemetry must record minimized metadata only. Bounded stdout/stderr previews are command result data, not audit data, and should not be projected to users as final content.

Promoted artifacts are managed artifacts scoped to the conversation. Internal workspace files remain hidden from user download surfaces.

## Known Limits

Docker isolation is acceptable for the first dedicated VPS deployment. A command shares the host's kernel, filtered only by Docker's default seccomp profile, and runs without a user namespace. Higher-risk environments may require rootless Docker, user namespaces, an own seccomp profile, gVisor, Firecracker, or a managed sandbox service before enabling `workspace.exec` for sensitive workloads.

Network-enabled execution, package installation, and cross-conversation file libraries are not part of the v1 security model.

pages.title: App bridge v1
pages.description: The messages and calls between an App and the interface that shows it, frozen as version 1.
pages.body:
An App, and a Page of a conversation, runs in a sandboxed frame without an origin. It holds no credential and reaches nothing but the interface that shows it. The two talk through the bridge: messages posted between the frame and the interface. The App Kit (`@work-shape/catalyst-app-kit`) is the App's half; an App calls the kit and never posts a message itself.

## Version 1 is frozen

The bridge protocol is version 1. Every message of either side carries `catalystBridge: 1`, and the interface drops a message without it. What this page lists is the contract an App can build on:

- Version 1 is the set of messages and calls listed on this page. Further calls of the platform's bridge design, such as `storage` or `files.open`, arrive additively within version 1.
- Changes to version 1 are additive only: a new message type, a new call of the kit, or a new optional field. An App written against version 1 keeps working.
- A new call needs a named App that cannot be built without it. It is added as a new member, never by renaming one.
- A breaking change, such as removing or renaming a message, a field or a call, or changing what one means, is version 2. Version 2 runs beside version 1, and the interface keeps answering version 1.
- A kit version is frozen too. An App names the exact kit version it was built with (`kit` in `app.yaml`) and keeps loading those files. A new Page or App names kit 1.4.0.

## Calls of the kit

| Call | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `getContext()` | Greets the interface and answers the context below. It waits up to 10 seconds, then rejects: a Page runs inside the platform. |
| `onThemeChange(callback)` | Calls back with `{ theme, mode }` whenever the colours or the mode of the interface change. Answers the function that stops it. |
| `navigate(path)` | Tells the interface the route the App shows. |
| `resize(height)` | Tells the interface the height of the App's content, in pixels. |
| `actions.call(name, input?, { idempotencyKey? })` | Kit 1.1.0 and later. Calls a named action of the manifest with the viewer's rights. Answers the result below, or rejects with an `AppCallError`. |
| `workflowRuns.get(runId)` | Reads a Workflow Run that a `workflow` action of the App started, as the viewer who started it. Kit 1.3.0 and later. |
| `useWorkflowRun(runId)` | A React hook that reads the run every second until it ended. Kit 1.3.0 and later. |
| `mountApp({ routeTree, element? })` | Renders a React App with its routes and the look of the interface. |

An App reaches a Connection, a Data Store or a Workflow only through a named action in its folder: `actions/<name>.action.yaml` for an operation of a Connection or a Workflow, `actions/<name>.sql` for a statement on a Data Store. Each call goes through the policy, the audit and the viewer's rights.

## Messages the App sends

| `type` | Fields | Answered with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ready` | none | `context` |
| `navigate` | `session`, `path` (a route of the App: one leading `/`, no host, at most 2048 characters) | nothing |
| `resize` | `session`, `height` (0 to 100000) | nothing |
| `action` | `session`, `requestId`, `name`, `input` (an object), optional `idempotencyKey` | `action_result` |
| `workflow_run` | `session`, `requestId`, `runId` | `workflow_run_result` |

Every message after `ready` names the session the interface gave in `context`. A message of another shape, with an unknown key, or naming another session is dropped.

### Retired: `connection_call`

Kits 1.1.0 to 1.3.0 have `connections.call(connection, operation, input)`, which sends `connection_call`; kit 1.0.0 had no call of a Connection, and kit 1.4.0 has none. The free call of a Connection from the browser was removed before version 1 was frozen. The interface answers it at once with an `action_result` whose error is `connection_call_removed`, not retryable, and whose message names the fix: an action file `actions/<name>.action.yaml` with `connection`, `operation` and `effect`, called with `actions.call('<name>', input)`. A call of it that waited for an approval when it was removed is ended when it is approved: it never reaches the Connection, and its run fails with the same message.

## Messages the interface sends

| `type` | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `context` | `session`, `context` |
| `theme` | `theme`, `mode` |
| `action_result` | `session`, `requestId`, `ok`, and `result` or `error` |
| `workflow_run_result` | `session`, `requestId`, `ok`, and `run` or `error` |

The context holds `viewer` (`kind: member`, `id`, `displayName`), `workspace` (`id`, `name`, or `null`), `locale`, `theme` (seven colours: `surfaceColor`, `backgroundColor`, `textColor`, `mutedTextColor`, `borderColor`, `accentColor`, `accentStrongColor`), `mode` (`light` or `dark`), `pageId`, `fileSetNumber`, `initialRoute`, and `can`: for each action, what a call of the viewer would come to now (`allow`, `confirm`, `approval` or `deny`). `can` is a hint for what the App shows; each call is checked again.

The result of an action is one of:

- `{ runId, status: "done", result }`: the operation ran, and `result` is what it answered.
- `{ runId, status: "pending_approval" }`: the call waits for another person's approval. The run says how it ends.
- `{ status: "dry_run", message, result }` (kit 1.3.0 and later): a draft or a Page of a conversation carried nothing out. `message` is the platform's sentence of what the call would have done; show it as it is.

A run (`workflow_run_result`) holds `id`, `workflow`, `status` (`queued`, `running`, `waiting`, `done`, `failed`, `cancelled` or `limit_reached`), and where known `output` or `outputTruncated`, `error`, `startedAt` and `finishedAt`.

An error holds `code` (such as `action_unknown`, `draft_safe_mode`, `forbidden`, `input_invalid`, `rate_limited` or `connection_call_removed`), `message`, and optionally `right` (the right a `forbidden` call lacks), `retryable` (`false` where the same call cannot come out differently) and `runId`. The kit rejects with an `AppCallError` that carries the same fields. A call nothing answers within 180 seconds rejects with `timeout`.

pages.title: What the release contains
pages.description: What the current release contains and what it does not contain yet.
pages.body:
Workshape Catalyst is an early product: configuration keys and package APIs can still change between releases.

## In The Current Release

The open platform contains:

- the chat API under `/api/v1` with streamed agent runs, described by an OpenAPI document, see the [API reference](/reference/api/)
- the standalone chat interface and an embeddable chat widget, with session tokens issued by a host backend
- agents and skills as config assets in the database, edited in Studio or synchronized with the `catalyst` CLI; skills may carry files of any type, and a few skills ship with the platform
- Pages an agent builds in a conversation, and Apps saved from them, with a draft whose changing actions are simulated, **Run live once**, and publishing (module `apps`)
- Workflows with a canvas, test runs, schedules, code steps and a list of runs, acting as a service principal (module `workflows`)
- Connections to remote MCP servers, created in Studio or in release config, with a key entered on the Connection's page (module `connections`)
- Data Stores: one Postgres database per store for Apps and Workflows (module `dataStores`)
- custom code tools through the tool SDK, and capabilities through the capability SDK
- data sources with guarded, read-only Postgres query tools
- generated views, web search and web fetch
- standalone sign-in, service principals with API keys, personal API keys and `catalyst login` (module `personalApiKeys`), roles, individual rights, Namespaces and grants
- retention for conversations and audit events, minimized audit events, usage records with budgets and a customer rate card, and rate limits
- modules, mail for invitations and password reset, and the background jobs page
- execution workspaces with a sandboxed command runner, off unless an instance enables them
- approval requests for skill changes that an agent proposes, and for calls the operation policy holds, decided in the Inbox
- guardrails that check saves, operation calls, publishes and approval requests: the operator's floor in release config, and further guardrails written as assets, tested, dry-run and published with the CLI; Studio > Guardrails lists them read-only with their hits
- the chat dock, which keeps a conversation open beside any page
- Docker images, Compose files, an explicit migration step, and the `/health` and `/ready` probes

Document processing, the artifact helper commands for execution workspaces and the private data view are paid capabilities. They are not in the open repository.

## Not In The Current Release

- A connector for a plain HTTP or OpenAPI system. A Connection reaches a remote MCP server only.
- Writing, testing or publishing a guardrail in the interface. Studio > Guardrails reads; the CLI writes.
- A platform MCP server for a local agent such as Claude Code or Codex. A local agent works through `catalyst login` and the CLI.
- Tools with the permission mode `approval_required`. An agent run cannot pause for a person's decision and continue afterwards, so startup refuses such a tool.
- An approval for a call an agent makes. The operation policy value `approval` holds a person's call for a decision in the Inbox, see [Operation policy](/configure/release-config/#operation-policy). An agent's run cannot pause for such a decision and continue, so startup refuses a tool of the release whose calls would wait.
- Editing a sent message and exporting a conversation.

Each page of these docs describes the current release unless it says otherwise.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.description: The terms these docs and the interface use, with the German screen names.
pages.body:
## Customer

An organization that uses the agent chat platform for its own internal users and domain workflows.

## User

A person authenticated by a customer application or standalone login path who may interact with the chat.

## Client Instance

A separately deployed product instance for one customer, with its own infrastructure and operational boundary.

## Instance Operator

The party responsible for running a client instance. This may be Workshape or the customer.

## Operated Dedicated Instance

A dedicated instance hosted and maintained by an operator for one customer.

## Self-Operated Instance

A dedicated instance run by the customer in its own infrastructure or chosen hosting environment.

## Customer-Hosted Integration

A customer system, API, MCP server, or data source that a client instance calls but does not operate.

## Client Assembly App

The TypeScript application that imports platform packages, registers client tools, loads release config, and builds the deployable client-specific server image.

## Release Config

Version-controlled configuration deployed with the client assembly app. It sets what needs a deployment to change: modules, model providers and bindings, tool enablement, the guardrail floor, Connections from config, egress, retention, usage policy, mail and infrastructure. Agents, skills, Apps, Workflows and guardrails written as assets are not in it; they live in the database and change at runtime.

## Module

One optional feature of the product with one switch in release config, `modules.<name>.enabled`, such as `apps`, `workflows` or `connections`. The interface lists them under **Settings > Instance > Modules** (German: **Module**). See [Modules](/configure/modules/).

## Workspace

Where your conversations and Apps live. Your **Personal workspace** (German: **Persönlicher Arbeitsbereich**) is yours alone. A **Shared workspace** (listed under **Geteilte Arbeitsbereiche** in German) has members; its owners manage them under **Settings > Workspace** (**Einstellungen › Arbeitsbereich**).

## Studio

The area of the interface where builders make and look after agents, skills, Connections, Data Stores and guardrails. It has the same name in German. Only a person who may read one of these sees it.

## Agent

A configured AI behavior with instructions, model settings, available tools, and skills. Agents live in the database and are edited in Studio or with the CLI.

## Skill

Instructions an agent reads when a task calls for them, as a folder with a `SKILL.md` and optional files. Some skills ship with the platform and are read-only; **Copy to edit** makes an editable copy.

## Page

What an agent builds in one conversation and shows beside the chat: screens with their files, without a name or a history of its own. **Save as app** (German: **Als App speichern**) turns it into an App.

## App

Screens plus named actions that work with data outside a chat, saved in a workspace. An App has a draft and a published revision: members of the workspace see the published one, and changing actions in the draft are only simulated, unless a person who may edit the App uses **Run live once** (German: **Einmal live ausführen**) for one call. See [Build an App](/apps/build/).

## Workflow

A fixed sequence of steps the platform runs without a conversation, started by hand or on a schedule. It acts as one service principal, whoever starts it. A Workflow is drafted, tried with a test run and published. It has its own row in the main rail, **Workflows**.

## Connection

The access to one outside system, today always a remote MCP server. It holds the address and, stored encrypted, one key for everyone who may use it. Agents call the operations it offers once a person has accepted them. In the interface: **Studio > Connections** (German: **Studio › Verbindungen**).

## Data Store

A SQL database the platform hosts for Apps and Workflows, one per store, changed only through the migrations of its definition. In the interface: **Studio > Data stores** (German: **Datenspeicher**).

## Guardrail

A rule that checks an action just before it happens, such as saving an asset, calling an operation or publishing an App, and answers allow, warn, ask for an approval, or block. The operator's floor comes from release config; further guardrails are written as assets and published. In the interface: **Studio > Guardrails** (German: **Studio › Leitplanken**). See [How rights work](/operate/how-rights-work/#guardrails).

## Inbox

Where requests for approval wait: skill changes an agent proposes, and calls that the policy or a guardrail holds. German: **Eingang**. A person who may decide sees **To decide** (**Zu entscheiden**) and **Decided** (**Entschieden**); everyone else sees their own requests.

## Custom Code Tool

A tool implemented with customer-specific code that runs inside the client instance or one of its execution runtimes.

## Embed Surface

The customer-facing integration point that renders chat inside a customer application.

## Conversation

A persisted chat history owned by an authenticated user and retained according to the client instance retention policy.

## Audit Event

A minimized governance record of a security, data, tool, config, or lifecycle action. It is not a full transcript.

pages.title: Your first conversation
pages.description: Pick an agent, start a chat, add files, and find your way around Catalyst.
pages.body:
In Catalyst you work with **agents**: assistants set up for a task, such as answering client questions or drafting offers. You talk to one in a chat. The German interface shows the labels in quotes.

## Start a chat

1. Click **New chat** ("Neuer Chat") in the main rail. If your workspace offers only one agent, this starts a chat with it.
2. If your workspace offers more than one agent, the rail also shows **Agents** ("Agenten"). It lists them; pick one to start a chat with it.
3. Type what you need and press Enter.

To add files, click **Add attachment** ("Anhang hinzufügen") or drop them onto the chat.

If the agent offers more than one model, the chat shows a picker with **Model** ("Modell") and **Reasoning** ("Denkaufwand"). More reasoning takes longer and uses more of your quota.

## Find it again

**Recent** ("Zuletzt") in the main rail lists your conversations, and **Search** ("Suchen") finds them. A conversation may be deleted after a while, as your organisation set it; the chat then says "Will be deleted automatically on …" ("Wird am … automatisch gelöscht").

## What appears beside the chat

- When the agent builds something for you, such as a small tool with screens, it shows it beside the chat. You can keep it as an App: see [Apps for people](/automate/apps/).
- When you open a chat from another page, for example with **Edit with the agent** on an App, the chat stays open on the left of that page as you move on. **Close chat** ("Chat schließen") hides it, **Chat** brings it back, and **Open as full chat** ("Als ganzen Chat öffnen") gives it the whole window.

## The rest of the main rail

Which of these you see depends on your rights and your workspace.

- **Apps**: the Apps of your workspace.
- **Workflows**: work the platform does by itself. See [Workflows](/automate/workflows/).
- **Inbox** ("Eingang"): requests waiting for an approval.
- **Studio**: where agents, skills and connections to other systems are made. It shows only for people who build them. On an agent's card, **Edit in Studio** ("Im Studio bearbeiten") opens it there.
- Your name at the bottom of the rail opens **Profile** ("Profil") and **Language and appearance** ("Sprache und Darstellung"). Your **API keys** ("API-Schlüssel") are on the same Settings page. Workspace owners and administrators also get a **Settings** ("Einstellungen") button.

Next: [Workspaces](/start/workspaces/).

pages.title: Workspaces
pages.description: Your personal workspace, shared workspaces, and who sees what.
pages.body:
A workspace is where your conversations and Apps live. The German interface shows the labels in quotes.

- Your **personal workspace**, shown as "Anna's workspace" ("Annas Arbeitsbereich"), is yours alone.
- A **shared workspace** has members. Its conversations, agents and Apps are there for the team.

## Switch, create or join

Open the workspace menu in the main rail (**Switch workspace**, "Arbeitsbereich wechseln").

- Pick a workspace to switch to it. The rail then shows its agents, Apps and conversations.
- **Create** ("Erstellen") makes a new shared workspace. You are its owner.
- **Browse** ("Durchsuchen") lists the shared workspaces you may find. **Request access** ("Zugriff anfragen") asks their owners to let you in.

## Who sees what

In a shared workspace the owners choose, under **Settings > Workspace > General**, whether **New conversations are** ("Neue Unterhaltungen sind") **Private to their author** or **Visible to the workspace** ("Für den Arbeitsbereich sichtbar"). A change applies to new conversations only.

Published Apps of a workspace are open to all its members. Which agents a workspace offers is set in Studio.

## Manage members

Owners manage a shared workspace under **Settings > Workspace** ("Einstellungen › Arbeitsbereich"):

- **Members** ("Mitglieder"): **Add member** ("Mitglied hinzufügen"), give someone the role **Owner** ("Besitzer"), **Admin** ("Administrator") or **Member** ("Mitglied"), or remove them. Open access requests wait here too.
- **General** ("Allgemein"): the name, whether the workspace is **Discoverable** ("Auffindbar") or **Private** ("Privat"), and who sees new conversations.
